Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who will not write down this profound perfection of wisdom, nor recite it, nor explain it, nor study it, nor attend to it with proper mental application, and who will create obstacles for it, are of little intelligence, of dull intelligence, and of limited intelligence.

And their minds will not enter into those most sublime dharmas, if they do not write down this profound perfection of wisdom, do not retain it, do not recite it, do not study it, do not attend to it with proper mental attention, and so on, up to not cultivating it.

And they will create obstacles for others as well, up to those who are practicing meditation. Furthermore, Subhūti, although these works of Māra will arise while this profound perfection of wisdom is being written down,

up to being meditated upon, yet, Subhūti, if— when these sons of good family and daughters of good family are writing down, reciting, teaching, and properly attending to this profound perfection of wisdom—
For those who cultivate this, the works of Māra will not arise; furthermore, they will fulfill the perfection of meditation,
and they will fulfill the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.
They will fulfill all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
all the gateways of samādhi, dhāraṇīs, and liberations, the immeasurable meditations, the formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the ten bodhisattva stages,
the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a buddha, and so on, up to omniscience itself.

Subhūti, it should be understood that this is due to the power of the Buddhas, by which no obstacles will arise for these sons of good family and daughters of good family who write, recite, explain, study, and properly attend to this profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, they will fulfill all the perfections;
they will fulfill all the emptinesses, all the factors conducive to awakening, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, and all the doors of liberation;
they will fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges.
They will fulfill the ten bodhisattva stages;
they will fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they will fulfill omniscience. Furthermore, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the ten directions, teaching the Dharma—
They, too, will exert themselves for the sake of those sons of good family and daughters of good family who write down, recite, study, and properly attend to this profound perfection of wisdom;
and those bodhisattvas in the ten directions who are irreversible shall likewise [exert themselves] for the sake of those sons of good family and daughters of good family.
And they will apply themselves with diligence and provide support for those who write, recite, teach, study, properly attend to, and cultivate this profound perfection of wisdom;
just as, Subhūti, it might be that some woman has many sons.
Whether five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand,
they would all exert themselves for this mother who is ill.
"How might no obstacle befall our mother? How might our mother live long? How might no unpleasant touch descend upon our mother's body?"

"This is our mother, the giver of our bodies and the sustainer of our lives; they should attend upon her as she stands before them, protecting her well, so that there may be no obstacle to her life, nor physical weakness, nor the affliction of gadflies, mosquitoes, or reptiles, nor the suffering of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the like."

In this way, those sons would provide for their mother all the requisites of happiness; in this way, they would cherish and honor that mother who has been well-nourished, thinking, "She is the one who showed us this world. In the very same way, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, constantly and continuously attend to this profound perfection of wisdom with their Buddha-eye. For what reason is that?
For this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all our Buddha-qualities and the producer of the light of wisdom;

even those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the ten directions, they too constantly and continuously attend to this very *prajñāpāramitā* with their Buddha-eye. Why is that?
For this profound perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas and the revealer of this knowledge of omniscience;
therefore, out of gratitude, the Tathāgatas constantly and continuously attend to this profound perfection of wisdom with their Buddha-eye. Why is that?
For from this have emerged the Tathāgatas’ perfections of meditation, vigor, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity;
for from this have emerged the Tathāgatas’ internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;

and from this have emerged the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
From this the three gates of liberation have emerged;
from this the four noble truths have emerged;
from this the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments have emerged.
From this are born the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments;
from this are born all samādhis and all doors of dhāraṇī;
from this are born the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
From this the six superknowledges are born;
from this the omniscience of all Buddhas is born;
from this the immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-qualities are born.
From this have emerged the stream-enterers, the once-returners, and the non-returners;
from this have emerged the arhats and the pratyekabuddhas;
from this have emerged the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Whatever [beings there may be], Subhūti, even those...

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— all of them have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying on this profound perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Great Vehicle and [rely on] this profound [perfection of wisdom]...

Subhūti, all those sons of good family and daughters of good family who will write down the Perfection of Wisdom, uphold it, read it, recite it, study it, and attend to it with wise reflection, are constantly and continuously kept in mind by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones with their Buddha-eye.
And the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will constantly and continuously provide protection, shelter, and defense such that they shall not fall away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, by means of the illustration and examples beginning with the great jewels of Jambudvīpa, their great majesty has been described; the faults have been stated.
Subhūti said: "As for what the Blessed One has said—

that the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the revealer of this world— how, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom the [mother] of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones?"
And how, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom the revealer of this world?
And how, Blessed One, is the Tathāgata generated by the perfection of wisdom?
And what is the world that has been described by the Tathāgata?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, by means of this profound perfection of wisdom, the ten powers of a Tathāgata are generated;

the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great compassion, great loving-kindness, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, are generated."
And it is by means of these dharmas, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata is manifested;
therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is brought forth by this profound perfection of wisdom. Thus, Subhūti spoke regarding the knowledge of the manifestation of the Tathāgata:
"But what, Blessed One, has been designated by the Tathāgata as 'the world'?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the five aggregates have been designated by the Tathāgata as 'the world'."
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, have the five aggregates been shown by means of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom does not show these five aggregates as being broken down, nor does it show them as being completely disintegrated, nor does it show them as arising.
It shows them as they are not being ceased, nor does it show them as being afflicted or purified;
it shows neither increase nor decrease.
He does not demonstrate dharmas as involving grasping or rejection, nor as past, future, or present. Why is that?
For emptiness is neither broken nor disintegrated, and the signless is neither broken nor disintegrated.
The wishless is neither broken nor disintegrated;

the unconditioned, the non-arising, the non-ceasing, the non-existence, and the absence of intrinsic nature are neither broken nor disintegrated. For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata has declared the profound perfection of wisdom to be the revealer of the world. This is the knowledge of the world.

Subhūti, even those who know the mental activities of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings—those immeasurable beings who possess the knowledge of others' minds—they too know them by relying on the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, in this profound perfection of wisdom, neither a being nor the designation of a being is apprehended;
neither form nor the designation of form is apprehended.
Neither feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations,
nor consciousness is apprehended, nor is the designation of consciousness apprehended;
neither eye nor form, nor eye-consciousness, nor eye-contact, nor feeling conditioned by eye-contact is apprehended.
The designation "eye" and "form" is not apprehended;
the designation "eye-consciousness" is not apprehended;
the designation "eye-contact" is not apprehended.
The designation of feeling conditioned by eye-contact is not apprehended;

likewise, there is no ear, no sound, no nose, no odor, no tongue, no taste, no body, no tangible object, no mind, no mental phenomenon, no mental consciousness, no mind-contact, and no designation of feeling conditioned by mind-contact.

It is not apprehended. In this way, neither the perfections, nor the factors conducive to awakening, nor the gates of liberation, nor the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, nor the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including the designation of the knowledge of all aspects, is apprehended.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that this profound perfection of wisdom is the one that reveals the world to the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, this profound perfection of wisdom does not show form, nor does it show anything up to and including omniscience. Why is that?
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom itself is neither found nor apprehended within the perfection of wisdom;
how then could form be apprehended?
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—
how much less could consciousness be apprehended, and how much less could even the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended?
This is the knowledge of the conduct of all minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as many beings as are designated by the designation "being"— whether they have form or are formless,

whether they possess perception, lack perception, or are neither percipient nor non-percipient— be they in this world-system or in other world-systems in the ten directions, whatever contracted minds or distracted minds those beings have, those...

He understands, as it truly is, "contracted minds" and "distracted minds. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata understand those contracted minds and distracted minds of those beings as they truly are?
By means of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), Subhūti, the Tathāgata understands those contracted minds and distracted minds of those beings as they truly are.
Subhūti said:
"By what nature of phenomena, Blessed One, does the Tathāgata know, in accordance with reality, that the minds of those sentient beings are contracted or distracted?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, in that *dharmatā* where even *dharmatā* itself is not apprehended, how much less so contracted minds or distracted minds?

By means of this *dharmatā*, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows the contracted minds and distracted minds of those sentient beings as they truly are. This is the knowledge of the contraction of the mind. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, [knows] the contracted minds of those sentient beings from the perspective of the inexhaustible.

He understands distracted minds and concentrated minds as they truly are. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata understand those beings' concentrated minds and distracted minds as they truly are from the perspective of their inexhaustibility?
Here, Subhūti, the Tathāgata understands those minds of those beings as they truly are from the perspective of cessation and abandonment.
By way of tranquility, by way of emptiness, and by way of solitude, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha knows, as it truly is, the contracted minds and the distracted minds of those beings.
This is the knowledge of the aspect of the non-exhaustion of the mind.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the mind with passion of those beings as "a mind with passion."
He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from passion as "a mind free from passion";
he understands, as it truly is, a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred";
he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred."
He understands, as it truly is, a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," and he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion.
Subhūti said:

How, Blessed One, does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, truly know the mind of those beings as "a mind with lust" when it is a mind with lust; truly know the mind as "a mind with hatred" when it is a mind with hatred; and truly know the mind as "a mind with delusion" when it is a mind with delusion?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that which is the state of the mind possessing passion, hatred, and delusion is not the mind's suchness. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the mind is not apprehended as it truly is, nor are mental factors; how much less so [the mind] with passion?"
or with hatred, or with delusion, he will not perceive such a mind. For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on the perfection of wisdom, knows the minds of those beings as they truly are:
"a mind with passion is a mind with passion," and he knows a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred" as it truly is.

He understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion" according to reality. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata understand the minds of those beings that are free from passion as "minds free from passion" according to reality?
He understands a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred" according to reality.
Does one know, as it truly is, that "the mind is free from delusion, the mind is free from delusion"?
Subhūti, that which is the mind’s freedom from passion is not the mind’s state of being possessed by passion. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, there is no conjunction of two minds. Likewise, Subhūti, that which is the mind’s freedom from hatred is not the mind’s state of being possessed by hatred.
Subhūti, that which is the mind’s freedom from delusion is not the mind’s state of being deluded. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, there is no conjunction of two minds. In this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds of those beings that are free from passion as "minds free from passion," and he knows, as it truly is, their minds that are free from hatred as "minds free from hatred."
He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata [knows] the minds of other beings and other persons, such as those possessed of passion and so forth.

He understands as it really is: "a vast mind, a vast mind. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand as it really is that the minds of other beings and other individuals are vast, [thinking] "a vast mind, a vast mind"?

In this regard, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata perceives that for other beings and other persons there is no expanded mind and no contracted mind; for the mind does not increase, nor does it decrease;
it does not come, nor does it go.
He understands the mind as it truly is. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the mind is not apprehended—that by which it would be expanded, or even where it might come from.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, relying upon this perfection of wisdom, [knows] other beings and other persons.

He understands, as it truly is, "the vast mind is a vast mind. Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the exalted mind of other beings and other persons as "an exalted mind. And how, Subhūti, does he do so?

“Does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the vast mind of other beings and other persons as it truly is, thinking, ‘the mind is vast’? Subhūti, in this regard, the Tathāgata knows that those minds of those other beings and other persons have no coming and no going, no arising, no cessation, no staying, and no alteration.”
He perceives thus. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of those thoughts does not exist, such that it could come or go, arise or cease, remain, or become otherwise.

In this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the vast mind of other beings and other persons as "a vast mind. This is the knowledge of the vast mind. Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata [knows] the minds of other beings and other persons...
He understands, as it truly is, that the mind is immeasurable, that the mind is immeasurable. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata,
by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, that the minds of other beings and other persons are immeasurable, that the minds are immeasurable?
In this regard, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata perceives the minds of other beings, of other persons, as neither abiding nor non-abiding, neither fixed nor non-fixed.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the stream of mind is without support and immeasurable.

For they have no basis whereon they might be established. In this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the immeasurable minds of other beings and other persons as "immeasurable minds."
Thus is the knowledge of immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the mind of other beings and other persons is invisible, [and] that the mind is invisible. And how, Subhūti, does he do so?

Does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the invisible mind of other beings and other persons as it truly is, thinking, "the invisible mind, the invisible mind"? In this regard, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, [knows] the signless states of other beings and other persons.
He understands thoughts as they truly are—thoughts devoid of intrinsic nature—by way of the emptiness of specific characteristics.

For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, understands the invisible mind of other beings and other persons as it truly is: "the invisible mind, the invisible mind. This is the knowledge of the invisible mind.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the invisible mind of other beings and other persons as "the invisible mind. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata,
by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the invisible mind of other beings and other persons as "the invisible mind"?
Does he know this as it truly is?

For indeed, Subhūti, those thoughts of others do not come within the range of the five eyes of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha [knows] this perfection of wisdom.
Having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the invisible mind of other beings and other persons as "invisible mind.
Furthermore, Subhūti, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata [knows] the invisible minds of other beings and other persons...

And he understands, as it truly is, the mental expansions, contractions, withdrawals, and extensions of beings. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as they truly are, the mental expansions, contractions, withdrawals, and extensions of other beings and other persons?

In this regard, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata perceives the expansions and contractions, the withdrawals and extensions, of the minds of other beings and other persons— whatever such expansions, contractions, withdrawals, or extensions of the minds of beings arise as they occur—
all of these are dependent upon form (*rūpa*).
Feeling, perception, and mental formations arise dependent upon consciousness.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows as they truly are the expansion and contraction, the withdrawal and extension of the minds of those beings.

"That the Tathāgata exists after death" is a form of clinging to form; "he does not exist," "he both exists and does not exist," [or "he neither exists nor does not exist"]— these too are forms of clinging to form.
"That the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death" is included within form;
"feeling," "perception," and "formations" [are likewise];
"that the Tathāgata exists after death" is included within consciousness.
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death? Does he both exist and not exist? Does he neither exist nor not exist?"—this pertains to consciousness.
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*);
[or] they are non-eternal, or both eternal and non-eternal.
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal are the self and the world; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*).
Likewise for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Eternal are the self and the world; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"The self and the world are non-eternal; they are both eternal and non-eternal; they are neither eternal nor non-eternal—this alone is the truth, all else is delusion": this pertains to consciousness.
Thus, "the self and the world are finite; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*).
Likewise, regarding feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*):

"the self and the world are finite; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Similarly, "the self and the world are infinite; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"Feeling, perception, and mental formations;

the self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness. "The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"Feeling, perception, and mental formations;

the self and the world are both finite and infinite—this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness. "The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite—this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
That "feeling, perception, and mental formations;
that the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite—this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness.
That "the self and the world exist after death—this alone is true, all else is delusion"—[this pertains to consciousness].
Thus, this pertains to form:
it does not exist,
and it both exists and does not exist.
"Neither does the self and the world exist nor do they not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*).

"The self and the world exist after death; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"The self and the world neither exist nor do they not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"— this belongs to the sphere of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"That the soul is that body, or the soul is one thing and the body another— 'this alone is the truth, everything else is delusion'— this pertains to form (*rūpa*). That the sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) [are the soul], or the soul is one thing and the body another— 'this alone is the truth, everything else is delusion'— this pertains to consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

It is thus. For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the expansions and contractions, the withdrawals and extensions of the minds of other beings and other persons. This is the knowledge of the expansions and contractions of the mind.
Furthermore, Subhūti, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata perceives form. How does he perceive form?

One perceives in such a way that one perceives true suchness (*tathatā*)— which is non-falsehood, unchanging, non-conceptual, signless, effortless, non-proliferated, and non-apprehensible— as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. How does consciousness perceive?

He perceives it in such a way that it is thusness— unfailing, unchanging, non-conceptual, signless, effortless, non-proliferated, and non-apprehensible. For in this manner, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, knows the opening and closing, the contraction and expansion, of other beings and other persons exactly as they are in thusness.
It is non-falsity, unchanging, non-conceptual, signless, effortless, non-proliferated, and non-apprehensible.
Thus, Subhūti, that which is the suchness of opening, closing, contracting, and extending is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination;
and that which is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination is the suchness of all phenomena.
That which is the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the six perfections;
that which is the suchness of the six perfections is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
that which is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness of all the emptinesses.

The suchness of all the emptinesses is the suchness of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments; the suchness of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments is the suchness of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; the suchness of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments is the suchness of the four noble truths.

The suchness of the four noble truths is the suchness of the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the suchness of the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is the suchness of the six superknowledges;
the suchness of the six superknowledges is the suchness of all meditative concentrations.
The suchness of all samādhis is the suchness of all dhāraṇī-doors;
the suchness of all dhāraṇī-doors is the suchness of the ten powers of a Tathāgata;
the suchness of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is the suchness of the four grounds of self-confidence.
The suchness of the four grounds of self-confidence is the suchness of the four analytical knowledges;
the suchness of the four analytical knowledges is the suchness of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
and the suchness of great loving-kindness and great compassion is the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the suchness of omniscience;
the suchness of omniscience is the suchness of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;

the suchness of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena is the suchness of worldly and transcendent phenomena, of those with outflows and without outflows, of those blameworthy and blameless, of those with afflictions and without afflictions, of those subject to defilement and free from defilement, and of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The suchness of phenomena— that which is the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena— is the suchness of past, future, and present phenomena;
that which is the suchness of past, future, and present phenomena is the suchness of the dharma of the stream-enterer.
That which is the suchness of the dharma of a stream-enterer is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry;
that which is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the dharma of a once-returner;
that which is the suchness of the dharma of a once-returner is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning.

That which is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the dharmas of the non-returner; that which is the suchness of the dharmas of the non-returner is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning;
that which is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning is the suchness of arhatship.

That which is the suchness of arhatship is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship; that which is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship is the suchness of a pratyekabuddha; that which is the suchness of a pratyekabuddha is the suchness of pratyekabodhi;
and that which is the suchness of pratyekabodhi is the suchness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The suchness of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is the suchness of the Tathāgata;
the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all sentient beings. Thus, that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata and that which is the suchness of all sentient beings—
This suchness is one alone, the inseparable suchness;
that which is inseparable suchness is inexhaustible, and that which is inexhaustible is non-dual by virtue of its inexhaustibility. Subhūti, this is the suchness of all phenomena.
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom, by relying upon which the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment,
is thus the suchness of the Tathāgatas and their mother;
for in this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the revealer of the world.

For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, knows the suchness of all phenomena; he knows their non-falsity and their non-otherness, and it is by virtue of that suchness that he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Subhūti said:

"O Blessed One, profound indeed is the suchness of all dharmas—their non-falsity and their non-other-suchness. O Blessed One, by means of this suchness, the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is revealed. Who, O Blessed One, will have faith in this?"
"Except for irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, or persons endowed with right view, or arhats whose outflows are exhausted—these dharmas, Blessed One, are profound.
The Blessed One said:
"For such is the inexhaustible suchness, Subhūti. Why is it inexhaustible?"
Because all phenomena are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible.

Subhūti, this is that suchness which the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, has proclaimed—namely, the suchness of all phenomena. Thus [are] the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the awakening to suchness, his subsequent proclamation, his designation, and his wisdom.
Then, as many sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form as there are in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system...
Taking up divine sandalwood powders, they all approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, this profound perfection of wisdom is being revealed. Blessed One, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
“O sons of the gods, this profound perfection of wisdom has emptiness as its characteristic.”
For, O sons of the gods, this profound perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of the signless; for, O sons of the gods, this profound perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of the wishless.
Thus are the characteristics of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless.

O sons of the gods, [all phenomena] have the characteristic of non-arising, the characteristic of non-cessation, the characteristic of non-defilement, the characteristic of non-purification, the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of lack of intrinsic nature, the characteristic of non-reliance, the characteristic of space, the characteristic of non-eternality, the characteristic of non-annihilation, the characteristic of non-conditioning, the characteristic of non-identity, the characteristic of non-difference, the characteristic of non-coming, and the characteristic of coming; indeed, they are characterized by the absence of characteristics.
This is the profound perfection of wisdom. O sons of the gods, this profound perfection of wisdom has such characteristics;

it is expressed by the Tathāgata through worldly convention, but not in terms of the ultimate truth. Thus, the knowledge of non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth—O sons of the gods—these characteristics cannot be subverted by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Why is that?
For even the world with its gods, humans, and asuras has that very characteristic;
thus, O sons of the gods, a characteristic does not disturb a characteristic,
nor does a characteristic perceive a characteristic.
One does not perceive a characteristic as being without characteristic;
for indeed, both characteristics and non-characteristics, as well as characteristics-and-non-characteristics—
of these two, neither has any real existence.
"By what one would know, or who would know"—
this is the knowledge that does not disturb the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
For, O sons of gods, these characteristics are not conditioned by form (*rūpa*).
In the same way, feeling, perception,
and mental formations are not conditioned by consciousness, nor conditioned by the elements, nor conditioned by the sense bases,
nor conditioned by dependent origination, nor conditioned by the perfection of generosity, nor conditioned by the perfection of ethical discipline, nor conditioned by the perfection of patience.

They are not conditioned by the perfection of vigor, nor conditioned by the perfection of meditation, nor conditioned by the perfection of wisdom; they are not conditioned by all the emptinesses, nor conditioned by the factors of enlightenment, nor conditioned by the noble truths, nor conditioned by the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative attainments;
nor are they conditioned by emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
It is not conditioned by the superknowledges, nor conditioned by all meditative concentrations, nor conditioned by all doors of dhāraṇī, nor conditioned by the powers of a Tathāgata,
nor conditioned by the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, nor conditioned by omniscience. This is the knowledge of non-conditioning.
"O sons of the gods, these marks do not belong to humans or non-humans, nor are they with-outflows or without-outflows, worldly or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned.
Then the Blessed One said this to those sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm:
"Sons of the gods, if someone were to ask: 'What is the characteristic of space?'"
If one were to speak thus, would he be speaking correctly?
The sons of the gods replied: "No, Blessed One, he would not be speaking correctly. Why is that?"
"Indeed, Blessed One, space does not exist by means of any characteristic, because the space-element is unconditioned. Thus the Blessed One spoke of non-conceptual knowledge:
"O sons of the gods, whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this stability of the dharma-realm remains established with such characteristics."
Just as the causal characteristic exists, so has it been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata;
therefore, the Tathāgata is called "Tathāgata.
The sons of the gods said:

"O Blessed One, these characteristics realized by the Tathāgata are profound. Because of the realization of these characteristics, the Tathāgata possesses unattached knowledge; and by abiding in these characteristics, all characteristics have been fully revealed by the Tathāgata. It is through the full revelation of the perfection of wisdom, O Blessed One, that those characteristics have been fully revealed. It is marvelous, O Blessed One, how deep this perfection of wisdom of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, is!"
It is the domain of the perfectly awakened ones;
it is where the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, while practicing, fully realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
and having fully realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment, made the differentiation of all characteristics.

The differentiation has been made of the characteristic of form, the characteristic of feeling, the characteristic of perception, the characteristic of mental formations, and the characteristic of consciousness; likewise, the differentiation has been made of the characteristics of the aggregates, the characteristics of the elements, the characteristics of the sense bases, and the characteristics of dependent origination, up to the differentiation of the characteristic of omniscience.
This is the knowledge of differentiation.
Then the Blessed One said this to those sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm:
"Sons of the gods, the characteristic of forms is form;
thus has that been awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics."
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of grasping signs; mental formations have the characteristic of volitional construction.

The Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to the fact that consciousness, which has the characteristic of individual representation, is without characteristics; that the aggregates have the characteristic of a heap;
and that the elements have the characteristic of a lineage.
The sense bases (āyatana) have the characteristic of being gateways for the arrival [of consciousness];
dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) has the characteristic of being a causal complex; these the Tathāgata has awakened to as being without characteristics (alakṣaṇa);
and the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) has the characteristic of relinquishment.
That has been realized by the Tathāgata as being without marks: the perfection of ethical discipline has the mark of non-burning; the perfection of patience has the mark of non-anger;
the perfection of vigor has the mark of being uncrushable.
The perfection of meditation has the characteristic of gathering;

the perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of non-attachment, and that has been realized by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics. The four meditations, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments have the characteristic of being undisturbed.

Those [dharmas] have been awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*), which have the characteristic of leading to liberation, have been awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics. That which has the characteristic of solitude, the characteristic of peace, the signless (*animitta*), and the effortless characteristic of the wishless (*apraṇihita*)—that has been awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics. Those liberations (*vimokṣa*) which have the characteristic of liberation have been awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics. [The concentrations] have the characteristic of being well-ascertained.
The grounds of self-confidence have the characteristic of being well-established;
the analytical knowledges have the characteristic of being indestructible;
and great loving-kindness has the characteristic of bringing about benefit.
Great compassion has the characteristic of providing protection;
sympathetic joy has the characteristic of serene confidence and gladness regarding the Buddha-dharma;
equanimity has the characteristic of indifference toward all faults and virtues, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, fame and insignificance, and blame and praise.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), which have the characteristic of being unassailable, have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Even up to the omniscient knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) that has the characteristic of direct perception, that too has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics. It is in this way, O sons of the gods, that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as being without characteristics; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
He is called one who possesses knowledge free from attachment. Thus [is] the knowledge of the absence of characteristics.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is that by which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, is brought forth; she is his mother."

And because she is the revealer of the world, for that reason the Tathāgata dwells relying upon this Dharma of the perfection of wisdom. Thus, through the very knowledge of dwelling in reliance upon his own Dharma, he honors, reveres, respects, worships, adores, and venerates this Dharma. This, Subhūti, is that...
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the perfection of wisdom; therefore, the Tathāgata honors, reveres, respects, worships, adores, and venerates this perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, it is from this perfection of wisdom that the manifestation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, occurs.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is grateful and appreciative.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those who would rightly say of the Tathāgata, "He is grateful and appreciative," would indeed be speaking rightly if they said, "He is grateful and appreciative. And how, Subhūti, is the Tathāgata grateful and appreciative?
Subhūti, by whatever vehicle the Tathāgata has come,

and by whatever practice he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— precisely that vehicle and that practice the Tathāgata honors, reveres, respects, worships, adores, and venerates.
He favors and protects them;
Subhūti, this should be seen as the Tathāgata’s gratitude and thankfulness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the fact that all dharmas are uncreated, based on the non-existence of an agent—this is the knowledge of honor and so forth.

"They are unmodified," [the Tathāgata] has perfectly awakened to this by way of the non-existence of any suppression; Subhūti, this too should be seen as the Tathāgata’s gratitude and thankfulness. Thus, having relied upon the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to all phenomena as uncreated. This is the knowledge of the uncreated.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata’s unconditioned knowledge regarding all phenomena has proceeded;

it proceeds by way of this convention of non-proceeding. In this manner, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world. Thus is the all-pervading knowledge.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, since all dharmas are without a knower and without a seer,
how then is the perfection of wisdom the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. All dharmas are without a knower and without a seer.
And how, Subhūti, are all dharmas without a knower and without a seer?"
For all phenomena, Subhūti, are empty, hollow, vain, and without essence;
by this method, Subhūti, all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer.
Furthermore, Subhūti, all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer.
And how, Subhūti, are all dharmas neither knowing nor seeing?
Subhūti, all dharmas are non-dependent and non-included;
in this manner, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither knowing nor seeing. It is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world.
Furthermore, because form is unseen, she is its revealer;
likewise, because feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are unseen, she is their revealer.

Because the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination are not seen, she is their "revealer. Likewise, up to and including omniscience, because it is not seen, she is its "revealer.
In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world.
Subhūti said:
How, O Blessed One, is it that by the non-seeing of form, and how by the non-seeing of feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, does [the Prajñāpāramitā] become the revealer?
"How is it that she reveals the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields by not seeing their dependent origination?
How is it that she reveals everything up to omniscience by not seeing it?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, when consciousness does not arise with form as its object,

then, Subhūti, because form is not seen, it is the "showing" [of form]. Likewise, Subhūti, when consciousness does not arise with feeling, perception, or mental formations as its objects, and when consciousness does not arise with consciousness itself as its object—

Thus, because consciousness is not seen, it is the "revealer. When consciousness does not arise with the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, or dependent origination as its object, it is the "revealer" because these are not seen. When consciousness does not arise with the perfections as its object, it is the "revealer" because the perfections are not seen. Likewise for all the emptinesses and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the five superknowledges, all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges;

When consciousness does not arise with the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) as its object, it is thus a "revealer" because the unique qualities of a Buddha are not seen. Subhūti, when consciousness does not arise with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as its object, it is thus a "revealer" because omniscience is not seen. For in this way, Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, Subhūti, how is it that the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world?
Here, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom indicates that the world is empty. How does it indicate that the world is empty?
It indicates that the five aggregates are the world that is empty.
It indicates that the world of the twelve sense bases is empty;
it indicates that the world of the eighteen elements is empty;
it indicates that the world of the ten paths of wholesome action is empty.
It indicates that the world is empty of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
it indicates that the world is empty of the twelve-linked dependent origination conditioned by ignorance;
and it indicates that the world is empty of the sixty-two types of views preceded by the view of a self-identity.
It indicates that the world of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is empty;

it indicates that the world of the six perfections is empty. Likewise, it indicates that the world of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, is empty. In the same way, [it indicates that] the ten powers [are empty].
It indicates that the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are an empty world;
it indicates that omniscience is an empty world. For in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom makes known that the world is empty.
In what sense does the world indicate that it is empty?
The world indicates that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are empty;
it indicates that dependent origination, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are empty.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to and including omniscience, demonstrate that the world is empty. For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the progenitor of the Tathāgata and of this world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom shows the Tathāgata that the world is empty. How does it show that the world is empty?
It shows that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four meditative concentrations, and the four... [are empty].

It demonstrates that the immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the sixty-two types of views preceded by the view of a self-identity, the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, all modes of emptiness, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a buddha, and so on up to the knowledge of all aspects— all these are empty of the world. For it is in this way, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom [is the mother] of the Tathāgata.
She is the mother of this world and its revealer.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the wisdom of the perfection of wisdom reveals to the Tathāgata the cognitions that indicate the aspect of emptiness and the cognitions that demonstrate [reality]. How does it reveal that "the world is inconceivable"? What is meant by revealing that "the world is inconceivable"?

It shows that the five aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, up to the knowledge of all aspects, are the world, and that this world is inconceivable. It shows that it is thus secluded, absolutely empty, and empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom shows the Tathāgata’s world to be peaceful. How does it show that the world is peaceful?
It shows that from the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and dependent origination, up to the knowledge of all aspects, the world is peaceful.
For in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world.
Thus is the inconceivable knowledge of peace.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom shows that the world of the Tathāgata is emptiness itself. In what way does it show that the world is emptiness itself?
It shows that the five aggregates are the world and are emptiness itself;
likewise, it shows that the elements and sense-fields are the world and are emptiness itself.

He shows that the factors of dependent origination are the world, which is emptiness itself. In this way, he shows that everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the world, which is emptiness itself. For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgata and the revealer of this world. Furthermore, Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom reveals the world to the Tathāgata in such a way that there is neither a notion of this world nor a notion of a future world. Why is that?
For those phenomena do not exist by which one might form the notion of this world or the notion of the other world.
This is the knowledge of the cessation of the notion of the world. Subhūti said: "This is the characteristic of knowledge."

"Indeed, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of a great task for the Blessed One; it has appeared, Blessed One, for the sake of an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, an incalculable task, and a task equal to the unequaled for the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is present for the Tathāgatas for a great task. And how, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom present for a great task?

This, Subhūti, is the great task of the Tathāgatas, namely, the sense of not abandoning the protection and refuge of all sentient beings. And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom [present] for an inconceivable task?"

"Subhūti, Buddhahood, the state of a Tathāgata, the state of a Self-Existent One, and omniscience are inconceivable. It is through such inconceivable activity, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is present for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom present through incomparable activity?"

For indeed, Subhūti, there is no being whatsoever to be found among the classes of beings who would be able to weigh the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is by this method, Subhūti, through this incomparable function, that the perfection of wisdom is present for the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas. And how?

Subhūti, is it because of the immeasurable task of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that this perfection of wisdom is present? Subhūti, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, Self-Become-hood, and omniscience are immeasurable; they cannot be measured by anyone. Subhūti, it is in this sense that this perfection of wisdom of the Tathāgatas has an immeasurable task.
It is present. And how, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom present through the incalculable activity of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas?

Subhūti, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, self-existence, and omniscience are incalculable; they cannot be calculated by anyone. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that it is present through incalculable activity.
The perfection of wisdom is present for the Tathāgatas. And how, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom present through its function of being unequaled and equal?

Subhūti, there is no one equal to the Tathāgatas, let alone superior. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is present for the Tathāgatas through its function of being unequaled and equal. Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, Self-Existent-hood, and Omniscience inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, self-existence, and omniscience are inconceivable.

Likewise, Subhūti, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, self-existence, and omniscience are incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled. Form, too, Subhūti, is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Subhūti, are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled.

Likewise, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled. Thus, even up to omniscience itself is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable.
Subhūti, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequally equal.
Subhūti, in that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, neither mind nor mental factors (*caitasika dharma*) are to be apprehended. Why is that?
For form (*rūpa*), Subhūti, is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequally equal; it is not cognized.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Subhūti, are indeed inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; they are not known. In the same way, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; they are not known.
"Even omniscience itself is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; it is not perceived.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is form inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled, such that it is not perceived?"

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; they are not perceived. Likewise, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; they are not perceived. In the same way, Blessed One, for what reason is even omniscience itself inconceivable and incomparable?
“Is it not the case that the objects of cognition (*prameya*)—innumerable and unequaled—are not perceived?
The Blessed One said:

“Even for form (*rūpa*), its contemplation, weighing, measurement, calculation, and its state of equality or inequality are not perceived. In this same way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), its contemplation, weighing, measurement, calculation, and its state of equality or inequality [are not perceived].”
It is not discerned.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is it that [the nature] of form, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects, is not discerned?"
“Is it not the case that reflection, weighing, measuring, counting, and the state of being equal or unequal are not discerned?
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.”

Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled, because it is devoid of intrinsic nature. In the same way, the intrinsic nature of the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable.

"It is equal to the unequaled because it is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). In this way, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), its intrinsic nature is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled because it is without intrinsic nature. What do you think, Subhūti? Is form—which is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled—perceived therein?"

Feeling, perception, and mental formations— Subhūti, as for that consciousness which is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled— is consciousness apprehended therein? Those elements, sense-bases, and dependent originations which are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled— [are they apprehended?]

"Are the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination perceived therein? Subhūti, as for that omniscience which is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled—is omniscience perceived therein?
Subhūti replied: "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"By this method, Subhūti, all dharmas are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
These, Subhūti, are the Tathāgata’s Tathāgata-dharmas; they are inconceivable because they have transcended thought."
They are incomparable because they have transcended comparison;
they are immeasurable because they have transcended measurement;
they are incalculable because they have transcended calculation.

They are "unequaled by the unequaled" because they have ceased from both the even and the uneven. By this method, Subhūti, all dharmas are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled by the unequaled.
These, Subhūti, are the Tathāgata’s Tathāgata-dharmas: they are inconceivable, having transcended thought; they are incomparable, having transcended comparison.
They are immeasurable, having transcended all measure; they are incalculable, having transcended all calculation;
they are unequaled, having transcended both the equal and the unequal. "Inconceivable," Subhūti, is a designation for that which cannot be conceived.
"Subhūti, 'incomparable' is a designation for that which cannot be weighed; Subhūti, 'immeasurable' is a designation for that which is without measure;
Subhūti, 'incalculable' is a designation for that which cannot be counted."
"O Subhūti, 'the unequaled' is a designation for that which is neither equal nor unequal.
O Subhūti, these qualities of a Tathāgata are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled. O Subhūti, they are 'inconceivable' because space is inconceivable;

likewise, they are incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled because space is unequaled. Thus indeed, O Subhūti, the qualities of a Tathāgata are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable."
They are unequaled by the unequaled;

they cannot be conceived, weighed, measured, or numbered by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, nor even by the world including all its gods, nor can their equality or inequality be determined. Thus immeasurable are the Buddhas.
The qualities of a Buddha are immeasurable.

Furthermore, while this Dharma discourse— the chapter on the inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled— was being spoken by the Blessed One, the minds of five hundred monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.

The minds of twenty thousand bhikṣuṇīs were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified for sixty thousand upāsakas and twenty thousand upāsikās;
and twenty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.

And they have been prophesied by the Blessed One that they will become Buddhas in this very Fortunate Aeon. Thus, through such distinctions as inconceivability and so forth, there are four moments regarding suffering.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is profound.

O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task; it has appeared, O Blessed One, for an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an incalculable task, an immeasurable task, and a task equal to the unequaled."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task."

Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is present by means of inconceivable activity, incomparable activity, immeasurable activity, incalculable activity, and activity that is equal to the unequaled. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, within this profound perfection of wisdom, the five perfections are fully integrated. For here, Subhūti, within this profound perfection of wisdom, internal emptiness is fully integrated, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
It is conjoined with the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,

the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. For herein, Subhūti, within this profound perfection of wisdom, are the four meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

The four noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the six superknowledges, all samādhis, and all dhāraṇī-doors are joined herein. For it is in this profound perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, that the ten powers of a Tathāgata are joined.
The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are associated with it.
For here, Subhūti, in this profound perfection of wisdom, the stage of a Buddha is associated, up to and including omniscience.
It is just as if, Subhūti, there were a consecrated Kṣatriya king who has attained power and valor over his realm.

Whatever royal duties there may be, all of them are carried out in conjunction with ministers; thus the king has little concern and is relieved of his burden, whether regarding royal affairs or the affairs of the realm. In the same way, Subhūti, whatever dharmas there are—whether those of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas, or the Buddhas—all of them are conjoined with the perfection of wisdom.
The perfection of wisdom performs their task. Therefore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task;
this perfection of wisdom has appeared for an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, and an incalculable task. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the profound perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the non-appropriation and non-attachment to form.

It is established for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment toward the knowledge of all aspects.

It is present for the sake of non-appropriation and non-adherence to the fruit of stream-entry. Likewise, it is for the sake of non-appropriation and non-adherence to the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, is this perfection of wisdom present for the sake of non-appropriation and non-adherence to form?"
How, O Blessed One, is it with regard to feeling, perception, and mental formations?
How, O Blessed One, has this perfection of wisdom appeared for the sake of non-appropriation and non-adherence to consciousness?
And how, O Blessed One, has it appeared for the sake of non-appropriation and non-adherence to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, do you perceive that form which is the form by which one might grasp or become attached?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One; [the same applies to] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, do you perceive that consciousness by which one might grasp or become attached?
Likewise, Subhūti, do you perceive that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment which one might grasp or become attached to?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

Subhūti, I too do not perceive that form which I might grasp or adhere to, nor that which anyone else might grasp or adhere to; and this applies likewise to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, I too do not perceive that consciousness which I might grasp or adhere to, nor that which might grasp or adhere to it; and so on, Subhūti, up to that [feeling].
I do not perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; not perceiving it, I do not grasp it; not grasping it, I do not adhere to it.
Subhūti, I likewise do not perceive the stage of a Buddha, omniscience, the knowledge of all modes, the state of a Tathāgata, or Buddhahood.
Not perceiving them, I do not grasp them; not grasping them, I do not adhere to them.
Therefore, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not grasp form, nor should they adhere to it. The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, consciousness should not be grasped nor should it be adhered to by bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination should not be grasped;

likewise, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments [should not be grasped].

The emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not to be grasped and not to be adhered to; even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is not to be grasped and not to be adhered to. In this same way, Buddhahood, omniscience, and the knowledge of all aspects [are not to be grasped and not to be adhered to].
"The state of a Tathāgata is not to be grasped, nor is it to be adhered to.
Thus, by way of the excellence of including all noble persons, there is the first moment regarding the Truth of Origination.
Then, those sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm said this to the Blessed One:

“O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound; it is difficult to see, difficult to realize, beyond reasoning, outside the sphere of reasoning, peaceful, subtle, and to be known by the wise and learned. O Blessed One, those bodhisattvas will indeed have performed their duties under previous Victors.”
Those who have faith and resolve in this profound perfection of wisdom,
O Blessed One, will be bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are sustained by spiritual friends and have planted roots of merit. Indeed,
those who have faith and resolve in this profound perfection of wisdom will be such bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Thus, by way of the distinction of being experienced by specific types of persons, there is the second moment regarding the origin [of suffering]. Blessed One, if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become followers by faith,
followers of the Dharma, those of the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats;
Even if there were Pratyekabuddhas,

and whatever knowledge and whatever abandonment they possess, compared to a single day’s worth of patience, interest, reflection, weighing, examination, and calculation regarding this profound perfection of wisdom, this alone is superior to all of that.
Whoever here possesses such a taste for and acceptance of this perfection of wisdom— for what reason is that?

Because the knowledge and the abandonment of those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are all [contained within] the acceptance of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then the Blessed One addressed those sons of the gods:
"So it is, sons of the gods, so it is; such is the knowledge of the pratyekabuddhas, and such is their abandonment."
This is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thus, by way of this distinction of uncommonness, is the third moment regarding the origin [of suffering].
If any son of good family or daughter of good family should hear this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),...

Having heard it, one should write it down; having written it down, one should recite it and attend to it thoroughly. Furthermore, O sons of good family and daughters of good family, the more rapid attainment of final nirvāṇa is to be expected for these [practitioners] than for those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas who are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and who practice according to other sūtras. Why is that?

For it is in this profound perfection of wisdom that the preeminent dharmas are taught in detail, wherein those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, and those who are at the eighth stage must train;
wherein stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle must train;
and wherein the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, while training, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, by way of this distinction of swift superknowledge, there is the fourth moment regarding the origin [of suffering].
Then indeed, those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form uttered this inspired utterance:
"O Blessed One, this is a great perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom."

"Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the inconceivable perfection, the incomparable perfection, the immeasurable perfection, the incalculable perfection, and the perfectly equal perfection. For indeed, Blessed One, having trained in this profound perfection of wisdom, those who follow by faith shall go forth, those who follow by dharma shall go forth, as well as the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, and once-returners."
"Non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas—

in this [perfection] having trained, bodhisattva mahāsattvas have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Yet, neither a deficiency nor a fullness of this perfection of wisdom is perceived."
Thus, by virtue of this distinction of being neither deficient nor complete, there is the first moment of cessation.

Then indeed, those sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One. They did not go very far.
Having departed, they became invisible;
those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire returned to the desire realm,
and those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form returned to the form realm.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, from where has a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, gains resolute faith, passed away before being reborn here?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, shall have faith upon hearing it, and shall not be cowed, nor shrink back, nor become weary, nor doubt, nor be perplexed,
but shall rejoice in hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, and having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, by that very [faith]...
He will not be separated from mental attention; whether walking or coming, standing or sitting, or lying down, he will constantly and continuously maintain that mental attention,
and he will follow that person, the Dharma-preacher, constantly and continuously.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a cow with a young calf does not abandon her calf; even so, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of this profound perfection of wisdom, does not leave that Dharma-preacher until this perfection of wisdom has been committed to memory, mastered, recited, and thoroughly cultivated by the mind.

And having been observed and seen, and thoroughly penetrated—Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, a person belonging to the new vehicle, has passed away from among humans and has been reborn among humans. Why is that?
Because previously, by that bodhisattva mahāsattva of the new vehicle, this profound perfection of wisdom was [already]...

Having written it down and placed it in a book, he honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, and with rows of lamps all around.
By that root of merit, having passed away from among humans, he was reborn again among humans;
and upon merely hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he became resolved in faith toward it.
Thus, due to this particular intensity of realization regarding cessation, Subhūti spoke a second time:
"It might be, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these very qualities [is superior] to others."

Having attended upon other Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in various Buddha-fields, one who, having passed away from there, is reborn here and, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it; and having had faith, will write it down,
and having written it down, will take it up, recite it, study it, and attend to it with wise reflection.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Subhūti, there may be a way in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these very qualities [surpasses] others."

Having attended upon other Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in various Buddha-fields, one who, having passed away from there, has been reborn here, will—upon merely hearing this profound perfection of wisdom—have faith in it; and having had faith, will write it down, take it up, recite it, study it, and attend to it with wise reflection. Why is that?

For it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva heard this profound perfection of wisdom from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; having heard it, he took it up, retained it, recited it, studied it, and attended to it with his mind.
By that very root of merit and by those very mental attentions, he has been reborn here.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has passed away from among the Tuṣita gods and has been reborn here in the company of human beings should be known as being endowed with these very same qualities. Why is that?
