Because, Subhūti, by that bodhisattva mahāsattva [Maitreya]—the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya—[has been attended].
Having thoroughly inquired about this profound perfection of wisdom, he has been reborn here by virtue of that root of merit.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva did not hear this profound perfection of wisdom in the past,
and having heard it, did not inquire about it.

When he is reborn in the world of humans, there arises in him a state of doubt, a state of hesitation, and a dejection of mind; therefore, Subhūti, it is because this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has not heard this profound perfection of wisdom even in the past,
and having heard it, he did not inquire about it further.
When this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, there arises in him a state of doubt, a state of hesitation, and a dejection of mind;
and the same occurs regarding the perfection of concentration, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva [this has been done] from the past...
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) was neither heard nor inquired about in the past;
when this perfection of generosity is being spoken, he experiences hesitation, he experiences despondency, and his mind becomes cowed.
Moreover, Subhūti, by whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva [this has not been done] even from the perspective of the past..."

If internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, has not been heard or inquired about, then upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, there arises in him a state of doubt, a state of hesitation, and a dejection of mind. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is the case that by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, even from the past limit, has neither inquired about nor heard the four foundations of mindfulness.

Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, he becomes hesitant, he becomes paralyzed, and his mind becomes dejected. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has not previously heard, even from the past limit, of the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
And having heard it, he does not inquire further;
while this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, upon hearing it, he becomes hesitant, he becomes paralyzed, and his mind becomes cowed.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, even from the past limit, [has practiced] the four dhyānas...

The four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four noble truths, the five superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, all the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī, the ten bodhisattva stages,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have not been heard by them.
And having heard it, they do not inquire further;
upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they become filled with doubt, they become hesitant, and their minds become dejected.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is that bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment has not even been heard of in the past.
And having heard it, they do not inquire further;
upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being spoken, they become hesitant, they become stolid, and their minds become cowed.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom this profound *prajñāpāramitā* has not been heard even in the past, nor has it been inquired about—
If it has not been cultivated, not practiced extensively, and not attended to with proper mental focus—
whether for one day, two days, three days, four, five, six, or ten days—
then this profound perfection of wisdom is liable to be lost, and one becomes separated from the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
"It is so, Subhūti. For that bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom this profound perfection of wisdom has not been heard even in the past, nor inquired about, nor cultivated, nor practiced extensively,
nor properly attended to with right attention— for him there will be at one time a desire for this profound perfection of wisdom, and at another time no such desire."

Furthermore, he is withdrawn in this way by a wavering mind and becomes like a tuft of cotton wool. Moreover, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who has not long set out in the vehicle, who has not been taken hold of by spiritual friends, and who has not attended upon the perfectly awakened Buddhas. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should not...]
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* has been pointed out to him, but it has not been recited, nor has it been attended to with wise reflection, nor has he trained in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

He has not trained in the *dhyānapāramitā*, nor in the *vīryapāramitā*, nor in the *kṣāntipāramitā*, nor in the *śīlapāramitā*, nor in the *dānapāramitā*. He has not trained in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He was not trained in the applications of mindfulness;
he was not trained in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path;
nor was he trained in the five superknowledges, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, or the eight liberations.
He was not trained in the nine successive meditative attainments, nor in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he was not trained in the concentrations, nor in the gateways of mnemonic formulas, nor in the six supernormal knowledges.
They have not trained in the powers of a Tathāgata, nor in the grounds of self-confidence, nor in the analytical knowledges, nor in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
nor have they trained in the knowledge of all aspects. Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as having newly set out in the vehicle.

They are possessed only of a mere semblance of the Dharma, a mere semblance of faith, and a mere semblance of affection; they do not, however, honor this Perfection of Wisdom by writing it down, reciting it, teaching it, studying it, or attending to it with wise reflection, and so on, Subhūti, until such time as those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle [do so].
Or they will write down this perfection of wisdom,

but they will not teach it, nor recite it, nor attend to it with proper mental attention, nor will they benefit others through this profound perfection of wisdom. It is the same for the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of patience.

They will not be sustained by the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects. Nor will they experience this profound perfection of wisdom. Likewise, [they will not experience] the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.

In this way, until they have realized the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one of two stages should be expected for them—namely, either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because these sons of good family and daughters of good family have, from the very beginning, [not practiced] this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, [this perfection of wisdom] has not been written down, nor taught, nor recited, nor properly attended to; nor have they been sustained by this perfection of wisdom, nor has this profound perfection of wisdom been experienced by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Therefore, one should not expect those sons of good family or daughters of good family to attain the two stages. Thus, by way of the distinction in realization, this is the third moment regarding cessation.

Subhūti, it is just as if a sea-going ship were to break apart; in that case, those men who do not take hold of or grasp onto a piece of wood, a leather bag, or even a corpse should be known, Subhūti, as men who, before reaching their destination, will perish at sea.
On the other hand, those men who, while the sea-going ship has not yet broken apart, [take hold of] a piece of wood, a leather bag, or a corpse...
Subhūti, if they should think it ought to be taken up, or if they should take it up, you should know this: those men will not meet their end in the great ocean;
they will cross over the great ocean in safety.
They will remain unharmed, uninjured, and in safety upon dry land. In the very same way, Subhūti,
those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who are endowed with mere faith, mere serene confidence, and mere affection,
yet do not write down this perfection of wisdom, nor teach it, nor recite it, nor attend to it properly, nor take hold of it—
Subhūti, it should be understood that those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will fall into despondency midway along the path;
without having attained *sarvākārajñatā*, they will realize the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha,

so long as they do not write down, recite, or study the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity.

They will attend to it properly and will not become attached to it. Likewise, they will not [become attached] to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor to the four noble truths, nor to the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments;
nor to internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; nor to the eight liberations or the nine successive meditative attainments.

They will not write down, nor teach, nor recite, nor attend to with proper mental application, nor take up as their support the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor the superknowledges; nor all the meditative concentrations and attainments; nor all the doors of dhāraṇī; nor the ten powers; nor the grounds of self-confidence; nor the analytical knowledges; nor the unique qualities of a Buddha; and so on, up to the sūtras associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti, it should be understood that those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will fall into despondency midway along the path;
without having attained omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they will realize the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
However, Subhūti, for those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith and possess patience...
There is love, there is serenity, there is resolute intention, there is delight, there is conviction, there is zeal, there is renunciation,

and there is the non-abandonment of the burden in order to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and they will write down this perfection of wisdom, recite it, study it, rely upon it, and attend to it with wise reflection.

Behold, Subhūti, the faith, patience, love, serenity, high resolve, inclination, conviction, zeal, renunciation, and indefatigable persistence in the unsurpassed [enlightenment] of those sons and daughters of good family by whom the perfection of wisdom has been embraced, and by whom the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity have been embraced.

By those through whom internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations,
and the formless attainments have been embraced;
by those through whom the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the doors of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have been embraced.
Those by whom the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha have been grasped;
those by whom the gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas, as well as the five superknowledges, have been grasped;
and those by whom even the knowledge of all aspects has been grasped—they shall not fall into despondency along the way.

Having transcended the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and having brought sentient beings to maturity and purified the buddha-field, they will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, by way of the distinction of the object of focus, this is the fourth moment regarding cessation.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a woman or a man were to carry water in an unbaked jar.

Subhūti, it should be known that if one thinks water should be taken up with a vessel, this vessel will not endure for long; it will quickly perish and come to ruin. Why is that? Because the vessel is as yet unripened.

He will indeed reach the culmination of the stages. In the same way, Subhūti, although there may be faith, patience, affection, serene confidence, resolute intention, delight, conviction, zeal, renunciation, and an undaunted perseverance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment among sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, [they may still not reach the goal].
And they are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom, nor are they embraced by skill in means;
they are not embraced by the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity.
They are not grasped by internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
they are not grasped by the applications of mindfulness,
nor are they grasped by the right efforts.
They are not embraced by the bases of psychic power,
not embraced by the faculties,
and not embraced by the powers.
They are not embraced by the factors of enlightenment,
they are not embraced by the noble eightfold path,
and they are not embraced by the five supernormal powers.
They are not encompassed by the four dhyānas, nor by the four immeasurables; they are not encompassed by the four formless attainments, nor by the four noble truths.
They are not embraced by the eight liberations;
they are not embraced by the nine successive meditative attainments;
they are not embraced by the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Subhūti, it should be known that those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who are not sustained by the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to omniscience itself, will meet with disaster along the way.

They will fall into calamity. Why is that, Subhūti? Because what would constitute an obstacle for those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle—namely, the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha?
Subhūti, it is just as if a woman or a man were to carry water in a well-baked jar from a river, a well, a lake, a pond, or a fountain;
Subhūti, it should be known that this jar will reach home safely.
In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva there is faith, there is patience, and there is love—

There is serenity, there is resolute intention, there is interest, there is conviction, there is zeal, there is renunciation, and there is the non-laying-down-of-the-burden for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
provided that one is embraced by the perfection of wisdom.
He is embraced by skill in means,
embraced by the perfection of meditative concentration, embraced by the perfection of vigor, embraced by the perfection of patience, embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline,
and embraced by the perfection of generosity.

Subhūti, it should be understood that as long as [the bodhisattva] is sustained by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not fall into despondency midway— that is,

neither by the vehicle of the śrāvakas nor by the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas— but will, unhurt and uninjured, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Thus, by way of the excellence of the basis, this is the first [stage] on the path.
Subhūti, it is just as if a sea-going ship were not lashed together, not reinforced, and not secured, yet were launched upon the water.
Subhūti, it should be known that this ship will founder midway and meet with disaster;
the cargo will go one way and the ship another. In this way, that merchant should be known as unskilled in means.

He will be joined with great misfortune and excluded from great jewels. In the same way, Subhūti, although Bodhisattvas possess faith, possess patience, possess affection, possess clarity, possess resolute intention, possess inclination,
possess conviction, possess zeal, possess renunciation, and possess the quality of not laying down the burden for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

And they, being unencompassed by the perfection of wisdom and unencompassed by skill in means, are unencompassed by the perfection of concentration, unencompassed by the perfection of vigor, unencompassed by the perfection of patience, unencompassed by the perfection of ethical discipline, and unencompassed by the perfection of generosity;
they are unencompassed by all the modes of emptiness and unencompassed by the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
It is not encompassed by the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments; it is not encompassed by the noble truths; it is not encompassed by the eight liberations.
They are not encompassed by the nine successive meditative attainments;
they are not encompassed by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they are not encompassed by all the gateways of samādhi, dhāraṇīs, and superknowledges.

They are not sustained by the ten powers of a Tathāgata; they are not sustained by the grounds of self-confidence; they are not sustained by the analytical knowledges or the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Subhūti, it should be understood that as long as they are not embraced by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these bodhisattvas will meet with calamity midway on the path and will fall away from the great goal.
Namely, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is a heap of jewels.
Furthermore, Subhūti, what is the misfortune that befalls Bodhisattvas midway? It is namely the level of the Śrāvaka or the level of the Pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man of wise nature were on a well-reinforced ocean-going ship.

Subhūti, when it has been lowered into the water, the cargo has been loaded, and it is held steady by a favorable wind, you should know this: "This ocean-going ship will not meet with disaster along the way;
it will reach that destination for which it was intended."

And that merchant will obtain worldly jewels. In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva there is faith, patience, affection, clarity, resolute intention, delight, conviction, zeal, renunciation, and the quality of not laying down the burden regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
And he is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and embraced by skill in means;
he is embraced by the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity;

and he is embraced by all the emptinesses, by all the factors conducive to awakening, by all the meditative concentrations, by all the doors of dhāraṇī, and by the immeasurable meditations and formless attainments.
It is embraced by the noble truths;
it is embraced by the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments;
it is embraced by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He is embraced by the superknowledges;

he is embraced by the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; indeed, he is embraced by everything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not encounter misfortune on the way to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?

Subhūti, it is because for that bodhisattva mahāsattva there exists faith, there exists patience, there exists love, there exists clarity, there exists resolute intention, there exists preference, there exists conviction, and there exists zeal.
There is renunciation and the non-abandonment of the burden regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

and that [renunciation] is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and embraced by skill in means, and it is embraced by the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity. In this way, it continues until it is embraced by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
And that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka nor the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Thus, by way of the excellence of completeness, this is the second moment regarding the path.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a man two hundred years old by birth, decrepit, aged, and advanced in years, and some disease should arise in his body, whether caused by wind or by bile.
Or whether it be caused by phlegm or by a combination of all three humors—
what do you think,
Subhūti, would that man, being released, be able to climb out by himself?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, would that man rise up?
Subhūti said,
"Even though, Blessed One, that man might rise from his bed,"
And yet again, being powerless even to walk a distance of one *krośa*, he is worn out by that old age and those diseases;
and although he might rise from his bed,
he is nonetheless still unable to set out.

The Blessed One said: "In just this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses faith, possesses patience, possesses love, possesses clarity, possesses resolute intention, possesses inclination, possesses conviction, possesses zeal, possesses renunciation, and possesses the quality of not laying down the burden regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
And he is not embraced by the perfection of wisdom, nor is he embraced by skill in means;
he is not embraced by the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity;
he is not embraced by internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
It is not embraced by the foundations of mindfulness; it is not embraced by the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path;
it is not embraced by the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, or the noble truths;
it is not embraced by emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.

Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva, not being sustained by the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a buddha, will fall midway on the path onto the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because he is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom, nor sustained by skill in means, and so on, up to not being sustained by the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man, two hundred years of age by birth, decrepit, aged, and infirm;
he is exhausted by wind, bile, phlegm, or a combination of these humors.
Two strong men, supporting that weak man from both sides—on his left and right—would lift him up from his bed and say this:

"Come, my good man, wherever you wish; since you are supported by us, you will not fall in between until you have reached that destination. In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva there is faith, there is patience, there is love, there is serene confidence, there is resolute intention, and there is delight.
There is resolute faith, there is zeal, there is renunciation, and there is the non-laying-down of the burden regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and that bodhisattva is embraced by the perfection of wisdom, embraced by skill in means,
and embraced by the perfection of meditative concentration.
It is embraced by the perfection of vigor,
embraced by the perfection of patience, and embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti, it should be known that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is embraced by the perfection of generosity,
and is embraced by inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not fall away midway.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is capable of attaining that state, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because he is not separated from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, how is it that sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle— being unassisted by skillful means and the perfection of wisdom— fall into the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas?
The Blessed One replied:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, regarding this matter.
Here, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift from the very beginning, he gives it with a mental continuum fallen into the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine. When he guards his morality...”
Whatever patience he cultivates, whatever vigor he exerts, and whatever meditative concentration he enters,
Whatever wisdom he cultivates, he cultivates it with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine";
as he gives that gift, it occurs to him thus:
"I give this gift; I give this gift; I give this gift to this person; I observe moral discipline."
"I am observing this precept; I am virtuous; I am patient."
"I am accomplishing patience; I am patient;
I am exerting vigor."
"I have initiated vigor; I am possessed of vigor; I enter into meditative absorption."
"I meditate; I am one who possesses meditation;
I cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom."
"I am wise"; by means of that gift, he conceives [an ego], he conceives that gift, and he conceives, "The gift is mine"—
and likewise regarding ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.
By means of that wisdom, one conceives [of it]; one conceives of that wisdom; one conceives, "This is my wisdom. For what reason?
Because these conceptual constructions do not exist within the perfection of generosity. For what reason?
Because the perfection of generosity is indeed a non-perfection (āramitā).

Thus, these conceptual constructions do not exist in the perfection of ethical discipline, nor in the perfection of patience, nor in the perfection of vigor, nor in the perfection of meditative concentration, nor indeed in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because the perfection of wisdom is a "perfection" (pāramitā) [beyond limits], and that person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas knows neither the near shore (ara) nor the far shore (pāra).

Not embraced by the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—and thus not embraced even up to omniscience—he falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
he will not emerge into omniscience. And how does a bodhisattva become unskilled in means?

In this regard, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, from the very beginning, gives gifts without skillful means, guards ethical discipline without skillful means,
and accomplishes patience without skillful means, [they do not generate much merit].
He exerts effort without skillful means, enters meditative absorption without skillful means,
and cultivates wisdom without skillful means.
It occurs to him:
"I am giving a gift;
this is the gift I am giving."
"I maintain ethical discipline; I maintain this ethical discipline; I cultivate patience."
I accomplish this patience;
I exert vigor;
I exert this vigor.
"I enter into meditative absorption;
I enter into this meditative absorption;
I cultivate wisdom."
While cultivating this wisdom, he conceives of giving, conceives by means of giving, and conceives "giving is mine";
he conceives of morality, conceives by means of morality, and conceives "I am virtuous."

He conceives of patience; he conceives by means of patience; he conceives, "I am patient. He conceives of vigor; he conceives by means of vigor; he conceives, "Vigor is mine. He conceives of meditative concentration; he conceives by means of meditative concentration; he conceives, "I am possessed of meditative concentration."
One conceives of wisdom, one conceives by means of wisdom, and one conceives, "Wisdom is mine. For what reason?
Because no conceptual construction exists within the perfection of generosity as it is conceptualized by him. For what reason?
Because this perfection of generosity is, in fact, a non-perfection.
This is a crossing over, namely the perfection of ethical discipline; this is a crossing over, namely the perfection of patience;
this is a crossing over, namely the perfection of vigor.

This is a "far shore," namely, the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). Indeed, no conceptual construction exists within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) such as that by which one would construct [objects]. Why is that?
Because this perfection of wisdom is a "far shore," and that son of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle knows neither the near shore nor the far shore.

Not being embraced by the perfection of generosity, not being embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline, not being embraced by the perfection of patience, not being embraced by the perfection of vigor, and not being embraced by the perfection of meditative concentration—and thus continuing in this way up to not being embraced by the knowledge of all aspects—he falls either onto the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
he will not emerge into the knowledge of all aspects. For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva, through the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, [fails].
And being unaided, he falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. And how, Subhūti,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, supported by both the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, not fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha?
And how does he realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the very beginning when giving a gift,
does not give the gift with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine."
He does not guard ethical discipline with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine";
he does not cultivate patience with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine";
he does not exert vigor with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine."
He does not enter meditative absorption with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine," nor does he cultivate wisdom with a mind fallen into the notions of "I" and "mine";
it does not even occur to him thus:
"I am giving a gift; I give this gift; I give a gift to her.
"I am guarding my ethical discipline;
I guard this ethical discipline."
"In these I guard morality; I cultivate patience;
I cultivate this patience."
I cultivate patience for him;
I exert vigor.
I shall exert this vigor;
for the sake of this, I shall exert vigor; I shall enter into meditative absorption.
"I shall enter this meditative absorption," "I shall enter meditative absorption in these [states]," "I am cultivating wisdom."
"I cultivate this wisdom;
for the sake of this, I cultivate wisdom.
He does not conceive of giving, he does not conceive by means of giving, and he does not conceive, "Giving is mine."

He does not conceive of morality; he does not conceive by means of morality; he does not conceive "morality is mine. He does not conceive of patience; he does not conceive by means of patience; he does not conceive "patience is mine. He does not conceive of vigor; he does not conceive by means of vigor; he does not conceive "vigor is mine."
He does not conceive of meditation; he does not conceive by means of meditation; he does not conceive, "Meditation is mine.
He does not conceive of wisdom; he does not conceive by means of wisdom; he does not conceive, "Wisdom is mine. Why is that?
Because within the perfection of generosity, no conceptualization exists by which one might conceive.

In this way, no conceptualization exists within the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration by which one might conceive; likewise, no conceptualization exists within the perfection of wisdom by which one might conceive, for this perfection of giving is itself the perfection.

In this way, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration are all "this shore," namely, the perfection of wisdom.
And that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceive of either "this shore" or "the further shore";
he is embraced by the perfection of generosity.
When embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration,
and the perfection of wisdom, and so on up to being embraced by the knowledge of all aspects, one does not fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.

And he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and embraced by skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Thus, embraced by skill in means, he attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Thus, by way of this specific excellence of complete embrace, there is the third moment on the path.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how should a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?"
How should one train in the perfection of meditative concentration?
How should one train in the perfection of vigor?
How should one train in the perfection of patience?
How should one train in the perfection of ethical discipline?
How should one train in the perfection of generosity?
And how should one train in everything up to the unique qualities of a Buddha?

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom, who wishes to train in the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, and who wishes to train even up to the knowledge of all aspects, should attend upon and honor spiritual friends."
Those who are the teachers of this perfection of wisdom,
and the teachers of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity,
will teach this profound perfection of wisdom to him in this manner.

Come, son of good family, whatever gift you give, dedicate all of that toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; come, son of good family, whatever precept you observe, whatever patience you cultivate, [dedicate all of that toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment].
You exert vigor, you attain meditative concentration,
and you cultivate wisdom.
Dedicate all of that toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and you, son of good family, do not examine unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by way of form,
nor by way of feeling, nor by way of perception, nor by way of mental formations, nor by way of consciousness.
And you, son of good family, do not examine unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the perfection of giving;
do not examine it by means of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration,
or the perfection of wisdom.
Do not examine it by way of internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, nor internal-and-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
do not examine it by way of the applications of mindfulness, nor by way of the right efforts.
Do not examine it by means of the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path;

do not examine it by means of the five superknowledges; do not examine it by means of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments; do not examine it by means of the noble truths, the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative attainments.
Do not examine it by means of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

do not examine it by means of the meditative concentrations, nor the doors of dhāraṇī, nor the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the four grounds of self-confidence, nor the four analytical knowledges, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
And you, son of good family, do not grasp at anything from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment up to all-aspect omniscience. Why is that?
For form, when ungrasped, will attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; feeling, perception, and mental formations, when ungrasped, likewise [will attain it].
Ungrasped consciousness will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
ungrasped are the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration;
ungrasped is the perfection of wisdom.
Internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is untouched;
the applications of mindfulness are untouched;
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment are untouched.
The superknowledges are ungrasped;
the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are ungrasped;
the noble truths are ungrasped.
The eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments are untouched; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are untouched;
the gateways of concentration and dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four grounds of self-confidence are untouched.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are untouched, as are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*);

indeed, everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) remains untouched until one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, noble son, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, do not harbor desire for form.
Why is that?
For form, noble son, is free from longing; so too for feeling, perception, mental formations, and do not you, noble son, harbor longing for consciousness. Why is that?
For consciousness, noble son, is indeed free from longing;
therefore, noble son, do not harbor a longing for the perfection of generosity, and do not harbor a longing for the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.
Do not form a longing for the perfection of wisdom;
do not form a longing for internal emptiness; do not form a longing for anything up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

Do not conceive a longing for the applications of mindfulness; do not conceive a longing for the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, or the path; do not [conceive a longing] for the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments.
Do not conceive a longing for the noble truths;

do not conceive a longing for the eight liberations or the nine successive meditative attainments; do not conceive a longing for emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Do not harbor a longing for the gateways of all meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
nor, O son of good family, should you harbor a longing for omniscience. Why is that?
For omniscience, O son of good family, is indeed free from longing.

And you, son of good family, do not conceive a longing for the fruit of stream-entry; do not conceive a longing for the fruit of once-returning, nor for the fruit of non-returning, nor for arhatship, nor for solitary awakening; do not conceive a longing even for the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
"Do not conceive a longing for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, noble son, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Thus, Subhūti spoke regarding the specific characteristic of the fourth moment on the path, characterized by the absence of relishing:

“Indeed, Blessed One, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult, who aspire for unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment and desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment regarding phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.

For, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are doers of what is difficult, who long for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, desiring to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening within phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics."

Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have set out for the benefit of the world; Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have set out for the happiness of the world. Thinking, "We shall become a protection for the world," they have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. [Thinking], "We shall become a refuge for the world..."

Thinking, “We shall become a refuge for the world, a final resort for the world, islands for the world, leaders of the world, compassionate protectors, and a destination for the world,” they have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for the benefit of the world?

"In this regard, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having liberated beings from the five states of existence, establish them in the secure, fearless place of nirvāṇa. It is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment set out for the benefit of the world. Thus is their performance of benefit."
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for the happiness of the world?

Here, Subhūti, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas liberate all sentient beings from suffering, mental distress, and despair, and establish them in the fearless, secure state of nirvāṇa.

For it is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for the happiness of the worlds. Thus has been described their activity for the sake of happiness. And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment become a protection for the world? Here, Subhūti, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas rescue sentient beings from those sufferings that pertain to the realm of saṃsāra.
And they teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning those sufferings;

having heard that Dharma, they gradually attain final nirvana by means of the three vehicles. It is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a protection for the world.
Thus is the activity of providing protection.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment become a refuge for the world?

Here, Subhūti, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas [liberate beings] from the nature of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.

They liberate sentient beings from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; having liberated them, they establish them in the realm of nirvana without remainder. In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas become a refuge for the world.
Thus is the activity of providing refuge.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas become a refuge for sentient beings?

Here, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, teach the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may not cling to any phenomena. It is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas [become a refuge].
"Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they become a refuge for sentient beings.
Subhūti asked:
"But how, Blessed One, does there come to be a non-adherence to all phenomena?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that which is the non-adherence to form is the non-connection with form;
that which is the non-connection with form is the non-arising of form."
That which is the non-arising of form is the non-ceasing of form;
that which is the non-ceasing of form is the non-adherence to form;
[and so it is] for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, that which is the non-adherence of consciousness is the non-connection of consciousness;
that which is the non-connection of consciousness is the non-arising of consciousness;
that which is the non-arising of consciousness is the non-ceasing of consciousness.

That which is the non-cessation of consciousness is the non-adherence to consciousness. Likewise, it is so regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination;

regarding all the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Subhūti, that which is the non-attachment to the superknowledges, to all meditative concentrations, to all gateways of dhāraṇī, to the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha— that is the non-connection with omniscience;
that which is the non-connection with omniscience is the non-arising of omniscience.
That which is the non-arising of all-aspect omniscience is the non-cessation of all-aspect omniscience;

that which is the non-cessation of all-aspect omniscience is the non-adherence of all-aspect omniscience. It is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-adherence to all phenomena by all sentient beings.
Thus is the practice of providing shelter.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas who desire to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment become the refuge of the world?
Here, Subhūti, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas teach the Dharma to sentient beings in this way:
That which is the limit of form is not form;
that which is the limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
That which is the further shore of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination is not those aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination;
that which is the further shore of all perfections is not those perfections;
that which is the further shore of all emptinesses is not those emptinesses.
That which is the limit of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*) is not those factors conducive to enlightenment;

likewise, [the limit] of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges is not those [qualities];
that which is the limit of the unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) is not those unique qualities of a buddha.
To the extent that there is no further shore beyond omniscience, that is not omniscience;
and as it is with form, Subhūti, so it is with all dharmas, and so it is with omniscience.
Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, form is just as all dharmas are, then surely omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) has not been fully realized by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever on the far shore of form, nor of feeling, nor of perception, nor of mental formations.

There is no conceptualization whatsoever on the further shore of consciousness. There is no conceptualization whatsoever on the further shore of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or the factors of dependent origination. There is no conceptualization whatsoever on the further shore of the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including the further shore of the knowledge of all aspects. "This is form," [is a conceptualization].

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— up to: "these are the aggregates, these are the elements, these are the sense bases, this is dependent origination, these are the factors of dependent origination, these are the perfections, these are the emptinesses, these are the factors conducive to awakening, these are the noble truths, these are the superknowledges, and these are the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments."

"These are the gateways to the liberations, the meditative attainments, and the dhāraṇīs; these are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; these are the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
this is the knowledge of all aspects."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
For indeed, Subhūti, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever on the far shore of form."

There is no conceptual construction whatsoever on the far shore of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Likewise, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever on the far shore of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination;

nor is there any conceptual construction on the far shore of the perfections, all the modes of emptiness, the factors conducive to enlightenment, or the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.
There is no conceptualization whatsoever on the far shore of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha;

likewise, there is no conceptualization whatsoever on the far shore of even the knowledge of all aspects. Yet, Subhūti, is it not difficult for Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, that they contemplate such dharmas as these and yet do not become disheartened?

"In this way these dharmas are to be fully awakened to by me; and having thus fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, we shall proclaim these dharmas as so peaceful and so sublime. It is in this way, Subhūti, that bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, become the ultimate refuge for the world. Thus ends the section on acting as a true refuge.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become islands for the world?
It is just as, Subhūti, those places which are surrounded by water—whether in great rivers or in the great oceans—are called "islands," Subhūti.
In the same way, Subhūti, it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, [and consciousness].

Subhūti, consciousness is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits. In the same way, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
Likewise, the perfection of generosity is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits;
likewise, the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
Internal emptiness is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits; external emptiness is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits;

internal-external emptiness is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits; and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits;
the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
The immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits; the noble truths are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits;
and the doors of liberation, attainments, and dhāraṇīs are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
The superknowledges of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits;

the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities are delimited by the prior and subsequent limits; indeed, even the knowledge of all aspects is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits. Subhūti, by this delimitation of the prior and subsequent limits, all phenomena are delimited.
And whatever, Subhūti, is the delimitation of the prior and posterior limits of all phenomena—

this is peace, this is sublime, this is the true nature of things; namely, the non-apprehension of emptiness, the phenomenon of delimitation, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.

In this way, Subhūti, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas become islands for the world by teaching all phenomena as delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
And how, Subhūti, does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a light for the world?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, illuminating with wisdom the darkness of delusion and shattering the cataracts of the gloom of ignorance for those beings who have long been enveloped by the shell of the egg of ignorance and overcome by obscurity—

thus, Subhūti, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a light for the world. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a bearer of the torch and a maker of light for sentient beings?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, reveals to sentient beings the true meaning, in accordance with reality, of those discourses associated with the six perfections and the four means of attraction.
And therein he enjoins, settles, and establishes sentient beings;
for in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, becomes a bearer of the torch and a maker of light for sentient beings.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a caravan leader for sentient beings?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, teaches the single path to those beings who have set out upon wrong paths and are headed toward the four destinies— for the purification of beings, for the transcending of sorrow and calamity,
for the disappearance of suffering and dejection, for the realization of the noble Dharma, and for the direct realization of nirvāṇa.

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, becomes a caravan leader for sentient beings. Thus is his function as an island.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a guide for the world?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated great compassion toward the multitude of sentient beings, [strives for] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment...
Having attained perfect awakening, he teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of form;
he teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this way, he teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom. He teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the perfection of skillful means, the perfection of aspiration, the perfection of power, and the perfection of gnosis.

He teaches and elucidates the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, and non-purification of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
and likewise for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, and the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.
He teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

He teaches and proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatānimittāpraṇihita*). It is the same for all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).

He teaches and fully elucidates the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of all the gateways of dhāraṇī, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the knowledge of all aspects.

He teaches and elucidates the Dharma. He teaches and elucidates the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of pratyekabodhi. He teaches and elucidates the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the fruit of stream-entry. Likewise, he [teaches and elucidates the Dharma] for the sake of the non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purification of the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.

He teaches and fully illuminates the Dharma. For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, becomes a guide for sentient beings. Thus is described the activity of being a guide.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment become a refuge for sentient beings?
In this regard, Subhūti, after having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a refuge for sentient beings who have fallen into states of delusion.
He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "Form has space as its ultimate nature; so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations."

He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "Consciousness has the nature of space. He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "The aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination have the nature of space. In this same way, he teaches all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments.

He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "The noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the supernormal powers, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have the nature of space. He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "Omniscience has the nature of space. Form-emptiness has no coming or going; it does not come.
He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying that feeling, perception, and mental formations do not go;
he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying that the emptiness of consciousness, which has neither coming nor going, neither comes nor goes.

He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "The emptiness of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination is without coming or going; it neither comes nor goes.

Likewise, he teaches that the emptiness of all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs is without coming or going; it neither comes nor goes.
He teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying, "It does not go.

That emptiness of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path—being without coming or going—it neither comes nor goes; thus he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings. The emptiness of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments is likewise without coming or going.
She teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "It neither comes nor goes. Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, and emptiness itself are without coming or going;

she teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "It neither comes nor goes. The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and their emptiness are without coming or going; she teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying: "It neither comes nor goes. The emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects is without coming or going.

He teaches the Dharma to beings, saying, "It neither comes nor goes. For in this way, Subhūti, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a refuge for beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all phenomena have emptiness as their destination; they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of emptiness is apprehended. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the signless as their destination; they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of the signless is apprehended. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the wishless as their destination; they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived in that which is wishless. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have non-conditioning as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived in that which is unconditioned. Thus, Subhūti, all phenomena have non-arising as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. For what reason?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of non-arising is apprehended. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have non-cessation as their destination; they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of non-cessation is apprehended. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have non-affliction and non-purification as their destination; they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going is perceived for that which is without affliction or purification. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the nature of being unborn and non-existent; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going is perceived for that which is unborn and non-existent. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the nature of a dream; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, neither the coming nor the going of a dream is apprehended. Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of an illusion; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, neither the coming nor the going of an illusion is apprehended. Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of an echo; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of an echo is perceived. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have the nature of a reflection; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of a reflection is perceived. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have the nature of a magical creation; they do not transcend that nature. And why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of a magical creation is apprehended. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have the nature of a mirage; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of a mirage is apprehended. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have the nature of a city of the Gandharvas; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of a city of the Gandharvas is perceived. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have an infinite and boundless course; they do not transcend that course. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of the infinite and boundless is perceived. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have a course that is without extraction or re-extraction; they do not transcend that course.
For what reason?

Subhūti, for neither coming nor going is perceived in that which is without extraction or re-extraction. Subhūti, all dharmas are without coming; they do not deviate from that course. For what reason?

Subhūti, for neither coming nor going is perceived in that which is without coming. Subhūti, all dharmas have a course that is without gathering-in or casting-out; they do not deviate from that course. For what reason?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived for that which is without gathering or dispersing. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have as their movement non-union and non-separation, non-adherence and non-detachment; they do not transcend that movement. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived for that which is without union and non-separation, without adherence and non-detachment. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the self as their movement; they do not transcend that movement. That...
For indeed, Subhūti, neither the coming nor the going of a self is apprehended. Subhūti, all dharmas have the destiny of a sentient being;

Subhūti, all dharmas have the destiny of a living being, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, a seer, an arouser, and an originator; they do not transcend that destiny.
Why is that?

For, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, a sentient being does not exist; a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, a seer, an arouser, or an originator do not exist.

How then could there be for them any coming or going? For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of permanence; they do not deviate from that state. For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of happiness; they do not deviate from that state.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the self as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
for, Subhūti, all dharmas have purity as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
For, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, permanence, pleasure, self, and purity do not exist;
how then could there be any coming or going for these? Indeed, Subhūti, all phenomena have impermanence as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
all phenomena have suffering as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination.
For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the nature of selflessness; they do not transcend that nature.
For all dharmas, Subhūti, have the nature of impurity; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, what is impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure does not exist.

How much less, Subhūti, could there be any coming or going for these? For all dharmas, Subhūti, have passion as their destination; they do not transcend that destination. All dharmas, Subhūti, have hatred as their destination; they do not transcend that destination. All dharmas, Subhūti, have delusion as their destination; they do not transcend that destination.
Subhūti, all dharmas indeed follow the course of views; they do not transcend that course. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, a thing produced by views does not exist; how then could there be things produced by views?
How much less could there be any coming or going? For, Subhūti, all phenomena have suchness as their destination, and they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, neither a coming nor a going of suchness is apprehended;
for, Subhūti, all phenomena have the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as their destination, and they do not deviate from that destination.
For all phenomena, Subhūti, have the limit of reality as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
for all phenomena, Subhūti, have equality as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
for all phenomena, Subhūti, have the inconceivable realm as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived for the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), equality, or the inconceivable realm. For all phenomena, Subhūti, have a motionless course;
they do not deviate from that course. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, neither coming nor going is perceived for a phenomenon that is immovable.
Thus, this is the activity of bringing about the departure via the three vehicles and the direct realization of their fruits.
Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of form; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, form does not exist at all.
How much less, then, could there be any coming or going for it?
Subhūti, all phenomena have consciousness as their destination; they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, consciousness does not exist.

How much less, then, could there be any coming or going for it? For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the same destination as the aggregates, the elements, the sense-fields, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination; they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, the aggregates, the elements, the sense-fields, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination do not exist at all.
How much less, Subhūti, will there be any coming or going for these? For all dharmas have the perfection of giving as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the perfection of giving does not exist in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be any coming or going for it? In the same way, Subhūti, all dharmas have the perfection of ethical discipline as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination.
Subhūti, all dharmas have the perfection of patience as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
Subhūti, all dharmas have the perfection of vigor as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
Subhūti, all dharmas have the perfection of meditation as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination.
Subhūti, all dharmas have the perfection of wisdom as their destination, for they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
Subhūti, because the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom do not exist in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be a coming or a going of them? Subhūti, all dharmas have internal emptiness as their destination, for they do not transcend that destination.
Subhūti, all dharmas have the nature of reaching the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; they do not transcend that nature. Why is that?
Subhūti, because internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, does not exist in an ultimate sense.
How, then, could there be any coming or going for these? For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the *smṛtyupasthānas* as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the *smṛtyupasthānas* do not exist in an ultimate sense;

how, then, could there be any coming or going for them? In the same way, Subhūti, all dharmas have the *samyakprahāṇas*, *ṛddhipādas*, *indriyas*, *balas*, *bodhyaṅgas*, and the *mārga* as their destination, and they [do not transcend] that destination.
They do not transcend them. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path do not exist in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be any coming or going for them? Their destination is the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.

For indeed, Subhūti, all dharmas do not transcend that destination. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have as their destination the noble truths, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs; they do not transcend that destination. For all dharmas, Subhūti, have as their destination the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
For, Subhūti, all dharmas do not exist in an ultimate sense;
how, then, could there be any coming or going for them? Subhūti, all dharmas have the fruit of stream-entry as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination.
Subhūti, all dharmas have the fruit of once-returning as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the state of the fruit of non-returning as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination;
for, Subhūti, all dharmas have the state of arhatship and pratyekabuddhahood as their destination, and they do not transcend that destination. Why is that?
For, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas do not exist;
how then could there be any coming or going for them? Subhūti, all dharmas have as their destination unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and they do not deviate from that destination. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, unexcelled, perfect enlightenment does not exist.
"From where, then, will there be its coming or its going?
Subhūti said:
"Lord, who will have faith in this profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who will have practiced previously for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; who will have performed services under previous Victors; and who will have ripened roots of merit under previous Victors—"

They will have attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and being sustained by spiritual friends, they will have resolute faith in this profound perfection of wisdom. This is the activity of their destination; this is the characteristic of their activity.
Subhūti said: "But, Blessed One, what will be the marks, the forms, the signs, and the natures of those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who will understand this profound perfection of wisdom?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, will have a nature that is secluded from the discipline of passion;
Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, will have a nature that is secluded from the discipline of hatred and delusion. Thus is their nature secluded from the afflictions."
Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have a nature free from the marks of passion;

Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have a nature free from the marks of hatred and delusion. Thus, their nature will be one of freedom from those marks; Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have a nature free from the signs of passion.

And, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have as their intrinsic nature the discernment of the signs of hatred and delusion. Thus, they will have as their intrinsic nature the discernment of those signs; and, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have as their intrinsic nature the state of being secluded from passion and the absence of passion;
