and, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will have as their intrinsic nature the state of being secluded from hatred and the absence of hatred, and from delusion and the absence of delusion.
"Those who will have faith in this profound perfection of wisdom—
Subhūti asked:
'Blessed One, what will be the destiny of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas?'"
"Who will understand this profound perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, will have reached the state of the knowledge of all aspects."
“Those who shall understand this profound perfection of wisdom—
Subhūti said:
‘O Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have reached the state of omniscience become the refuge for all sentient beings.’”
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Subhūti, who have reached the state of omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), will become the refuge for all sentient beings."
“Those who will have faith in this profound perfection of wisdom.
Thus, having spoken on the nature of the distinction between the discordant factors and their antidotes,
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have donned this armor, thinking ‘We shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa,’ will be doers of what is difficult; for herein neither a sentient being nor the designation ‘sentient being’ is perceived.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is.

Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Subhūti, will be doers of what is difficult, who have donned this armor, thinking: 'We shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Subhūti, that armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not bound to form."
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, form does not exist at all;
neither does the bodhisattva nor the bodhisattva’s armor. Therefore, Subhūti, it is said that this armor is not bound to form.
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—moreover, Subhūti, that armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not connected with consciousness. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, consciousness does not exist, nor does the bodhisattva, nor the bodhisattva’s armor.

Therefore, Subhūti, it is said that this armor is not connected with consciousness. This armor is not connected with the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), the sense-bases (āyatanas), or the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpādāṅgas). Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, as well as the factors of dependent origination, are absolutely [non-existent].

Or rather, they do not exist, nor does the bodhisattva, nor the bodhisattva’s armor. Therefore, Subhūti, it is said that this armor is neither connected to dependent origination nor connected to the factors of dependent origination. In this way, Subhūti, in detail, this armor is not connected to a self, a being, a soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.
As long as, Subhūti, this armor is not connected with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, in an ultimate sense, omniscience does not exist, nor does the bodhisattva, nor the bodhisattva’s armor; therefore it is so called.

"As long as this armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not bound to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), so indeed is this armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva bound to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). For by those who practice this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and have thus donned this armor, [it is bound to all phenomena]."
"In this way we shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa. Subhūti, concerning the nature of this difficulty, said:
"Blessed One, regarding this bodhisattva mahāsattva who thinks, 'I shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa'..."
For one thus armored with the armor [of resolve], two states are not to be expected: the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.

It is impossible, O Blessed One, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus armored with the thought, "I shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa," should fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
This is not possible. Why is that?
Because the armor donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva for the sake of sentient beings is not bound by limits. Thus, its nature is exclusively [altruistic].
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Furthermore, Subhūti, with what purpose in mind do you say this:
that for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor, while practicing this profound perfection of wisdom,
neither of these two states— the level of a śrāvaka nor the level of a pratyekabuddha— is to be expected?
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, Blessed One, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has not donned the armor for the sake of limited beings;
rather, Blessed One, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the armor for the sake of the parinirvāṇa of all beings and for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
It is not for the sake of limited beings that the great armor has been donned by the bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is for the sake of the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings, and for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*), that the bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is profound; it is not to be cultivated by anyone, nor anywhere, nor in any manner. Why is that? Because it is not..."

For indeed, Blessed One, in this profound perfection of wisdom, the perfect accomplishment of any dharma whatsoever is not apprehended— neither one who might cultivate, nor that which might be cultivated, nor that by means of which one might cultivate.
This cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is a cultivation of space.
The cultivation of all dharmas is this, namely, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

the cultivation of non-existence is this, namely, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation of non-appropriation is this, namely, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; it is the cultivation and the elimination of cultivation, O Blessed One, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, to whom does this cultivation and non-cultivation belong, namely, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:

“Blessed One, this cultivation and non-cultivation of form is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; Blessed One, this cultivation and non-cultivation of feeling, perception, and mental formations is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; Blessed One, this cultivation and non-cultivation of consciousness is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
Blessed One, this cultivation and non-cultivation of a self is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”

This cultivation and non-cultivation of a being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer—this, namely, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

this cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of generosity—this, namely, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline—this, namely, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of patience—this, namely, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of vigor is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of meditation is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

This cultivation and analytical deconstruction of internal emptiness is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; up to and including this cultivation and analytical deconstruction of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

this cultivation and analytical deconstruction of the applications of mindfulness is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; and this cultivation and analytical deconstruction of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and non-cultivation of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

this cultivation and non-cultivation of the gateways to liberation, the meditative absorptions, the attainments, and the gateways to the dhāraṇīs is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truths is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the ten powers is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

This cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of stream-entry is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of once-returning is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the fruit of non-returning is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and elimination of the state of arhatship is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

this cultivation and elimination of the state of a pratyekabuddha is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this cultivation and elimination of the state of a bodhisattva is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"O Blessed One, this cultivation and non-cultivation of all-aspect omniscience is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, this cultivation and deconstruction of form is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and deconstruction of feeling, perception, and mental formations is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and deconstruction of consciousness is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

This cultivation and non-cultivation of the aggregates is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this cultivation and non-cultivation of the elements is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the sense bases is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of dependent origination is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; the cultivation and non-cultivation of the factors of dependent origination is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation and non-cultivation of the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling conditioned by eye-contact is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, the cultivation and non-cultivation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects; of mental consciousness, mental contact, and the feeling conditioned by mental contact—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation and non-cultivation of the earth element—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation and non-cultivation of the water element—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and elimination of the fire element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and elimination of the air element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and elimination of the space element is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this [is] the cultivation and elimination of the consciousness element.

That is to say, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the elimination of ignorance; that is to say, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the elimination of formative factors; that is to say, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the elimination of consciousness.
This is the cultivation and elimination of name-and-form;
this is the cultivation and elimination of the six sense bases;
this is the cultivation and elimination of contact.
This is the cultivation and elimination of sensation; this is the cultivation and elimination of craving; this is the cultivation and elimination of clinging.

This cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the elimination of existence; it is the cultivation of the elimination of birth; it is the cultivation of the elimination of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair. In this way, it is the cultivation of the elimination of all the perfections. What is this? It is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
This cultivation and non-cultivation of all emptinesses is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
this cultivation and non-cultivation of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

This cultivation and non-cultivation of the noble truths, the superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the doors of liberation, the concentrations, the meditative attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

this cultivation and non-cultivation of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific understandings, and the unique qualities of a Buddha is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
up to and including this cultivation and non-cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, Subhūti, in this profound perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be examined as being irreversible by way of the nature of non-apprehension.
Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not become attached to this profound perfection of wisdom should be examined as an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not become attached to the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity should be regarded as an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Likewise, one who does not become attached to internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, [should be regarded as such].
One should not become attached to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening;
one should not become attached to the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments;
one should not become attached to the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, or to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
One should not become attached to the gateways of meditative concentration and dhāraṇīs, nor to the superknowledges;
one should not become attached to the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not become attached to the knowledge of all aspects is irreversible.
He is a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom,
does not regard the words spoken by others or the counsels of others as being essential or authoritative, is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who, practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom, does not proceed by means of another’s faith, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible. Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who,
practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom, is not carried away by thought-moments accompanied by passion, nor by those accompanied by hatred or delusion.
By these productions of the thought of awakening, that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be examined.

Any irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva who, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, does not tremble, is not terrified, does not fall into fear, and neither shrinks back nor cowers— [he is to be known as irreversible].
And his mind does not turn back, nor is he ever separated from the perfection of wisdom;
he rejoices at hearing the perfection of wisdom, and having heard it, he takes it up, masters it, retains it, recites it, attends to it properly, and practices for the sake of suchness.
Subhūti, it should be known that this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva was likewise [endowed with these qualities] in the past.
This profound perfection of wisdom has been heard, taken up, mastered, retained, recited, properly attended to, and practiced for the sake of suchness. Why is that?
Because an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells here in this profound perfection of wisdom.
When this is being taught, he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror; he does not shrink back, nor does he become despondent;

his mind does not turn away, nor does it retreat. Furthermore, having heard what follows, he takes it up, masters it, retains it, recites it, attends to it with wise reflection, and practices in accordance with suchness. This is the nature of non-attachment.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught here,
does not tremble, does not become terrified, does not fall into fear, does not shrink back, and does not become despondent— "
"The mind becomes averse;
how, Blessed One, should this profound perfection of wisdom be investigated by that bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom should be investigated by that bodhisattva mahāsattva with a mental continuum inclined toward the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, how does the investigation of the profound perfection of wisdom occur for a bodhisattva mahāsattva through a mental continuum inclined toward the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is by means of a mental continuity inclined toward emptiness, sloping toward emptiness, and leaning toward emptiness, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices here in this profound perfection of wisdom; and by means of a mental continuity, Subhūti, inclined toward the signless, sloping toward the signless, and leaning toward the signless."
Subhūti, by means of a mental continuity that inclines toward the wishless, leans toward the wishless, and tends toward the wishless; Subhūti,
by means of a mental continuity that inclines toward space, leans toward space, and tends toward space.
Subhūti, as long as there is a continuity that inclines toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), flows toward the limit of reality, and tends toward the limit of reality;

Subhūti, as long as there is a continuity that inclines toward the absence of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*), flows toward the absence of volitional construction, and tends toward the absence of volitional construction—in this way, there is investigation into this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti, it is through a continuity that inclines toward dreams and inclines toward emanations [that this occurs].
Subhūti, by means of a continuum inclined toward illusion, inclined toward a mirage; Subhūti, by means of a continuum inclined toward an echo, inclined toward an optical illusion;
Subhūti, by means of a continuum inclined toward a reflection, and inclined toward a city of the Gandharvas—in this profound perfection of wisdom, there is such investigation.
Subhūti said: "As the Blessed One has thus spoken:
'With a mental continuity that inclines toward emptiness, leans toward emptiness, and tends toward emptiness, [one should train] here in this profound perfection of wisdom.'"

Subhūti, for bodhisattva mahāsattvas, there is an investigation [of phenomena] by way of a continuity that is signless, wishless, like space, unarisen, unceasing, unborn, non-existent, without affliction, without purification, suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, inconceivability, the limit of reality, the unconditioned, and like a dream, a magical creation, an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, a city of the gandharvas— low-lying, sloping, and inclining toward [the ultimate]. It is in this way, Subhūti, that for bodhisattva mahāsattvas, there is an investigation here in this profound [perfection of wisdom].
There is an investigation into the perfection of wisdom. But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva also investigate form? Does he investigate feeling, perception, and mental formations?
Does he also investigate consciousness?
Does he thus investigate the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination?
Does he investigate all the perfections, all the emptinesses, and all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, and dhāraṇīs?
Does he investigate the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening?
Does he investigate the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the supernormal powers?
Does he investigate the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha?
"Furthermore, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva investigate even up to the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
"No, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not investigate form."
He does not investigate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not investigate the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination;
he does not investigate any of the perfections or any of the emptinesses.

He does not analytically investigate the factors conducive to enlightenment; he does not analytically investigate the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, or the noble truths;
nor does he analytically investigate the doors of liberation, meditative absorptions, attainments, or the dhāraṇīs.
He does not conceptualize the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha;
nor, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva conceptualize anything up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, omniscience is not made by anyone, it has not come from anywhere, it has not gone anywhere, nor is it situated anywhere; it is neither located in a place nor located in a region, and it has no numerical designation.
Neither going nor coming is perceived;
and that which has neither number nor going nor coming perceived cannot be fully awakened to by anyone.

It is not by means of form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; not by means of the aggregates, nor the elements, nor the sense bases, nor dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination;

not by means of generosity, nor ethical discipline, nor patience, nor vigor, nor meditative concentration, nor wisdom, up to and including the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), can one fully awaken. Why is that?
Because form itself is omniscience.
Feeling itself, perception itself, mental formations themselves, and consciousness itself are omniscience. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that which is the suchness of form, [is the same as the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness].

That which is the suchness of omniscience and that which is the suchness of the Buddha-qualities— this is one single suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated; and it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and that which is the suchness of consciousness.
The suchness of omniscience and the suchness of the Buddha-dharmas are one and the same suchness— non-dual and indivisible;
and the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination is likewise.
The suchness of omniscience and the suchness of the Buddha-qualities are one and the same suchness— non-dual and indivisible—
and so too is the suchness of the aggregates, the elements, the sense-bases, and the factors of dependent origination.

The suchness of omniscience and the suchness of the Buddha-qualities are one and the same suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated. Likewise, the suchness of the perfections and the suchness of emptiness—
That which is the suchness of the factors conducive to enlightenment,

that which is the suchness of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, that which is the suchness of the noble truths, and that which is the suchness of the gateways of concentration, meditative attainment, and dhāraṇī—
That which is the suchness of the gateways to liberation, that which is the suchness of the superknowledges,
and that which is the suchness of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges;
The suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha,
the suchness of omniscience, and the suchness of the Buddha-qualities— all this is a single suchness, non-dual and indivisible.

Then indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, having taken divine sandalwood powders and having taken divine blue lotuses, white water lilies, red lotuses, fragrant lotuses, māndārava flowers, and mahāmāndārava flowers, scattered them toward where the Blessed One was; and having scattered them, (PSP_4:115)
They approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of reasoning and inaccessible to logic, peaceful, and subtle."
The awakening of the Tathāgatas— worthy ones, perfectly enlightened ones— is to be realized by those who are skillful, wise, and discerning, and it is contrary to the entire world;
for therein the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach this very Prajñāpāramitā, which is so profound and so subtle.
Form itself is omniscience, and omniscience itself is form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are omniscience, and omniscience itself is consciousness. For what reason?
That which is the suchness of form and that which is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects— this is one single suchness, non-dual and indivisible; and that which is the suchness of feeling...
And that which is the suchness of perception,
that which is the suchness of mental formations,
and that which is the suchness of consciousness—

And that suchness of the knowledge of all aspects is this very same single suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated. Thus, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination are themselves the knowledge of all aspects, and the knowledge of all aspects itself is the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination. For what reason?
Because that which is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination—

And that suchness of the knowledge of all aspects is this very same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. Likewise, from the suchness of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, up to the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, it is this very same suchness—non-dual and indivisible.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm:
"So it is, sons of gods; so it is.
Form itself, sons of gods, is omniscience, and omniscience itself, sons of gods, is form;
[so too are] feeling, perception, and mental formations."
"O sons of the gods, consciousness itself is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and omniscience itself, O sons of the gods, is consciousness. Why is that?

Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and the suchness of omniscience are one and the same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. And so too is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of mental formations."

The suchness of consciousness and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are one and the same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. In this way, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination are themselves the knowledge of all aspects; the knowledge of all aspects itself is the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination. Why is that? Because the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects are one and the same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. The perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) itself is the knowledge of all aspects.
The very knowledge of all aspects is the perfection of generosity;
likewise, it is the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
O sons of the gods, the perfection of wisdom itself is omniscience; O sons of the gods, omniscience itself is the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because the suchness of the perfection of giving and the suchness of omniscience are one and the same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. It is the same for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.

The suchness of the perfection of wisdom and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects are one and the same suchness, non-dual and indivisible. Internal emptiness itself is the knowledge of all aspects, and the knowledge of all aspects itself is internal emptiness;

likewise, up to and including, the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence itself is the knowledge of all aspects, and the knowledge of all aspects itself is the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. For what reason is that?

The suchness of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence and the suchness of all-aspect omniscience are one and the same suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated. The foundations of mindfulness are themselves all-aspect omniscience, and all-aspect omniscience itself is the foundations of mindfulness; likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are themselves all-aspect omniscience, and all-aspect omniscience itself is the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path. That...
For what reason?

That which is the suchness of the applications of mindfulness and that which is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects are one and the same suchness, non-dual and indivisible. Likewise, that which is the suchness of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, and that which is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, are one and the same suchness, non-dual and indivisible. The immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are themselves the knowledge of all aspects; the knowledge of all aspects itself is the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.
For what reason?

That which is the suchness of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments, and that which is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects—this is one single suchness, non-dual and indivisible.

In the same way, it applies to the noble truths, emptiness, the signless, the wishless, the superknowledges, the liberations, the concentrations, the attainments, the doors of the dhāraṇīs, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.

The unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are themselves the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects is itself the unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is that?

Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of the unique qualities of a Buddha and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects are one and the same suchness—non-dual and indivisible. It is the same for the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and the state of a pratyekabuddha.
The Buddhas themselves are the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects itself is the Buddhas. For what reason?

That which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Blessed Buddhas and that which is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects—this is one single suchness, non-dual and indivisible. This too, O sons of gods, is so.
Perceiving the necessity of the matter, the Tathāgata inclined his mind toward remaining with little exertion rather than teaching the Dharma. Why is that?

Because this Dharma—the awakening of the Tathāgatas—is indeed profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond logic, outside the sphere of reasoning, peaceful, subtle, to be realized by the wise and the learned, and contrary to the entire world.

It has not been fully awakened to by anyone, it was never fully awakened to, nor will it ever be fully awakened to anywhere; this is that profundity of phenomena, this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), wherein neither the occurrence of duality nor the occurrence of non-duality exists.
Such is the intrinsic nature of the objective support (*ālambana-svabhāva*).
O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because space is profound;

it is profound, O sons of the gods, because suchness is profound, because the realm of phenomena is profound, because the limit of reality is profound, and because the inconceivable realm of phenomena is profound;

it is profound because it is infinite and boundless, because there is neither coming nor going, because it is the sameness of non-arising and non-ceasing, and because it is the sameness of non-defilement and non-purification.

O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the equality of non-conditioning and the profundity of the self; it is profound because of the profundity of the sentient being, the living being, the creature, the nourished being, the person, the individual, the human, the man, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer. O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of form;
O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of the aggregates, the profundity of the elements, the profundity of the sense bases, the profundity of dependent origination, and the profundity of the factors of dependent origination; O sons of the gods, it is profound because of the profundity of the perfection of generosity, the profundity of the perfection of ethical discipline, the profundity of the perfection of patience, the profundity of the perfection of vigor, the profundity of the perfection of meditative concentration, and the profundity of the perfection of wisdom.
"O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of internal emptiness, up to the profundity of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;

O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of the applications of mindfulness, and because of the profundity of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path."

O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of the immeasurable meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the noble truths (*āryasatya*), emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it is profound because of the profundity of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the doors of all liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; and it is profound because of the profundity of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
"O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound because of the profundity of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
When this was said, the sons of the gods said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this Dharma that is being taught is contrary to the entire world. For what reason?"

"Blessed One, this Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping form, nor for the sake of non-grasping; it is not taught for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor for the sake of non-grasping."

The Dharma is taught neither for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of not grasping the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination. Likewise, the Dharma is taught neither for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of not grasping all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
The Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping all phenomena, nor for the sake of non-grasping;

this Dharma, Blessed One, is not taught for the sake of grasping the fruit of stream-entry, nor for the sake of non-grasping. Likewise, it is not for the sake of the fruit of once-returning, nor for the fruit of non-returning, nor for arhatship, nor for pratyekabuddhahood, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Dharma is taught neither for grasping nor for non-grasping, yet the world proceeds in grasping, thinking: "Form is mine,
feeling is mine, perception is mine, mental formations are mine, consciousness is mine."
"My aggregates, my elements, my sense bases; I am dependent origination, I am dependently originated;
my giving, I am the giver; my morality, I am the moral one; my patience, I am the patient one; my vigor, I am the vigorous one; my meditation, I am the meditator; my wisdom, I am the wise one."

"Internal emptiness is mine; I cultivate internal emptiness," up to "the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is mine; I cultivate the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. "The foundations of mindfulness are mine; the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are mine. The immeasurables, the meditations, and the formless attainments are mine. The noble truths are mine. The superknowledges are mine. The doors of liberation, concentration, attainment, and dhāraṇī are mine. Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are mine."
"I possess emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges are mine; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are mine;
the fruit of stream-entry is mine; I am a stream-enterer; the fruit of once-returning is mine; I am a once-returner; the fruit of non-returning is mine;
I am a non-returner; arhatship is mine; I am an arhat; pratyekabuddhahood is mine; I am a pratyekabuddha. My...
"I am omniscience; [all] omnisciences are I.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, sons of the gods, so it is."

"O sons of the gods, this Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping form, nor for the sake of non-grasping; it is not taught for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor for the sake of non-grasping. But those sons of the gods who practice for the sake of grasping form..."

Those who practice for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not capable of cultivating the perfection of wisdom. Those who practice for the sake of grasping the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination [are likewise not capable].

Those who practice for the sake of grasping all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the gateways of the meditative concentrations, the attainments, and the dhāraṇīs; those who practice for the sake of grasping the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.

Those sons of the gods who practice for the sake of grasping all-aspect omniscience are not capable of cultivating the perfection of wisdom, nor are they capable of cultivating the perfections of meditation, vigor, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, up to and including being incapable of cultivating all-aspect omniscience. Thus, its intrinsic nature is contrary to the entire world.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with all dharmas;
Blessed One, with what is this Dharma in conformity?"
“Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with the perfection of wisdom;

Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity;
Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with internal emptiness.”
“Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to the applications of mindfulness;
Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.”
“Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to the Noble Truths;

Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
Blessed One, this Dharma conforms to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges.”
"Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;

Blessed One, this Dharma is in conformity with the knowledge of all aspects. This Dharma is not obstructed anywhere: it is not obstructed in form, and likewise it is not obstructed in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
He is not obstructed regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination;
he is not obstructed regarding all the perfections and all the modes of emptiness;
he is not obstructed regarding the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
He is unimpeded regarding the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the liberations, the samādhis, the attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī;
he is unimpeded regarding emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities;
he is unimpeded regarding the knowledge of all aspects. Indeed, this dharma has the characteristic of being unimpeded.
By taking recourse in the equality of space, by taking recourse in the equality of suchness, and by taking recourse in the stability of the realm of phenomena.
Based on the equality of the limit of reality,
based on the equality of the inconceivable realm,
and based on the equality of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Based on the equality of non-arising and non-ceasing, and based on the equality of non-defilement and non-purification,
this dharma is non-arising, based on the non-arising and non-ceasing of form.
Feeling, perception, and mental formations,
by virtue of the non-arising and non-cessation of consciousness,
[are likewise empty] of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination.
Based on the state of non-arising and non-cessation,

all perfections, all emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, the superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, all liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī are based on the state of non-arising and non-cessation.

This is based on the non-arising and non-ceasing of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Thus, this dharma has the nature of being unimpeded;
it is trackless, based on the non-apprehension of the track of form, and based on the non-apprehension of the tracks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Based on the non-apprehensibility of the terms for the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination;

based on the non-apprehensibility of the terms for all the perfections, all the liberations, meditative concentrations, attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇīs; and based on the non-apprehensibility of the terms for the factors conducive to awakening.
By way of the non-apprehensibility of the terms for the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
by way of the non-apprehensibility of the terms for the noble truths, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha;
and by way of the non-apprehensibility of the term for the knowledge of all aspects.
"This Dharma is trackless; thus its nature is trackless.
Then those sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this Elder Subhūti is born after the Blessed One. For what reason?"
For indeed, whatever he teaches, he teaches the Dharma starting from emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Then, the venerable Subhūti addressed those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form:
"O sons of the gods, as you have said..."
“Lord, this Elder Subhūti is born after the Blessed One.
Why is it that because he is ‘born after,’ the Elder Subhūti is said to be born after the Tathāgata?
It is because, just as the Tathāgata’s suchness is neither come nor gone,”

In the same way, Subhūti, the suchness of Subhūti has neither come nor gone; for it is in this manner that the Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata. That which is the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all dharmas;
that which is the suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of the Tathāgata—unfailing suchness, non-other suchness.

For in this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the Tathāgata. That which is the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of stability; that which is the suchness of stability is the suchness of the Tathāgata.

For in this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is unchanging and immutable, so too the suchness of the Elder Subhūti is unchanging and immutable, just like the suchness of the Tathāgata.

In some cases it is obstructed. Thus, the suchness of all phenomena is not obstructed anywhere. That which is the suchness of the Tathāgata and that which is the suchness of all phenomena—this is one single suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated; it is never not suchness.

Since there is never a time when that is not suchness, therefore that suchness is non-dual and without division. In this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the manner of the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is all-pervading and non-conceptual, so too the suchness of Subhūti is all-pervading, non-conceptual, and free from conceptual construction. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is undivided—an indivisible suchness that is unapprehendable—[so too is the suchness of Subhūti].

In this way, Subhūti, the suchness of Subhūti is undifferentiated; it is the undifferentiated suchness that is non-apprehensible. For in this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the manner of the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is the non-other suchness of all dharmas—a suchness that is never not suchness, but is always suchness—so too is the Elder Subhūti a non-other suchness who, having been born after the manner of the Tathāgata, is not born anywhere at all.

In this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the manner of the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present, so too the suchness of all phenomena is neither past, nor future, nor present. In this way, the suchness of the Elder Subhūti is neither past, nor future, nor present;

it is for this reason that the Elder Subhūti is said to have been born after the manner of the Tathāgata. By the sameness of the suchness of the past, there is the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata; by the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the sameness of the suchness of the past.
The sameness of the suchness of the future is the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata; the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata is the sameness of the suchness of the future.
The sameness of the suchness of the present is the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata; the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata is the sameness of the suchness of the present.
Thus, the suchness of the past, future, and present and the suchness of the Tathāgata are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
The suchness of form is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of form;
[so it is with] feeling, perception, mental formations,
and the suchness of consciousness is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of consciousness.

For thus, the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Through the suchness of the aggregates, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata;
through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the elements; through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the elements.
Through the suchness of the sense bases, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the sense bases.
The suchness of dependent origination is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of dependent origination;
the suchness of the factors of dependent origination is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the factors of dependent origination.
For thus, the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination, and the suchness of the Tathāgata, are non-dual.
It is non-dual; it is not divided. Through the suchness of non-otherness, the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of non-otherness;

likewise, the suchness of a sentient being, a living being, a creature, a nourished being, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer, and the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are non-dual, they are not divided. Through the suchness of the perfection of giving, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the perfection of generosity;

likewise, the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom; and the suchness of the perfection of wisdom is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the suchness of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, and the suchness of the Tathāgata, are non-dual.
This is non-dual. The suchness of internal emptiness is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of internal emptiness;

likewise, up to the suchness of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is the suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
For indeed, the suchness of internal emptiness and the suchness of the Tathāgata are one and the same.

Up to the suchness of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence and the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are non-dual, they are not divided into two. By means of the suchness of the applications of mindfulness, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; by means of the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path. By means of the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the path. Thus, indeed, the suchness of the applications of mindfulness and the suchness of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path [are one].

And the suchness of the Tathāgata and this [suchness] are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Through the suchness of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments. Through the suchness of all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs.

For thus, the suchness of the immeasurable meditations, the formless attainments, and all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, and the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are non-dual and not divided into two. By means of the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; by means of the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The suchness of the noble truths is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the noble truths.
The suchness of the superknowledges is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the superknowledges.
For indeed, the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the suchness of the noble truths, and the suchness of the superknowledges are the suchness of the Tathāgata.
And this is non-dual and indivisible. Through the suchness of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata;
through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.
Through the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha, there is the suchness of the Tathāgata; through the suchness of the Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha.

For thus, the suchness of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the three kinds of analytical knowledge, and the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha, and the suchness of a Tathāgata—these are non-dual and not divided into two. Through the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, there is the suchness of a Tathāgata; through the suchness of a Tathāgata, there is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects.
For thus, the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects and the suchness of a Tathāgata are non-dual and not divided into two. This is...
Subhūti, it is by coming to that very suchness within the suchness of the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and thus he receives the name "Tathāgata. Furthermore, while this chapter on Suchness was being spoken, this great trichiliocosm shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways and with eighteen great omens.
It moves, it moves forward, it moves completely forward; it quakes, it quakes forward, it quakes completely forward;
it resounds, it resounds loudly, it resounds completely loudly.
It quivers, it quivers violently, it quivers intensely;
it roars, it roars loudly, it roars intensely;
the eastern direction rises while the western direction sinks.
The western direction rises and the eastern direction sinks;
the northern direction rises and the southern direction sinks;
the southern direction rises and the northern direction sinks.
It rises from the edges and sinks in the middle;
it rises from the middle and sinks at the edges.
Then indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm scattered divine sandalwood powder over the Blessed One and the Elder Subhūti, and spoke these words:

“It is wonderful, Blessed One, how this Elder Subhūti has been born after the Tathāgata by way of the suchness of the Tathāgata. Thus [is] the nature of non-going. Then the Elder Subhūti continued that very discourse to those sons of the gods: “For indeed, O sons of the gods, the Elder Subhūti has not been born after form, nor has he been born after the suchness of form.”
He is not born other than from the suchness of form; he is not born from feeling, perception, mental formations, nor from consciousness.

He is not born after the suchness of consciousness, nor is he born apart from the suchness of consciousness; he is not born after the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, nor is he born after the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, nor is he born apart from the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; he is not born after dependent origination.

He is not born after the suchness of dependent origination, nor is he born apart from the suchness of dependent origination. In the same way, [this applies to] all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the doors of liberation, samādhis, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; and to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
He is not born after the image of the knowledge of all aspects, nor is he born after the image of the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects;
yet he is not born apart from the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects. He is not born after the image of the unconditioned.
He is not born after the unconditioned suchness, nor is he born apart from the conditioned suchness. Why is that?
Because those phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended—neither one who would be born after them, nor that by which one would be born after them.
"Whether that which is produced or that by which it is produced—this is the nature of non-arising.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:

"O Blessed One, profound is this suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
Where form is not apprehended, nor the suchness of form;
when form itself is not apprehended, how much less will the suchness of form be apprehended?
Where there is no feeling, no perception, and no mental formations...
Where consciousness is not apprehended, nor the suchness of consciousness;

when consciousness itself is not apprehended, how indeed could the suchness of consciousness be apprehended? Where the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are not apprehended, nor the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;
when the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields themselves are not apprehended—

How much less, then, could the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases be apprehended? For where neither dependent origination nor the factors of dependent origination are apprehended, nor the suchness of dependent origination,
nor the suchness of the factors of dependent origination—
since neither dependent origination nor its very factors are apprehended.
How much less, then, could the suchness of dependent origination, or the suchness of the factors of dependent origination, be apprehended?

In the same way, [how could there be the apprehension of] all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; the noble truths; the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the superknowledges; the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha?
Wherein omniscience is not apprehended, nor the suchness of omniscience;
when omniscience itself is not apprehended—
"How much less, then, will the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended?
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is."
Profound, Śāriputra, is this suchness, wherein form is not apprehended,
nor is the suchness of form apprehended.
Form itself is not apprehended; how, then, could the suchness of form be apprehended?

Wherein neither feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness is apprehended, nor is the suchness of consciousness apprehended—consciousness itself is not apprehended; how, then, could the suchness of consciousness be apprehended?
Wherein the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination are not apprehended, nor is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination apprehended;

since the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination themselves will not be apprehended, how much less could the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination be apprehended? In this same way, up to: omniscience is not apprehended, nor is the suchness of omniscience apprehended.
Even omniscience itself is not apprehended;

how much less could the suchness of omniscience be apprehended? Furthermore, Śāriputra, while this very suchness—unfailing suchness, non-other suchness—was being taught, the minds of two hundred monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
The dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified for five hundred bhikṣuṇīs;

five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena; and the minds of sixty bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were subject to regression were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, perceiving that the minds of those bodhisattvas were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging, addressed the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which the minds of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging?
The Blessed One said:

And by these bodhisattvas, Śāriputra, five hundred Buddhas were attended upon; everywhere they gave gifts, maintained ethical discipline, perfected patience, exerted vigor, produced meditative concentrations, and cultivated wisdom. Yet, because they were devoid of the perfection of wisdom and not sustained by skill in means, they practiced in such a manner.
"We give gifts, we guard our morality, we perfect patience, we exert vigor, we attain meditative concentration, and we cultivate wisdom.
Because they were devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lacked skill in means, they cultivated giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Moving within the perception of multiplicity and through the apprehension of multiplicity, they did not enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva.

Without entering the fixed course of the bodhisattvas, they attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the attainment of arhatship; yet, Śāriputra, although there exists for bodhisattva mahāsattvas the path— whether emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness— if they are deprived of the perfection of wisdom and not sustained by skill in means, they [fall into] the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Having realized [this], they become śrāvakas.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, do they, having well cultivated those very dharmas that are empty, signless, and wishless, [become śrāvakas]?"

“Those who are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and not sustained by skill in means, having realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), become śrāvakas. But how is it, Blessed One, that bodhisattvas— having well cultivated those very dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and having relied upon the perfection of wisdom and skill in means— awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Śāriputra, one who is devoid of the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),
while cultivating the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, becomes a śrāvaka by not resorting to skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, another bodhisattva mahāsattva, never being separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*), while cultivating the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). It is just as if, Śāriputra, there were a bird whose body were a hundred yojanas in size.
Suppose his body were two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas in size,
and he thought he must come from the Heaven of the Thirty-three to Jambudvīpa,
yet that bird were to become wingless.

He would think that he must free himself from the thirty-three gods, [thinking], "I shall go to Jambūdvīpa. Then, while that bird, the winged creature, was half-fallen, this thought occurred to him: "O, would that I might remain among the gods of the Thirty-three! What do you think, Śāriputra, would that bird, the winged creature, be capable of remaining once again among the gods of the Thirty-three?
Śāriputra said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
If, however, in the midst of this,
it were to think, "Oh, that I might land in Jambudvīpa unharmed and uninjured," what do you think, Śāriputra, would that bird, that fowl, indeed land in Jambudvīpa unharmed and uninjured?
Śāriputra said:
"No, Blessed One.
Wounded and injured, Blessed One, he would meet his death before even reaching Jambudvīpa. For what reason?"
"It is so, Blessed One; it happens thus for one who has a large body but whose wings have not yet grown, and who falls from afar and from a great distance.
The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Śāriputra, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, practices giving, guards morality, accomplishes patience, exerts vigor, and enters meditative concentration— and although his setting out is great, his production of the thought of awakening is great, and his undertaking is immeasurable for the sake of fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
And being devoid of both the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, he falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has given gifts with a mind that is devoid of the knowledge of all aspects.

He has maintained ethical discipline, accomplished patience, exerted vigor, and generated the meditative concentrations; yet that bodhisattva was devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, and by that he falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Moreover, Śāriputra, even though that bodhisattva...

He attends to, accomplishes, and takes as a sign the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present;
yet he does not truly know the morality of those Tathāgatas, nor does he know their concentration, nor their wisdom, nor their liberation, nor their knowledge and vision of liberation.

Not knowing and not understanding, he hears of peace in emptiness, the signless, or the wishless; he takes that peace as a sign, and having taken it as a sign, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. By dedicating in this way, the bodhisattva will stand on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?

It is thus, Śāriputra: whoever is devoid of both the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, and does not dedicate their roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, falls to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. This is the nature of the non-apprehension of suchness.
Thus has the characteristic of intrinsic nature been explained.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, never being separated from the mind of omniscience,
practices giving, guards morality, accomplishes patience, exerts vigor, and enters the meditative concentrations.

And he does not take them as signs; he cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, yet he does not take them as signs, up to and including the cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not take it as a sign.
Thus is the general [explanation of] the stage conducive to liberation.
Not separated from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, he brings to mind the Buddhas of the three times;

and regarding the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those Blessed Buddhas of the past,
future, and present— he does not take any of that as a sign, nor does he take the concentration on emptiness, the signless concentration, or the wishless concentration as a sign.
Śāriputra, it should be understood that if he does not form a mental sign, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not abide on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Unhurt and unimpaired, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is the factor conducive to liberation consisting of faith.
Why is that?
Because, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, that bodhisattva mahāsattva has given gifts without making them into signs.
Ethical discipline has been guarded, patience has been perfected, vigor has been exerted, meditative concentration has been attained, and wisdom has been cultivated, yet no sign was made of them.
The ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, were not made into signs.
Śāriputra, this is the skillful means of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, by which they remain devoid of signs.

With the mind, one gives gifts, guards ethical discipline, accomplishes patience, exerts vigor, enters meditative concentration, and cultivates wisdom. One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
one cultivates the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
He enters into all the gateways of the liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
he cultivates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet does not form signs of them.

He cultivates the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities, up to practicing in the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not form signs of them. This is the factor conducive to liberation characterized by vigor.
Śāriputra said:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, Blessed One, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva whose intention is not separated from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, there is unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus is the stage conducive to liberation characterized by mindfulness.

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, by that bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, no phenomenon whatsoever has been apprehended— neither that which would awaken, nor that by which one awakens, nor that which is awakened to.
Whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

likewise, whether it be the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination; whether it be all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the noble truths, or the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.

Or whether it be all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; or emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;

or even omniscience itself—those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, O Bhagavat, are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and devoid of skill in means, will have doubts regarding these.
One should expect [attainment] in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?

Because, Blessed One, whatever gift was given by those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who were devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means—all that—
Having made it into a sign, they give;

likewise, whatever morality has been observed, whatever patience has been perfected, whatever vigor has been exerted, whatever meditative concentration has been attained, and whatever wisdom has been investigated—all that has been investigated by making it into a sign. Therefore, they have doubt regarding those [dharmas].
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle is to be expected.

Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must not be separated from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
Abiding in the perfection of wisdom through skill in means, by way of non-apprehension and with a mind accompanied by the signless,

one should give gifts, guard morality, fulfill patience, exert vigor, attain meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom. With a mind accompanied by the signless, one should cultivate internal emptiness.

One should cultivate the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*). With a mind accompanied by the signless (*ānimitta*), one should cultivate the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment;

with a mind accompanied by the signless, the noble eightfold path should be cultivated. With a mind accompanied by the signless, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments should be entered. With a mind accompanied by the signless, the noble truths should be cultivated. With a mind accompanied by the signless...

With the mind, one should cultivate all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs. With a mind accompanied by the signless, one should cultivate the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
with a mind accompanied by the signless, one should course in the knowledge of all aspects.
Thus ends the section on the factors conducive to liberation consisting of meditative concentration.
Then, indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, supreme perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize and difficult to have faith in."
For in this regard, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects, those phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, sons of the gods; so it is."
“O sons of the gods, supreme perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize and difficult to have faith in.
Yet, O sons of the gods, I too have fully awakened to all phenomena in all their aspects;
however, I have not apprehended any phenomenon whatsoever—that which would awaken, that by means of which one awakens, or that which is awakened to. (PSP_4:130)
For what reason?
O sons of the gods, it is because all phenomena are absolutely pure. Thus [ends] the stage conducive to liberation consisting of wisdom.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Regarding what the Blessed One has said— that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize—
I understand the meaning of the Blessed One’s words as follows, and this is how it appears to me:
In that same way, Blessed One, is unexcelled perfect enlightenment fully awakened to. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, no one awakens, nothing is awakened by anyone, and there is nothing to be fully awakened to;
for all phenomena, Blessed One, are empty.

O Blessed One, since all phenomena are empty, that phenomenon does not exist which would be fully awakened to, nor that by which one would be fully awakened, nor that which would be fully awakened. Why is that?
Because, O Blessed One, all phenomena are empty.
For the sake of increasing or abandoning whichever dharma one might give a gift,
or guard morality, or cultivate patience, or exert vigor, or enter meditative absorption—
even up to training in the knowledge of all aspects— [one should do so].
And those phenomena do not exist:
