that which would fully awaken, that by which one would fully awaken, and that which would be fully awakened—all these phenomena are empty. By this method, O Blessed One, the unsurpassed perfect awakening of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is their own.
perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form;
feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise empty].
Consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination,
as well as the factors of dependent origination, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the factors of dependent origination.
In this way, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions,

the formless attainments, the noble truths, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, and the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, [are empty] by virtue of the intrinsic nature of the unique qualities of a Buddha.
The knowledge of all aspects is empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects.
These are the superior aids to liberation.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this manner, venerable Subhūti, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize. Why is that?

Because, venerable Subhūti, it does not occur to space itself, 'I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. In the very same way, venerable Subhūti, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva [that he will do so]."
"I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, all phenomena are equal to space.
Moreover, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having resolved that all phenomena are equal to space, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If, however, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved that all phenomena are equal to space, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment were easy to awaken to, it would not be difficult to realize; yet such is not the case for bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

They would turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this manner, venerable Subhūti, it is understood that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize and not easily realized.
Thus are the weak factors conducive to liberation.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Does form turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable Subhūti. [The same applies to] feeling, perception, and mental formations."
Subhūti said:
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Does consciousness turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti.
It is thus [not so] in detail regarding the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination."

All the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; the factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; the noble truths, the doors of liberation, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Up until the point where the knowledge of all aspects turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"What do you think, venerable Śāriputra? Is there any dharma other than form which turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti, [it is not so] for feeling, perception, and mental formations."
Subhūti said:
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Is there any dharma other than consciousness that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti.

In this same way, it is not so for the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the factors of dependent origination, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors conducive to awakening, and the immeasurables, dhyānas, and formless attainments."

The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha—apart from omniscience itself—is there any dharma that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Does that which is the suchness of form turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

The suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and that which is the suchness of consciousness— that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this way, in detail, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the factors of dependent origination, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment [turn back].

The suchness of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, all the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, the doors of dhāraṇī, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the noble truths, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges— whatever is the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha, that would turn back from unexcelled, perfect, complete enlightenment; even up to whatever is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, that would turn back from unexcelled, perfect, complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
What do you think, Śāriputra? Is there any dharma other than the suchness of form that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Is there any [dharma] other than the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, or the suchness of mental formations?

What do you think, Śāriputra? Is there any dharma other than the suchness of consciousness that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? In this way, it should be stated in detail for everything other than the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination, and other than the suchness of the factors of dependent origination.
except for the suchness of all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
except for the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;
except for the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the noble truths, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the specific perfect knowledges.

Apart from the suchness of the unique qualities of a Buddha and apart from the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, there is no dharma whatsoever that turns back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra said:
"No, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "What do you think of that?"
"Venerable Śāriputra, does suchness turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra said:
"No, Venerable Subhūti.

Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), the fixed order of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭiḥ).
Śāriputra said:
"No, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "What do you think of that?"
"Venerable Śāriputra, the inconceivable realm turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:

"What do you think, venerable Śāriputra? Is there any dharma other than suchness that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? Likewise, [is there any dharma] other than the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), or the fixed order of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā)?"
Except for the inconceivable realm, there is no dharma that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"This being so, since those dharmas are not apprehended in terms of reality or stability, what is that dharma which turns back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:

"By that very nature of the Dharma-method which the Elder Subhūti has explained, no bodhisattva mahāsattva whatsoever will turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. As for these three types of persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who have been described by the Tathāgata..."

And there will be no distinction between these three persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle; there will be only one bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, the one belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, according to the teaching of the venerable Subhūti.
Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"But, venerable Śāriputra, does the elder Subhūti desire even a single bodhisattva mahāsattva?
First, the elder Subhūti must be questioned.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"But, venerable Subhūti, do you even accept the existence of a single bodhisattva belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti replied to the venerable Śāriputra:
"But, venerable Śāriputra, do you accept three bodhisattvas within suchness?"

"Do you desire a bodhisattva who belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or a bodhisattva who belongs to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or a bodhisattva who belongs to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas?
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"In that case, venerable Śāriputra, are three kinds of bodhisattvas perceived within suchness?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"But then, Venerable Śāriputra, is suchness perceived through one, two, or three aspects?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, do you perceive even a single bodhisattva within suchness?
Śāriputra replied: "No, venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"Since these dharmas are thus unapprehendable in terms of reality and stability, how could it occur to the Venerable Śāriputra to think:

'This is a bodhisattva belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas; this is a bodhisattva belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; this is a bodhisattva belonging to the vehicle of the Buddhas'?"
When this suchness of all phenomena is being elucidated, that bodhisattva mahāsattva whose mind does not shrink back,

does not become despondent, does not feel regret, and whose mind does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear— this bodhisattva mahāsattva shall go forth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! May your eloquence shine forth, Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is manifested when the suchness of all phenomena is being elucidated."
That bodhisattva mahāsattva whose mind does not shrink back, does not falter, does not become regretful, and whose mind does not tremble, does not fear, and does not fall into terror—
this bodhisattva mahāsattva shall go forth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, by means of which awakening will a bodhisattva mahāsattva set forth?
The Blessed One replied:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva will set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus, the middling factors conducive to liberation have been described. Regarding these factors conducive to liberation, the venerable Subhūti then said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment abide?"

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide in equanimity toward all sentient beings and should generate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings."
One should not give rise to an uneven mind;
all sentient beings should be taken as objects with an even mind,
and great loving-kindness should be generated toward all sentient beings.
Great compassion should be generated toward all sentient beings;
all sentient beings should be taken as the object of a mind of loving-kindness;
all sentient beings should be taken as the object of a mind of great compassion.

One should not regard all sentient beings with a human-like mind; rather, one should generate a state of humbled pridelessness toward them and regard all sentient beings with sincerity. Thus, in the stage of "mild heat" (*mṛdu-uṣmagata*), one should generate a mind of benevolence toward all sentient beings.
One should not give rise to a harmful mind;
all sentient beings should be taken as objects with a mind of benefit, and never as objects with a harmful mind.
One should generate a mind free from hostility toward all sentient beings;
one should not take all sentient beings as objects with a hostile mind;
and one should generate a mind of non-harming toward all sentient beings.

All sentient beings should not be taken as objects with a mind of malice. Thus, in the middle stage of "heat," one should generate toward all sentient beings a mind like that of a mother, a mind like that of a father, a mind like that of a brother, a mind like that of a sister, a mind like that of a son, and a mind like that of a daughter.

One should generate the thought of [them being] friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations; one should regard all sentient beings with the thought of them being mothers and the thought of them being fathers,
and one should regard them with the thought of them being brothers and the thought of them being sisters.

They should be regarded with the thought of a son, with the thought of a daughter, and they should be regarded with the thought of friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should abide.
Thus is the highest degree of the stage of heat (*adhimātram uṣmagatam*).
One should personally abstain from taking life, encourage others to abstain from taking life,
speak in praise of abstaining from taking life,
and [rejoice in] those others who abstain from taking life.
And one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval. In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should abide.
He himself must abstain from taking what is not given, and he should encourage others to abstain from taking what is not given.
One should speak in praise of abstaining from taking what is not given,
and one should speak in praise of and approve of those others who likewise abstain from taking what is not given.
One should personally abstain from sexual misconduct,
encourage others to abstain from sexual misconduct,
and speak in praise of abstinence from sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, one should speak in praise of and approve of others who abstain from sexual misconduct.
Likewise, one should abstain from false speech, harsh speech, slanderous speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and oneself from wrong view.
Furthermore, others should be encouraged to abstain from wrong view;
one should speak in praise of abstaining from wrong view, and one should acknowledge those others who have indeed abstained from wrong view.
And one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
Furthermore, one should personally attain the first dhyāna and encourage others to attain the first dhyāna as well.
One should speak in praise of the attainment of the first dhyāna,
and one should also speak in praise of and give approval to those others who have attained the first dhyāna.
In this way, one should personally attain the second dhyāna;
in this way, one should attain the third dhyāna;
and one should personally attain the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, others should be encouraged to undertake the fourth dhyāna; one should speak in praise of the attainment of the fourth dhyāna,
and one should speak in praise of and give approval to those others who have attained the fourth dhyāna.
One should cultivate loving-kindness oneself, encourage others to cultivate loving-kindness,
and speak in praise of the cultivation of loving-kindness.
One should speak in praise of and approve of those others who dwell in loving-kindness;
likewise, one should act toward those who dwell in compassion and sympathetic joy,
and one should oneself dwell in equanimity.
Others should be encouraged to dwell in equanimity; one should speak in praise of dwelling in equanimity,
and [one should honor] those others who dwell in equanimity.
One should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
Furthermore, one should personally attain the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space,
and should encourage others to attain the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
One should be a speaker of praise for the attainment of the sphere of infinite space,
as well as for those others who enter into the attainment of the sphere of infinite space.
And one should be a speaker in praise of them and give approval.

Likewise, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and by oneself, the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be entered.

Furthermore, others should be encouraged to attain the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; one should be a speaker in praise of the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and one should be a speaker in praise and a supporter of those others who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the stage of the "summit" (mūrdhan) at its mild level.
One should personally fulfill the perfection of generosity, encourage others to undertake the perfection of generosity,
and be one who speaks in praise of the perfection of generosity.
And as for others who fulfill the perfection of generosity, one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
The same applies to the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
One should personally fulfill the perfection of wisdom, encourage others to take up the perfection of wisdom,
and be one who speaks in praise of the perfection of wisdom.

And one should speak in praise of and give approval to those others who fulfill the perfection of wisdom. Thus, having reached the middle of the head, one should personally cultivate internal emptiness.
Furthermore, others should be encouraged to undertake internal emptiness;
one should speak in praise of internal emptiness;
and one should [rejoice] in those other beings who cultivate internal emptiness.
And one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
In this way, one should cultivate external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence by its own nature;
and others should be encouraged to undertake the emptiness of non-existence by its own nature.
One should speak in praise of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence,
and one should also speak in praise of and give approval to those other beings who cultivate the emptiness of the nature of non-existence.
One should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness oneself, encourage others to undertake the four foundations of mindfulness,
and be a speaker in praise of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, regarding other beings who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness,
one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
The same applies to the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
One should cultivate the noble eightfold path oneself, establish others in the noble eightfold path,
and be one who speaks in praise of the noble eightfold path.
And as for those other beings who cultivate the noble eightfold path, one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
One should personally cultivate the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should encourage others to undertake the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and one should be a speaker in praise of the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, one should speak in praise of and approve of those other beings who cultivate the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and one should personally cultivate the four noble truths.
Others should be encouraged to practice the cultivation of the noble truths, one should speak in praise of the noble truths,
and one should [rejoice] in those other beings who cultivate the four noble truths.
One should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
One should personally cultivate the eight liberations and encourage others to undertake the cultivation of the eight liberations.
One should be a speaker in praise of the eight liberations,
and one should be a speaker in praise and a follower of those others who attain the eight liberations.
One should personally undertake the nine successive meditative attainments, encourage others to undertake the nine successive meditative attainments,
and be one who speaks in praise of the nine successive meditative attainments.
Furthermore, one should speak in praise of and approve of those other beings who enter the nine successive meditative attainments;
and one should personally accomplish the superknowledges.
Others should be encouraged to attain the superknowledges; one should speak in praise of the superknowledges;
and as for other beings who have already attained the superknowledges, [one should rejoice in them].
One should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.
Furthermore, one should personally fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata and encourage others to undertake the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
One should speak in praise of the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
and one should also speak in praise of, and give approval to, those other beings who fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

In this way, one must personally fulfill the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and establish others in those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should be a speaker in praise of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and one should also be a speaker in praise of, and one should approve of, those others who bring the other unique qualities of a Buddha to fulfillment.
One should personally fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion, encourage others to undertake great loving-kindness and great compassion,
and be one who speaks in praise of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Furthermore, one should speak in praise of and give approval to those others who fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Moreover, one should personally enter into the meditative attainment of dependent origination in its forward and reverse order.

Furthermore, others should be encouraged to undertake the forward and reverse order of dependent origination; one should be a speaker in praise of the meditative attainment of the forward and reverse order of dependent origination,
and likewise for those others who enter into the meditative attainment of the forward and reverse order of dependent origination.
And one should speak in praise of them and give one's approval.

Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should stand. Thus, in the highest stage of the "Summits," he personally fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes its cessation, and cultivates the path.
He encourages others toward the full comprehension of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path;
he speaks in praise of the full comprehension of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path;
and he [rejoices] in those others who fully comprehend suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.
And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. This is the mild patience.
He himself generates the knowledge for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, yet he does not personally realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
and he encourages others toward the realization of the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry.
He speaks in praise of the realization of the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who generate the knowledge for the sake of realizing the fruit of stream-entry.
In this way, he himself generates the knowledge for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, yet he does not realize the limit of reality;
he himself generates the knowledge for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, yet he does not realize the limit of reality;
and he himself generates the knowledge for the realization of the fruit of arhatship, yet he does not realize the limit of reality.
He establishes others in the direct realization of the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship,
he speaks in praise of the direct realization of the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship,
and he [encourages] those others who generate the knowledge for the sake of the direct realization of the fruit of arhatship.
He speaks in praise of them and approves of them.
He himself generates the knowledge for the realization of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, yet he does not personally realize the realization of the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;
rather, he establishes others in the realization of the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
He speaks in praise of the realization of the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha,
and of those others who generate the knowledge for the sake of realizing the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. This is the middling degree of patience (*madhyā kṣānti*).
Furthermore, he himself enters the bodhisattva's state of certainty (*bodhisattvanyāma*), and he encourages others to enter that same state of certainty in the bodhisattva.
He speaks in praise of the entry into the bodhisattva’s certainty, and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those other bodhisattvas who enter into that certainty.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide. Thus, with superior patience,
he ripens himself and others, and he encourages others toward the ripening of sentient beings.
He speaks in praise of the ripening of sentient beings,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who have risen up for the sake of ripening sentient beings.
He himself purifies the buddha-field, encourages others to purify the buddha-field,
and speaks in praise of the purification of the buddha-field.
And he speaks in praise of and approves of others who are established in the purification of Buddha-fields. These are the soft supreme dharmas;
and he himself produces the superknowledges of a bodhisattva.
He encourages others to undertake the superknowledges of a bodhisattva, speaks in praise of the bodhisattva superknowledges,
and is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those other bodhisattvas who cultivate the superknowledges. These are the supreme mundane dharmas (madhyāgradharmāḥ).
He himself generates the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, encourages others to adopt the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects,
and speaks in praise of the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects.
Furthermore, he speaks in praise of and approves of others who generate the knowledge of all modes,
and he himself abandons all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and residual impressions.
He encourages others to abandon all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and habitual traces,
he speaks in praise of the abandonment of all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and habitual traces,
and he rejoices in those others who likewise abandon all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and habitual traces.
And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them. He himself acquires excellence of longevity,
and he encourages others to acquire excellence of longevity.
He speaks in praise of excellence of lifespan,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of those other great persons who abide in excellence of lifespan.
He himself upholds the endurance of the true Dharma, and he encourages others to do so as well.

He speaks in praise of the endurance of the true Dharma, and he becomes one who speaks in praise of and approves of those other great men, the bulls among beings, who uphold the endurance of the true Dharma.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [should train].

It must be so. Subhūti, it is precisely in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom and in skillful means. For one who trains in this manner and abides in this way, form will become unobstructed, feeling will become unobstructed, perception will become unobstructed, and mental formations will become unobstructed.
"Consciousness will be unobstructed;
thus, in detail, up until: the endurance of the true Dharma will be unobstructed. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, such a form has not been grasped by the bodhisattva mahāsattva from the very beginning."
There is no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness that is grasped;
likewise, up to and including omniscience, nothing is grasped. Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, that which is the non-appropriation of form is not form; that which is [the non-appropriation] of feeling, perception, and mental formations is likewise not those;
for in this way, that which is the non-appropriation of consciousness is not consciousness. And so on, up to that which is [the non-appropriation] of the knowledge of all aspects.

Non-appropriation is not that omniscience in all its aspects. Furthermore, while this station of the bodhisattva was being taught, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena. These are called the supreme mundane dharmas;
thus has been explained the stage conducive to penetration.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what are the modes, and what are the signs, of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible?"
What are the signs?
Or how, Blessed One, shall we know that "this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva"?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"Subhūti, that which is called the stage of ordinary persons, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, and the stage of Tathāgatas— all these are, by virtue of suchness, non-conceptual, free from conceptualization, non-dual, and without division."
And just as that suchness is free from conceptual construction, so too one does not construct it; thus one enters by means of non-conceptualization.
Having entered in this way, having heard how suchness is, one transcends it and does not construct anything at all.
For those [words] do not arise from suchness as being either one or the other, nor from both, nor from neither;
nor does he become a speaker of idle chatter. He speaks words endowed with meaning, not words devoid of meaning, and he does not look upon the deeds done or left undone by another.

And he is one who seeks out well-spoken words. Subhūti, by these aspects, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. Thus, Subhūti spoke on the general characteristics of irreversibility.
By what modes, Blessed One, by what marks, and by what signs [is this known]?
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
The Blessed One said:
"For, Subhūti, all dharmas are without form, without marks, and without signs."
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas are without aspect, without mark, and without sign, by means of which dharmas, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible shown to be 'irreversible'?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has turned away from form, turned away from feeling, turned away from perception, and turned away from mental formations,"
Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva who has turned away from consciousness should be known as irreversible.

Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has turned away from the aggregates, turned away from the elements, turned away from the sense bases, turned away from dependent origination, and turned away from the factors of dependent origination— this [bodhisattva]...

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has turned back from the perfection of generosity, and likewise from the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— [is irreversible].

He has turned away from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; he has turned away from the applications of mindfulness, and likewise from the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

He has turned away from the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; he has turned away from all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
he has turned away from the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.

Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has turned back from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and has turned back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; for what reason?

For in this way, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form does not exist; likewise, the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva might abide. In this same way, the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination does not exist.

Thus, up to and including unexcelled perfect enlightenment, no intrinsic nature exists wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva could be established. This is the characteristic of irreversibility for one who abides in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding those ascetics and brahmins outside of this [Dharma] whom a bodhisattva mahāsattva looks toward, thinking:
"These venerable ascetics and brahmins know what is to be known and see what is to be seen; they possess right view and wisdom..."

It is impossible that they would designate [them as such]. He does not fall into doubt, he does not cling to rules and observances, he does not succumb to wrong views, he does not believe in purification through auspicious ceremonies or charms, and he does not pay homage to other gods. [He does not honor them] with flowers, perfumes, incense, or ointments.

Or with powders, or robes, or parasols, or banners, or flags— Subhūti, one should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs is irreversible, provided he does not think that [these things] should be given to others or performed for others.
Thus, this is the second characteristic of irreversibility for one who abides in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not hold wrong views;
he is not reborn in the hells, nor in the world of Yama, nor in the animal realm, nor among the asuras, nor in the borderlands.
He is reborn in the [human] realms; he does not become dull-witted or mute; he is not reborn among the long-lived gods; and he does not assume the female state.
Subhūti, by these modes, these characteristics, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
This is the third characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, conducts himself accordingly; he himself abstains from taking life, he encourages others to abstain from taking life,
and he speaks in praise of abstaining from taking life.
Furthermore, those others who abstain from taking life, he speaks in praise of them and approves of them.
Likewise for [abstaining from] taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, and malice.
He himself abstains from wrong view, encourages others to abstain from wrong view,
and speaks in praise of abstaining from wrong view.
And those others who abstain from wrong view—
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible, provided he also speaks in praise of them and approves of them.
Furthermore, Subhūti, even when in a dream, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not commit the ten unwholesome paths of action.
By these modes, by these signs, and by these marks, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known.
Thus, this is the fourth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in the perfection of generosity, abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, abides in the perfection of patience, abides in the perfection of vigor, and abides in the perfection of meditative concentration, [he is irreversible].
When one abides in the perfection of wisdom, then for the sake of all sentient beings one gives gifts,
likewise guards ethical discipline, accomplishes patience, exerts vigor, enters meditative concentration, and cultivates wisdom for the sake of all sentient beings.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.

Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever teachings an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva masters— whether sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, itivṛttakas, up to avadānas and upadeśas— as he gives that gift of Dharma, it occurs to him thus:
"By this gift, may the righteous aspirations of all sentient beings reach fulfillment.
Having made that gift of Dharma common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti, by these modes, these characteristics, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who is irreversible.
Thus, this is the fifth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, there is no doubt, no perplexity, and no hesitation regarding profound dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva have no doubt, no perplexity, and no hesitation regarding profound dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:
"It is because, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever."
Whether he perceives form, or feeling, or perception, or mental formations, or consciousness; or the aggregates, or the elements, or the sense bases;
or dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination;
or all the perfections, or all the emptinesses, or all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; or the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.

or he does not perceive dharmas, or the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, or the noble truths, or emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, or the ten powers of a Tathāgata, or the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha; nor does he perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, wherever there may be longing, perplexity, or doubt,
one should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs is irreversible.
Thus is the sixth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses smooth bodily action that is pleasing, smooth vocal action that is pleasing, and smooth mental action that is pleasing and lovely.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is constantly and continuously possessed of loving-kindness.
He is endowed with agreeable and loving bodily action, agreeable and loving vocal action, and agreeable, lovely mental action. Subhūti,
by these characteristics, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Thus ends the seventh [section] on the characteristics of the non-retrogressive one who abides in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell together with the five hindrances:
sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Thus ends the eighth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no latent tendency whatsoever in any way at all.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one endowed with the state of non-retrogression.
This concludes the ninth [section], the characteristics of non-retrogression for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible walks forward or walks backward, he does so with an undistracted mind as he walks forward or walks backward.

Whether walking forward or returning, he walks with mindfulness established; indeed, he returns with mindfulness established. Possessed of mindfulness, he goes, steps, stands, sits, and prepares his bed; he does not lift his feet suddenly from the ground, nor does he set them down suddenly on the ground, nor does he place his feet down on the ground with haste.
Mindful indeed he lifts his feet, withdraws them, and sets them down;
he steps upon the ground only while looking at it.
Subhūti, endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva is irreversible.
He should be known as a mahāsattva.
This is the tenth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, in the use of robes, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not feel disgust toward his body.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from lice, is clean in his conduct, pure in his conduct, and has little illness.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known.
This is the eleventh characteristic of irreversibility for one in the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, those eighty thousand families of worms that dwell within the body and consume the body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva do not exist at all within the body of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, those roots of virtue of the bodhisattva mahāsattva have transcended the entire world.

Therefore, those eighty thousand families of worms do not exist within the body of that bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, to whatever extent these roots of virtue belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, to that same extent the bodhisattva mahāsattva acquires purification of body, purification of speech, and purification of mind.
Subhūti, it should be known that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs is irreversible.
Thus, the twelfth [topic], the characteristics of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration, has been explained.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But how, Blessed One, does the purification of body, the purification of speech, and the purification of mind come to be for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, in whatever measure those roots of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva increase, to that same extent there arises the state of the wheel of body, the state of the wheel of speech, and the state of the wheel of mind, as well as the rectitude of body, speech, and mind."
By means of those roots of merit, he purifies them. Subhūti, this is the purification of body, the purification of speech, and the purification of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Through that purification of body, purification of speech, and purification of mind, he transcends the level of the śrāvaka and the level of the pratyekabuddha. Subhūti, this is [the purification] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind— Subhūti, by these aspects, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Thus ends the thirteenth [section], the characteristics of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not value gain or honor, nor does he value alms-food, up to and including robes;
he abides in the undertaking of the twelve ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*).
By these modes, by these signs, and by these marks, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known.
Thus, this is the fourteenth mark of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, in an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, no thought of stinginess arises, no thought of immorality arises, no thought of agitation arises, and no thought of laziness arises.
A mind that is not concentrated does not arise; a mind of faulty wisdom does not arise; a mind of envy does not arise.
Subhūti, by these modes, these characteristics, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who is irreversible.
Thus, the fifteenth [mark] of the irreversible one who abides in the factors of penetration is as follows:
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses a firm intellect and listens to the Dharma from others with reverence.

Whatever Dharma he hears from others, he harmonizes it all with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Whatever worldly tasks there may be, he accomplishes them all by relying upon the perfection of wisdom.

He harmonizes with the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), yet he does not perceive that phenomenon which is not conjoined with the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); he perceives everything as being conjoined when it is being applied to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti, this should be known as the characteristic of irreversibility of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus ends the sixteenth characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One [will appear] to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Having manifested eight great hells before him, in each of those great hells he saw many hundreds of bodhisattvas,
many thousands of bodhisattvas, many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas,
being burned and cooked, experiencing painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.
He creates such an emanation and speaks thus: "These bodhisattva mahāsattvas, who have been prophesied by the Tathāgatas as irreversible, have been reborn in these great hells."
You too are a denizen of hell according to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly awakened ones, you who have been prophesied for the state of non-retrogression;
yet you once again renounce this thought of awakening.
In this way, you will not be reborn in the great hells;
from that, you will go to the heavenly realms.
Subhūti, if the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not agitated, does not waver, and does not doubt, [he shall attain it].
It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has been predicted by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;

this bodhisattva mahāsattva is fixed in the state of non-retrogression. Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva should be reborn in the hells, or among animals, or in the world of Yama, or among the hosts of asuras.
This is not possible;
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, one should know that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is irreversible.
Thus ends the seventeenth [section], the characteristics of irreversibility for one who has reached the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a śramaṇa and say:
"That which you previously heard—
that the perfection of giving should be purified by me in this way— [is not so]."
In this way, I must purify the perfection of ethical discipline;
in this way, I must purify the perfection of patience;
in this way, I must purify the perfection of vigor; in this way, I must purify the perfection of meditative concentration.
"In this way I must purify the perfection of wisdom; in this way I must fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—
confess all that you have previously [concealed] regarding the Tathāgatas, Arhats, [and Perfectly Enlightened Ones] of the past, future, and present.

"From the first production of the thought of awakening until the duration of the true Dharma of the perfectly awakened ones together with their community of disciples—whatever root of virtue exists within this interval, rejoice in all of that; confess it; relinquish it!
What you have heard is not the word of the Buddha, it was not spoken by the perfectly awakened one; it is a composition made by a poet, mere poetry."
"If what I speak is the word of the Buddha, spoken by the Tathāgata,
and yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes agitated, feels doubt, or falls into uncertainty,
it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not been predicted by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is indefinite;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide in the state of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not shaken, does not hesitate, and does not doubt,
he relies upon the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
he relies upon non-conditioning and non-arising.
He does not proceed by faith in another, and he becomes independent of others;

he becomes independent of others regarding the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, up to and including unsurpassed [enlightenment].

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, an Arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted does not proceed by faith in another, but acts through direct perception regarding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and cannot be led astray by Māra, the Evil One; even so, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is unassailable by those belonging to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.

He becomes one whose nature is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—whether by those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, or the vehicle of the buddhas.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is fixed in the state of non-retrogression and is no longer led by others;
he does not proceed even by faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
How much less could those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the buddhas; how much less Māra the Evil One;
how much less other non-Buddhist wanderers or ascetics—could they proceed with faith [in this]? Such a thing is impossible. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever.
With faith in whomsoever one might go—whether in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
or in the suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, or the suchness of consciousness;
likewise in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, the factors of dependent origination, or all the perfections.

He does not perceive all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; he does not perceive the factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, the superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; indeed, he does not perceive the suchness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Thus ends the eighteenth characteristic of irreversibility for one in the stage of the summit (*mūrdhagata*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, approaching an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a monk, will speak thus:
"This is the wandering of saṃsāra; this is not the practice for the knowledge of all aspects.
Right here, you must bring an end to suffering.
Furthermore, that wicked Māra will indeed teach the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva a counterfeit path.

That which is a counterfeit path, consisting of mundane modes belonging to the realm of saṃsāra—whether it be a perception or [the states] from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—he will teach as follows:
"Venerable one, this is the path, this is the practice; by means of this path and by means of this practice you will attain the fruit of stream-entry."
The fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning—the path by which you will attain arhatship:
by this path, Venerable One, and by this practice, make an end of suffering right here; you shall no longer experience those sufferings belonging to the realm of saṃsāra.
"O, would that this very body of yours here were not brought to cessation; why then do you think you must take up another body?
If, however, Subhūti, the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither agitated nor shaken, [he is established in the perfection of wisdom].
And further, this thought occurs to him:
"This monk is very helpful to me, who teaches what is a counterfeit of the path; for that which is a counterfeit of the path does not lead to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry."

It does not lead to the realization of the fruit of once-returning; it does not lead to the realization of the fruit of non-returning; it does not lead to the realization of the fruit of arhatship; it does not lead to the realization of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
It does not lead to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, joy arises in him:
"This monk has been very helpful to me, who teaches me these factors, by understanding which I must train in all three vehicles."

When Māra the Evil One perceives that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is thus gladdened, he will say to him: "Noble son, do you wish to see those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas by whom Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were attended upon and honored with robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick?"

And in the presence of as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, the perfection of giving was fulfilled, the perfection of ethical discipline was fulfilled, the perfection of patience was fulfilled, the perfection of vigor was fulfilled,
the perfection of meditative concentration was fulfilled, and the perfection of wisdom was fulfilled.

He has attended upon, questioned, and interrogated Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, for the sake of this very Bodhisattva vehicle: "How should Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, stand within the Bodhisattva vehicle?

How should one practicing the perfection of giving, practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, practicing the perfection of patience, practicing the perfection of vigor, practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, and practicing the perfection of wisdom [proceed]?"
How should one practice and abide?

In this way, [one should practice] regarding the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, all the emptinesses, all the doors of liberation, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī;
up to the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Should one abide practicing great loving-kindness and great compassion? Even by abiding, practicing, and applying oneself to yoga exactly as it was taught by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, those very Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, have still not fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Even by those who have practiced in such a way, been instructed in such a way, remained in such a way, and trained in such a way, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) was not attained; how much less so will you attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
If, while being thus analyzed, the mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not undergo any change, and he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror,"

And joy arises in him: "This monk is very helpful to me, who teaches me these factors by which the fruit of stream-entry is attained, as well as the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and even the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects."
Then Māra, the Evil One, perceiving that the mind of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was not dejected, manifested a great many monks right there on that spot of earth and spoke these words:
"These are those Arhats whose outflows are exhausted; they were those who set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but now they abide in Arhatship."
How much less, then, will you fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Furthermore, if it should occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "Alas, this is Māra, the Evil One, who teaches a counterfeit path,"

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, nor does he fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; moreover, it occurs to him:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of generosity or the perfection of ethical discipline..."
Practicing in the perfection of patience, practicing in the perfection of vigor, practicing in the perfection of meditative concentration, practicing in the perfection of wisdom;
practicing in internal emptiness, practicing in external emptiness, up to practicing in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;

practicing in the applications of mindfulness, practicing in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; practicing in all the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; [and] practicing in the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
Practicing in the superknowledges of the noble truths,

cultivating the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha, and cultivating omniscience, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"This possibility does not exist.
This is the nineteenth mark of irreversibility for one who has reached the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as follows:

If, having trained in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from that conduct as it was taught by the Tathāgata, and is not separated from these mental attentions associated with the perfections, then he does not fall away from the perfection of generosity,
he does not fall away from the perfection of ethical discipline, he does not fall away from the perfection of patience, and he does not fall away from the perfection of vigor.

He does not fall away from the perfection of meditation; he does not fall away from the perfection of wisdom; he does not fall away from internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; he does not fall away from the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
he does not fall away from the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, or the [three] doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and the superknowledges.

He does not fall away from all the gates of liberation, samādhis, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs; he does not fall away from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
he does not fall away from the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it occurs to him thus:

He who understands the deeds of Māra does not fall away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. This is the twentieth [section], the characteristics of irreversibility for one in the stage of having reached the supreme dharmas.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, from what is a bodhisattva mahāsattva known as 'irreversible'?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, he has turned away from the perception of form; he has turned away from the perception of feeling, the perception of perception, the perception of mental formations, and the perception of consciousness; he has turned away from the perception of the elements, the perception of the sense bases, the perception of dependent origination, the perception of the factors of dependent origination, and the perception of passion, hatred, delusion, and views.

He has turned away from the notion of the perfection of generosity, the notion of the perfection of ethical discipline, the notion of the perfection of patience, the notion of the perfection of vigor, the notion of the perfection of meditative concentration, and the notion of the perfection of wisdom;

he has turned away from the notion of internal emptiness up to the notion of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; and he has turned away from the notion of the applications of mindfulness, the notion of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, as well as the notion of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.

He has turned away from the notion of the gates of all liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; he has turned away from the notions of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he has turned away from the notion of the superknowledges; he has turned away from the notions of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
and he has turned away from the notion of the knowledge of all aspects.

He has turned away from the notion of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; he has turned away from the notion of a bodhisattva, up to and including the notion of a buddha. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva [perceives] all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaśūnya).
He has entered the fixed course of the bodhisattvas. He does not apprehend even that dharma; not apprehending it, he does not form it;
not forming it, he does not produce it. Therefore, he is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpādakṣāntika*).
Subhūti, by these modes, these signs, and these marks, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Thus, regarding the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena concerning suffering on the path of seeing:
furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva and attempt to dissuade him, saying:
"This so-called omniscience is equal to space; it is a cultivation like space, characterized by emptiness through the nature of non-existence."

These dharmas, too, are equal to space, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva*), and are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*). Among these dharmas—equal to space, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and empty of their own characteristics—not a single dharma is apprehended: neither that which awakens, nor that by which one awakens, nor that which is awakened to. All these dharmas are equal to space, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and are empty of their own characteristics. You are being needlessly distressed; this is merely the manifestation of the work of Māra, namely, that this is "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
"This was not spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One. Therefore, noble son, you should withdraw these mental preoccupations, lest they lead to your misfortune, suffering, and ruin for a long time.
In that situation, those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, having heard such insults, should investigate as follows:

Those are the works of Māra which divert me from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, although all phenomena are equal to space, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature and being empty of their own characteristics, sentient beings do not know them, do not see them, and do not awaken to them.

Therefore, having donned the armor of the emptiness of own-characteristics regarding all phenomena—which are equal to space and have non-existence as their intrinsic nature—and having fully awakened to the knowledge of all aspects, [we shall act] for the sake of sentient beings.
We shall teach the Dharma; we shall establish immeasurable sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry and in the fruit of once-returning.

"We shall establish them in the fruit of non-returning and in arhatship; we shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; we shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In that regard, by the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—
Starting from the first production of the thought of awakening, having heard these teachings, they must become firm-minded, unshakable-minded, and unassailable-minded;
endowed with this firmness of mind, unshakeability of mind, and unassailability of mind, they will enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva while practicing the six perfections.
Thus [is] the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible be called 'irreversible,' or should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is reversible be called 'irreversible'?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible should be called irreversible;
yet, Subhūti, even a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is reversible should be called irreversible."
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible to be called 'irreversible'? And how is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is reversible to be called 'irreversible'?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has turned back from the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha—Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be called irreversible; he is irreversible."

Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not turned back from the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas—Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be called irreversible; he is to be called irreversible. Subhūti, it is by these aspects, these marks, and these signs that one endowed with them is an irreversible [bodhisattva].
The characteristics of the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood;

by which modes, which marks, and which signs a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such that he cannot be diverted from unexcelled [enlightenment] by Māra, the Evil One— this is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣāntiḥ*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva who so desires enters the first dhyāna, up to entering the fourth dhyāna, and even enters the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

Desiring [these qualities], an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the four foundations of mindfulness; he enters into the right exertions, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path;
he enters into the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and he brings forth the five superknowledges.
He achieves mastery through these four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation;

he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; he enters the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet he does not grasp at the fruits of the dhyānas.
As long as he does not grasp at the fruit of the attainment of cessation, nor grasp at the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor arhatship,
nor does he grasp at solitary enlightenment— even while desiring these— he intentionally takes up a physical existence with such a body as that.

He acts for the benefit of all sentient beings and assumes that physical existence (*ātmabhāva*). Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
This is the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, being endowed with mental attention and never separated from the thought of awakening, does not regard form as weighty; he does not regard moments [of existence] as weighty; he does not regard outflows as weighty; he does not regard generosity as weighty; he does not regard ethical discipline as weighty; he does not regard patience as weighty; he does not regard vigor as weighty; he does not regard meditative concentration as weighty; and he does not regard wisdom as weighty.

He does not become one who values the immeasurables; he does not become one who values the formless realms; he does not become one who values the meditative attainments; he does not become one who values the supernormal powers;

he does not become one who values the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he does not become one who values all the liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments; he does not become one who values emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he does not become one who values the noble truths; he does not become one who values the grounds of self-confidence.
He does not regard analytical knowledge as heavy; he does not regard perfect awakening as heavy; he does not regard the maturation of sentient beings as heavy;
he does not regard the vision of the Buddhas as heavy; he does not regard the planting of roots of virtue as heavy. Why is that?
Because all those phenomena are equal to space, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and are empty of their own characteristics. Furthermore, he...

Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with this mental attention, proceeds and does not retreat by means of the four modes of conduct; he does not come with a distracted mind, nor does he go with a distracted mind, nor will he walk back and forth with a distracted mind.
He will not stand, he will not sit, and he will not lie down; rather, being mindful, he will come, go, walk back and forth, stand, sit, and lie down.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
This is the acceptance of the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin [of suffering].

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dwelling in a household, teaches the five strands of sensual pleasure through skillful means for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
he gives gifts to all sentient beings,
giving food to those who desire food.
He gives drink to those who desire drink, and so on, up to giving various other human requisites;
he himself practices the perfection of generosity,
he encourages others to practice the perfection of generosity, and he speaks in praise of the perfection of generosity.
And he speaks in praise of those others who practice the perfection of generosity, and approves of them;
likewise for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration;
and he himself practices the perfection of wisdom.
He encourages others to practice the perfection of wisdom,
speaks in praise of the perfection of wisdom,
and is one who commends and approves of those others who practice the perfection of wisdom. This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin [of suffering].
Furthermore, Subhūti, that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, while living at home, gives a gift by filling Jambudvīpa with the seven precious jewels;

likewise, he gives a gift by filling a world-system of four continents, a thousandfold world-system, a two-thousandfold world-system, and even up to a great trichiliocosm world-system with the seven precious jewels.
Furthermore, he does not indulge in the qualities of sensual pleasure, but remains constantly and continuously a practitioner of celibacy (*brahmacārī*);
nor does he produce any form of disparagement toward anyone by which another might become displeased.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.

Furthermore, Subhūti, for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi will be constantly and continuously attached to him until that bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— just as he has been constantly and continuously attached to me since I awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— and until the five families of Vajrapāṇis are constantly and continuously attached to him.

He cannot be overcome or crushed by humans or non-humans; he cannot be surpassed by anyone in the world—whether by a god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else—in accordance with the Dharma. This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering].
His mind is not distracted from the mental engagement with awakening until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The faculties of that bodhisattva mahāsattva will not be deficient—the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. That person will be a true being, not an untrue being. Subhūti said:
"To what extent, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become a true person and not an untrue person?
The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, it is when the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perish."
To this extent, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a true person (*satpuruṣa*) and not an untrue person.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with those mental orientations toward awakening (*bodhimanasikāra*).

He does not, in any way whatsoever or in any manner at all, employ or cause others to employ any of those methods for the subjugation of women— whether through spells, sciences, herbs, or medicinal drugs; nor does he perform any act of subjugating women,
nor does he exercise any power of command or miraculous display over either a woman or a man.
Either a son will be born to you or a daughter will be born to you;
he will be of noble birth, or he will be long-lived. For what reason?
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any sign among phenomena that are empty of their own defining characteristics; not perceiving a sign,
he dwells with a completely pure livelihood.
Subhūti, by these aspects, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. This is the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering].

Furthermore, Subhūti, as for those aspects, those marks, and those signs of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva—by which aspects, by which marks, and by which signs he is endowed with irreversibility—[he should be known as such].
One should know him as a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
I shall teach those aspects, those marks, and those signs— listen to them, attend to them well and thoroughly, and I will speak.
"So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
