"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is not separated from the mental engagements of awakening, nor is he intent upon the application to the aggregates."

He dwells; he does not dwell devoted to the application of the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*). He does not dwell devoted to the application of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Why is that?

Because, being established in emptiness, he does not perceive the inferiority or superiority of any dharma whatsoever. This is the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
He does not dwell devoted to the application of talk about thieves. Why is that?

For in this way, among phenomena that are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), he does not perceive the taking up or the discarding of any phenomenon whatsoever. This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*).
He does not dwell engaged in talk about armies. Why is that?

For, established in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*), he does not perceive the smallness or the greatness of any phenomenon whatsoever. This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhe 'nvayajñānakṣāntiḥ*).

He does not dwell devoted to the practice of talk about war. Why is that? Because, established in the true nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmatā*), he perceives neither attachment nor aversion toward any phenomenon whatsoever. He does not dwell devoted to the practice of talk about villages. Why is that? Because, established in universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*), he perceives neither accumulation nor non-accumulation of any phenomenon whatsoever. He does not dwell devoted to the practice of talk about cities. Why is that?
For he, established in the emptiness of space, does not perceive the inclusion or exclusion of any dharma. He does not dwell devoted to the practice of talk concerning villages.
Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, being established at the limit (*koṭi*), he does not perceive the transgression or non-transgression of any dharma. He does not dwell devoted to the practice of talk concerning the self.

Thus, he does not dwell engaged in discourse concerning a being (*sattva*), a living soul (*jīva*), a creature (*jantu*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*puruṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), a human (*manuja*), a man (*mānava*), an agent (*kāraka*), an experiencer (*vedaka*), a knower (*jānaka*), or a seer (*paśyaka*). Why is that?

Because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are absolutely pure; rather, he dwells engaged in discourse concerning the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and he is never separated from mental attentions (*manasikāra*) associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhe ’nvayajñāna*).
Practicing the perfection of generosity, he does not dwell engaged in talk of stinginess; practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, he does not dwell engaged in talk of immorality;
practicing the perfection of patience, he does not dwell engaged in talk of resentment.
While practicing the perfection of vigor, he does not dwell engaged in talk concerning laziness;
while practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, he does not dwell engaged in talk concerning distraction;
while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not dwell engaged in talk concerning lack of wisdom.
Dwelling in the emptiness of all phenomena, he desires only the Dharma and not what is not the Dharma;
moving within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he does not speak in praise of any divisible phenomenon;
he desires friends and not enemies toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas.

He also encourages, introduces, and establishes those great beings as well as those sons of good family belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
he yearns for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
In whichever world-system they abide, remain, and maintain themselves for the sake of being seen, he desires to be reborn there;
he dwells day and night with these mental attentions, namely, mental attentions directed toward the Buddha. For what reason is that?

For it is generally so, Subhūti, that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having produced mental orientations associated with the desire realm and abiding by the ten paths of wholesome action, are reborn in those buddha-fields where Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are present, remaining, and maintaining themselves.

Having produced the first dhyāna up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are reborn there where Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in person.

Subhūti, by these modes, these signs, and these marks, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. This is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, when an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells in internal emptiness, up to dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; when he dwells in the applications of mindfulness; when he dwells in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; and when he dwells in the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments—

For one who stands firm in the noble truths, who stands firm in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—who stands firm in all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, and who stands firm in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha, it does not occur to them:
"I am irreversible," nor does the doubt arise: "Am I irreversible or not? And they become free from uncertainty regarding their own stage. Why is that?

For he does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that either turns back or does not turn back. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a stream-enterer established on the level of the fruit of stream-entry has no doubt and no uncertainty regarding his own level; likewise, [he has no doubt] regarding the levels of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship.
Established on the level of a Buddha, he neither wavers nor doubts;
in the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established on his own level, neither wavers nor doubts. Established there on the level of non-retrogression, he purifies a buddhafield.
He brings sentient beings to maturity,
recognizes each and every demonic deed as it arises,
and does not fall under the power of those demonic deeds.

He recognizes all those deeds of Māra, and having recognized them, he disperses and thins them out. Subhūti, it is just as if a man who has committed an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) were never separated from the thought of that immediate retribution until the time of his death; that thought of immediate retribution simply persists.
And therein he is not able to suppress the mind of immediate retribution;

rather, that outburst of passion persists with him until the time of death. In the very same way, Subhūti, the genuine and stable mind of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva remains fixed upon the stage of irreversibility.
That mind is unshakable;
it cannot be turned back by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Why is that?

Because that irreversible mind has transcended the world of gods, humans, and asuras and has entered the fixed course of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*). Abiding in its own stage, it attains the supreme perfections of the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*).
He purifies the buddha-field, brings sentient beings to maturity,
and travels from buddha-field to buddha-field.
Having planted roots of merit in those buddha-fields, he questions, interrogates, and attends upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, remaining thus,
recognizes each and every māra-activity as it arises.
He does not fall under the sway of whatever demonic activities (*mārakarman*) arise;
through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), he purifies those demonic activities at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, he has no longing for nor doubt regarding his own stage (*bhūmi*). Why is that?
For he is free from doubt regarding the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); he does not conceptualize the limit of reality as being one or two.
Although he has turned away from birth, the thought of the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas does not arise in him. Why is that?

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), does not perceive the arising or the cessation, nor the defilement or the purification of any phenomenon whatsoever.
This is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the path.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics...
He does not perceive the arising or the cessation, nor the defilement or the purification of any dharma whatsoever.
Even one who has turned away from birth does not think:
"I shall not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"I shall indeed fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is empty of its own specific characteristics.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus established in his own stage,"
He is not dependent on others regarding his own stage; he is uncrushable regarding his own stage. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible, being established in this way, becomes endowed with a knowledge that cannot be taken away.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if Māra, the Evil One, should approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha and say: "Attain arhatship right here! You have not been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, you have not attained the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
by which you were prophesied for unexcelled perfect enlightenment by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
nor do those modes, marks, and signs exist within you.

By whatever forms, whatever marks, and whatever signs a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with when he is predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— if, moreover, Subhūti, having heard those words, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not shrink back, does not sink down, is not startled, is not terrified, and does not fall into terror, and his mind does not undergo any change, it should be known that [he will be so predicted].

"Subhūti, I have been predicted by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is that? Because those qualities exist in me by which Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, are predicted for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, if Māra, the Evil One, should approach a Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, in the guise of a Buddha and say:
"Or perhaps a person is possessed by Māra, who says: 'O son of good family, you have been prophesied for the state of a Śrāvaka, not for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
what use have you for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Subhūti, if such a thought should arise in a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,"
"Surely this is Māra the Evil One who has approached in the guise of a Buddha, or a person possessed by Māra;
for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not urge a bodhisattva mahāsattva toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, if Māra the Evil One approaches this bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha and speaks thus:"

"This was not spoken by the Buddha, nor was it spoken by the Śrāvakas; these sūtras in which you move are spoken by Māra. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand: "This is surely Māra the Evil One, or a person possessed by Māra, who seeks to separate me from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it should be understood that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has been predicted by those previous Tathāgatas.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has been established in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones, and is on the stage of non-retrogression. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, those modes, those marks, and those signs that belong to bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible are found in this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these modes, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, even renounces his own self and renounces his very life.
Indeed, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva applies himself solely to the task of upholding the true Dharma.
He undertakes the preservation of the true Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
In this regard, what is that Dharma for the sake of which a bodhisattva mahāsattva even abandons himself and even abandons his life?
In this regard, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, teaches the Dharma that all phenomena are empty.
Therein, certain deluded persons reject and oppose it, saying, "This is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.

For the sake of this [Dharma], Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva even performs the relinquishing of self and the relinquishing of life. In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should think thus:

"Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who shall teach the Dharma—I too shall be included therein; I too have been prophesied there; this very Dharma is mine, for the sake of which I relinquish myself and relinquish my life. Subhūti, it is seeing this purpose that I do so."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, renounces himself and renounces his very life.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is teaching the Dharma, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has no doubt and no hesitation.

Whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak, he grasps it all; and having grasped it in such a way, he does not let it perish. For what reason? Because he has attained the dhāraṇīs. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, by the acquisition of which dhāraṇī do the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata not perish for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has acquired the dhāraṇī of retention, the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata do not perish.”
Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, it is only that which is spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha; it is not that which is spoken by Śrāvakas, nor that which is spoken by gods, nor that which is spoken by nāgas, nor that which is spoken by yakṣas, nor that which is spoken by gandharvas, nor that which is spoken by asuras, nor that which is spoken by garuḍas."
[He does not rely on] the speech of *kiṃnaras*, nor the speech of *mahoragas*.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, regarding whatever sounds, conventions, or vocal expressions there may be, everywhere the bodhisattva mahāsattva has no doubt and no hesitation. For what reason?"
"Subhūti, it is because he has attained such dhāraṇīs and dhāraṇīs that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with great qualities; Blessed One, this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with immeasurable qualities; Blessed One, this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with limitless qualities."

The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with great qualities; Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with immeasurable qualities."
Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with limited qualities. Why is that?
Because he has attained infinite and boundless knowledge that cannot be taken away by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;

and established in that knowledge, the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), by means of which analytical knowledges, once brought forth, [he is not surpassed] by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
"He cannot be overcome by the world.
This is the subsequent knowledge regarding the path; such is the characteristic of the non-retrogression of one established on the path of seeing.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, is capable of describing for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges the forms, marks, and signs by which an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is characterized; it is well.

"Blessed One, please teach those very profound points, abiding in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the six perfections, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path."
He fulfills them;
he fulfills everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
he fulfills the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.
He fulfills the superknowledges of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he fulfills all the gateways of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
and he fulfills the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
One fulfills the knowledge of all modes. Thus is the profound path of cultivation.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
It is indeed excellent, Subhūti, that you, for the sake of the irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, inquire about these most profound points.

"Profound," Subhūti, is a designation for emptiness; it is a designation for the signless, the wishless, the unconditioned, non-arising, non-ceasing, non-extinction, the non-quiescent, suchness, the limit of reality, and the realm of phenomena. These, Subhūti, are those most profound points.
“This is a designation for those things which are called ‘nirvāṇa.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, is this a designation only for nirvāṇa, and not, Blessed One, for all dharmas?”
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, this term 'profound' is indeed a designation for all dharmas. For what reason?
Subhūti, form is profound."
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also profound;
even the eye, Subhūti, is profound.
In the same way, Subhūti, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also profound;
form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena are also profound, Subhūti; and visual consciousness, Subhūti, is also profound.
"Subhūti, eye-contact is profound;
Subhūti, feeling conditioned by eye-contact is profound. Likewise, Subhūti, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness are profound."
Subhūti, mental contact is profound;
Subhūti, feeling conditioned by mental contact is profound;
Subhūti, even the earth element is profound.

In this way, Subhūti, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are profound. Subhūti, dependent origination is profound; ignorance, Subhūti, is profound.

Likewise, the formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age and death—along with sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, Subhūti—are profound.
Subhūti, all the doors of the emptinesses, all the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative attainments, and the dhāraṇīs are profound.
Subhūti, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are profound.
Subhūti, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the noble truths are profound.
Subhūti, the three gateways to liberation are profound;
Subhūti, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha are profound;
even awakening, Subhūti, is profound. And how, moreover, Subhūti, is form profound?
As is the suchness of form, so is it profound;
as is the suchness of feeling, so is it profound;
as is the suchness of perception, so is it profound.
As is the suchness of formations, so is it profound;
as is the suchness of consciousness, so is it profound;
as is the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, so is it profound.
As the suchness of dependent origination is profound, so too is it profound;
as the suchness of the factors of dependent origination is profound, so too is it profound;
likewise, as the suchness of all the perfections is profound, so too is it profound.
As deep as the suchness of all emptinesses, so deep is it; as deep as the suchness of the factors conducive to awakening, so deep is it;
as deep as the suchness of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, so deep is it.
As deep as the suchness of all the doors of liberation, samādhis, meditative attainments, and dhāraṇīs is, so deep is it;
as deep as the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges is, so deep is it;
as deep as the suchness of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha is, so deep is it.
"As the suchness of awakening is, so is the profound. Thus Subhūti spoke regarding the profundity of the path of cultivation:
"How, O Blessed One, is the suchness of form?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, in that suchness where there is no form, nor anything other than form; Subhūti, in that suchness where there is no feeling, nor anything other than feeling."
Subhūti, in that suchness there is no perception, nor is it apart from perception;
Subhūti, in that suchness there are no volitional formations, nor is it apart from volitional formations;

Subhūti, in that suchness there is no consciousness, nor is it apart from consciousness. Likewise, Subhūti, in that suchness there are no aggregates, elements, or sense-fields, nor is it apart from the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields.
Subhūti, in that suchness there is no dependent origination, nor is it apart from dependent origination;
Subhūti, in that suchness there are no factors of dependent origination, nor is it apart from the factors of dependent origination;
Subhūti, in that suchness there are no all-perfections, nor is it apart from all-perfections.
Subhūti, in that suchness there is no all-emptiness, nor is it apart from all-emptiness;
Subhūti, in that suchness there are no factors conducive to awakening, nor is it apart from the factors conducive to awakening;

Subhūti, in that suchness there are no doors of all liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs, nor is it apart from the doors of all liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs.
Subhūti, in that suchness where there are no noble truths, immeasurables, dhyānas, or formless attainments, yet nothing other than the noble truths, immeasurables, dhyānas, and formless attainments;

Subhūti, in that suchness where there are no superknowledges, ten powers, fearlessnesses, or analytical knowledges, yet nothing other than the superknowledges, ten powers, fearlessnesses, and analytical knowledges;
Subhūti, in that suchness where there are no unique qualities of a Buddha, yet nothing other than the unique qualities of a Buddha.
“Subhūti, in that suchness there is no awakening, nor is suchness elsewhere than in awakening.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:

“It is wonderful, Blessed One, how by such a subtle means the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has been turned away from form and yet pointed toward nirvāṇa; and so it is with feeling and perception.”
It is excluded from consciousness and nirvāṇa is indicated;

even within the summary of all phenomena, it is excluded from the mundane and supramundane, the contaminated and the uncontaminated, or from both the contaminated and the uncontaminated, and nirvāṇa is indicated.
Thus, the path of cultivation is free from the extremes of superimposition and denial.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates, weighs, and reflects upon these most profound points associated with the perfection of wisdom—
this is the path of cultivation."
"I must abide in this way as it is commanded in the *Prajñāpāramitā*; I must train in this way as it is explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā*;
I must practice in this way as it is pointed out in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva, thus accomplishing, thus concentrating his mind, thus examining, thus applying himself, thus striving, and thus exerting himself—
this is the path of cultivation consisting of the factors of penetration.

By that production of the thought of awakening, he will acquire incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite roots of merit; for immeasurable eons, he will cast off, turn his back upon, and bring to an end cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
How much more so when, practicing unadulteratedly in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he dwells with mental attentions associated with awakening?
Subhūti, it is just as if that man, who is prone to passion and prone to discursive thought, were with a certain woman...

Suppose a man were to make an appointment with a woman who is beautiful, pleasing, and lovely to behold, yet that woman is under the protection of another and is unable to leave her home. What do you think, Subhūti, with what would the thoughts of that man be associated?
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, such thoughts connected with women would indeed occur to that man:
'This woman has come to me; I shall sit with her, walk with her, and enjoy her company.'"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? With the passing of either a night or a day, how many thoughts would arise in that man?"
Subhūti said: "Many, Blessed One; many, Sugata, would be the discursive thoughts of that person as the day passes by or as the night passes by.
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, as many thoughts as arise for that person during the passing of a day or the passing of a night,
for so many eons does that bodhisattva mahāsattva cast off, turn his back upon, and bring to an end cyclic existence,
provided he trains in, examines, and meditates upon this profound perfection of wisdom exactly as it has been taught.

In such and such a way he applies himself to yoga, so that he avoids those faults by which bodhisattva mahāsattvas turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus devoted to yoga, Subhūti, by this—
The root of merit accumulated in a single day by one dwelling in the dwelling as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* does not approach even a hundredth part,
nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of that [other] root of merit by which world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā would be filled.

It does not even approach— by way of a hundred thousand million-billionth part, nor by way of calculation, nor by way of comparison, nor by way of analogy, nor by way of resemblance, nor by way of nearness, nor by way of cause— even so much as that. Thus is the threefold benefit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to give gifts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges to the Three Jewels—the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṃgha. What do you think, Subhūti?
Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
Thus is the counter-fault that is the highest of the high.
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, this very son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit than that, who applies himself to yoga here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught. For what reason?"
For this is the path of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by which they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, this is the weak-weak counteragent.
What do you think?

Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā and establish offerings among stream-enterers; likewise, were he to establish offerings among once-returners, non-returners, and arhats;
and were he to establish offerings among pratyekabuddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. What do you think?
"Subhūti, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti replied: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
Thus, the adverse side is of the highest-middle degree.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Subhūti, this son of good family or daughter of good family would produce even more merit."
Whoever here applies themselves to the practice of this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught— for what reason is that?

For by practicing here in this perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva, and eventually awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus is the weak-middling counteragent.
What do you think,
Subhūti, regarding a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, [remains for] as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges...
Remaining for eons, one might give gifts, guard morality, accomplish patience, exert vigor, enter meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom; on that basis, one would generate much merit.
Subhūti said:
"Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
Thus is the counter-fault that is intense-mild.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much more merit who,
abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, were to practice giving for even a single day,
guard morality, fulfill patience, exert vigor, attain meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom.
One should cultivate it. For what reason?

Because this Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas; indeed, this Perfection of Wisdom is the progenitor of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. For it is here in the Perfection of Wisdom, Subhūti, that the Bodhisattvas abide.
Great beings bring all dharmas to fulfillment.
Thus, this counteractive measure ranges from weak to intense.
What do you think of this?

"Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges and bestow the gift of Dharma upon sentient beings. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti replied:
"Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
Thus [is] the medium and intense degree of the adverse side.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, remaining here for even a single day in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, were to give the gift of Dharma to sentient beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom is thus.
He is not separated from the knowledge of all aspects, Subhūti, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom and is not separated from the knowledge of all aspects.
Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must remain unseparated from the perfection of wisdom.
Thus is the counteragent that is medium-weak.

What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to apply himself to yoga for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments—
One should apply oneself to yoga by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,

the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; one should apply oneself to yoga by means of the four noble truths, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments.

He would apply himself to the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. What do you think, Subhūti, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
Thus ends the middle-of-the-middle section on the adverse factors.
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much more merit if they were to apply themselves to yoga for even a single day here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught."

By means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

...up until he attains union with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. For what reason? Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom should turn back from omniscience; such a thing cannot occur. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is indeed possible...
"And it is possible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, should turn back from omniscience;
such a case exists. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must not be devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus is the middle-of-the-middle counteragent."

What do you think, Subhūti? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, giving those gifts of material things and gifts of Dharma, and through those two, mental attentions associated with solitary seclusion, [dedicated] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment...
One should dedicate it. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said:
“Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
Thus ends the middling-mild degree of the adverse side.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit,

who, abiding here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, for even a single day practices that gift of material things and that gift of Dharma, and through those two, applies mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom and meditative seclusion toward unexcelled [enlightenment].

One should dedicate it toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment. Why is that? Because this is the supreme dedication, namely, the dedication of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, any dedication that is devoid of the perfection of wisdom is not a true dedication. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should dedicate] toward unexcelled...
"One who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled perfect enlightenment must possess roots of merit dedicated through the perfection of wisdom. This is the moderate-to-intense counteractive measure.
What do you think?

Subhūti, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and having rejoiced in all the roots of merit of the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples, were to dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. What do you think?
“Subhūti, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: “Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.”
Thus, the adverse side is both weak and intense.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much more merit [than that]."

If someone, remaining here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, were to dedicate even for a single day whatever root of virtue they have toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— this indeed is the supreme dedication through sympathetic joy, namely, the dedication through sympathetic joy in the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment must possess the root of virtue consisting in the dedication through sympathetic joy in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, the counteragent is "intense-weak.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But, Blessed One, when it was stated by the Blessed One that volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) is conceptualized (*kalpita*), then how is that [to be understood]?"
Would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce more merit?
Furthermore, Blessed One, it is not possible through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*) to attain right view or enter the fixed course (*niyāma*), nor to realize the fruit of stream-entry,
the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or even the state of a pratyekabuddha.
or to attain awakening, to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus, the adverse factors are weak and middling.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

For indeed, it is not possible through volitional effort to enter into right view or the path of certainty, nor to attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship; nor is it possible to attain pratyekabuddha-enlightenment or to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Moreover, Subhūti, even that volitional formation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is described as being merely empty, merely hollow, and merely vain.
It is declared to be utterly essence-less. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is well-trained in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
thus, this is the superior-middling counteractive measure.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as that bodhisattva mahāsattva, remaining here in this emptiness, examines conditioned formations in whatever manner,

in that very manner the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes not devoid of the perfection of wisdom; and as the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes not devoid of the perfection of wisdom, in that very manner he generates incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite merit.

Thus, Subhūti spoke the characteristics of the irreversible one abiding on the path of cultivation, stating that the extremely mild counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) for the extremely mild discordant factor (*vipakṣa*) implied by this meaning is the extremely intense [counteragent]:
"Blessed One, what is the distinction between the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*aprameya*), and the infinite (*aparimāṇa*)?"
"What is the distinction?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, 'incalculable' refers to that for which no number exists and which does not fall within the scope of calculation."
"Subhūti, that which is called 'incalculable' or 'immeasurable' is that for which no measure can be found among past, future, or present phenomena.
Subhūti, that which is called 'limitless' is that which cannot be measured.
Subhūti said:
"Could it be, Blessed One, that form also would be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite;
and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also, Blessed One, would be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, there may be a way in which form (*rūpa*) would be incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), immeasurable (*aprameya*), and infinite (*aparimāṇa*);
and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*),
and consciousness (*vijñāna*) would likewise be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite— this is an illustration of the terms beginning with "incalculable."
By what method, Blessed One, would form be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite; and how would feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness also be incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, form is empty, incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite;
so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations."
“Consciousness, Subhūti, would be empty, incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite.
Subhūti said: “But, Blessed One, is it only form that is empty?”
Are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness alone empty, while all other phenomena are not empty?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Have I not declared that all phenomena are empty?"
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, all dharmas have been declared by the Tathāgata to be empty; and those, O Blessed One, which are empty are also inexhaustible."
They are incalculable, they are immeasurable, they are infinite;
O Blessed One, no number can be found for emptiness.
Neither a measure nor a quantity is perceived; such is the defining characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the "incalculable" and so forth.
"Therefore, Blessed One, no distinction between these dharmas is perceived, whether in terms of their meaning or their phrasing.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
No distinction between these dharmas is perceived, whether in terms of their meaning or their phrasing. Subhūti, this which has been spoken by the Tathāgata is ineffable;
it is spoken of as "inexhaustible," or "incalculable," or "immeasurable," or "boundless," or "empty," or "signless," or "wishless," or "unconditioned," or "non-arising," or "dispassion."

"Whether it be 'cessation' or 'nirvāṇa,' Subhūti, this is a teaching that issues from the Tathāgata’s inexhaustibility, [extending] from 'the inexhaustible' up to 'nirvāṇa'; it is a teaching issuing from the Tathāgata’s compassion, preceded by a formal inquiry. When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
It is marvelous, Blessed One, how this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is taught by the Tathāgata;
yet that true nature is inexpressible. As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, Blessed One, so all phenomena are inexpressible.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. All dharmas, Subhūti, are ineffable."
"Subhūti, that which is the ineffability of phenomena is emptiness,
and emptiness cannot be expressed in words.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is there increase or decrease of an ineffable object?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti; there is neither increase nor decrease of an ineffable object."
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, if there is neither increase nor decrease in the ineffable reality, then there will likewise be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of generosity."

In this way, there will be neither increase nor decrease in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration; there will be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of wisdom;
and there will be neither increase nor decrease in the four applications of mindfulness.

In this way, there will be neither increase nor decrease of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment; there will be neither increase nor decrease of the noble eightfold path; there will be neither increase nor decrease of the eight liberations; there will be neither increase nor decrease of the nine successive meditative attainments, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges.

There will be neither increase nor decrease in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, or the four analytical knowledges; there will be neither increase nor decrease in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

There will be neither increase nor decrease of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). Blessed One, if there is neither increase nor decrease of these six perfections (*pāramitā*), up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, then, Blessed One, one would be incapable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment characterized by omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, this is an objection based on the state of neither decrease nor increase regarding that which is ineffable.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. There is neither increase nor decrease in the meaning that is ineffable. Furthermore, Subhūti, if for a bodhisattva..."

For a mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the perfection of wisdom, and applies himself to yoga in the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in means, it does not occur to him:
"I am increasing by means of the perfection of wisdom."
"I increase by means of the perfection of meditation; I increase by means of the perfection of vigor;
I increase by means of the perfection of patience."
"I am increasing through the perfection of ethical discipline;
I am increasing through the perfection of generosity. Furthermore, it occurs to him:
"This which is called the perfection of generosity is merely a name."
While practicing the perfection of generosity,

he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of the thought of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and he dedicates them in such a way that they become unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

In this way, while practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, one dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of the thought of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening— just as unexcelled, perfect,
and complete awakening is. This is the response.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"And what, Blessed One, is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
"The suchness of all dharmas is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti asked:
"Lord, what is this suchness of all dharmas which is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that which is the suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness;

likewise, that which is the suchness of the aggregates, the suchness of the elements, the suchness of the sense bases, the suchness of dependent origination, and the suchness of the factors of dependent origination—"
In this way, up to the point that the suchness of nirvāṇa is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;

it neither increases nor decreases. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells frequently and extensively, never separated from the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the increase or the decrease of any dharma whatsoever. Thus indeed, Subhūti, for an ineffable reality, there is neither increase nor decrease.

And thus, Subhūti, there is neither increase nor decrease of the perfection of generosity; likewise, there is neither increase nor decrease of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
and likewise, [there is neither increase nor decrease] of the emptinesses, the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, and the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments.

There is neither increase nor decrease in all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; in the superknowledges; in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; in the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should practice] in the perfection of wisdom.
"One should practice by means of a yoga that is neither increasing nor decreasing.
Thus Subhūti spoke regarding the characteristic of awakening.

In that regard, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening, or rather, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final production of the thought of awakening?
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [awakens] by means of the first production of the thought of awakening...
When one awakens to perfect complete enlightenment,

that initial production of the thought of awakening does not coexist with the final production of the thought of awakening, and the final production of the thought of awakening does not coexist with the initial production of the thought of awakening.
"Blessed One, since the mind and mental factors do not coexist in this way, how can roots of virtue be accumulated?
For it is not possible to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment without having accumulated roots of virtue.
This is the objection based on the non-coexistence of the two minds.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Subhūti, I shall give you a simile to clarify this very point;
for by means of a simile, some wise people here will understand the meaning of what is said. What do you think?"
"Subhūti, when an oil lamp is burning with its wick aflame, is that wick burned by the first incidence of the flame, or is it burned by the final incidence of the flame?
Subhūti replied:

"It is not, Blessed One, that the wick is burned by the initial impact of the flame, nor is it burned without depending on the initial impact of the flame; it is not, Blessed One, that the wick is burned by the final impact of the flame, nor is it burned without depending on the final impact of the flame."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Has that wick been burned?"
Subhūti said:
"Burnt, Blessed One; burnt, Sugata. The Blessed One said:
In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening,
nor does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without relying on the first production of the thought of awakening;
yet, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final production of the thought of awakening.

And yet, without relying on the final production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And yet, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
for herein, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [relies upon] the first production of the thought of awakening.
Having relied upon and fully perfected the ten stages, one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, what are the ten stages that a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fully perfect in order to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, having fulfilled the stage of pure insight (*śuklavipaśyanābhūmi*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

likewise, having fulfilled the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage (*aṣṭamakabhūmi*), the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanubhūmi*), the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*), and the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtāvībhūmi*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He awakens; having fulfilled the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
having fulfilled the bodhisattva stage, the bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having fulfilled the Buddha-ground, the bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therein, while training in the ten grounds, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening alone,
nor does he awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without relying upon that first production of the thought of awakening.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final production of the thought of awakening,
nor does he awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without depending upon the final production of the thought of awakening;
yet, he does indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, with the illustration of the lamp, the refutation was stated;
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, dependent origination is profound."

And yet, Blessed One, it is not by means of the first production of the thought of awakening that a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor, Blessed One, is it without having relied upon the first production of the thought of awakening; and yet, Blessed One, it is not by means of the final production of the thought of awakening [that he does so].
And yet, without depending upon the final production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and yet, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Will that mind which has ceased arise again? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. Thus [the Blessed One spoke] regarding the profundity of arising:
"What do you think?"
“Subhūti, is that mind which has arisen subject to cessation?
Subhūti replied, “It is subject to cessation, Blessed One; it is subject to cessation, Sugata.”
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Will that which has the nature of cessation cease?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. Thus [regarding] the profundity of cessation, the Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Will it remain just as suchness remains?
Subhūti said:
"In that very way, Blessed One, it will abide, just as suchness abides.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
“Subhūti, it will remain just as suchness and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are.
Subhūti said: “Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is suchness profound?"
Subhūti said:
"Profound, O Blessed One. Thus the Blessed One spoke regarding the profundity of suchness.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the mind exactly as suchness is?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti, is the mind other than suchness?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. Thus ends the profundity of the object of knowledge.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does suchness perceive suchness?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. Thus [regarding] the profundity of knowledge, the Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Does he who practices in this way practice in the profound perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, he who courses in this manner courses in the profound perfection of wisdom."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? He who practices in this way—"
"Where does he course?
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, he who courses in this manner..."
He does not course anywhere. For what reason?

Because, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of wisdom, these mental activities do not exist and do not manifest; for one who stands in suchness, Blessed One, nothing at all manifests.
"Nor does anyone practice therein. Such is the profundity of practice. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, as for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, wherein does he practice?"
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, he courses in the ultimate truth where the occurrence of duality is not found.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Does one who courses in the ultimate truth course in conventional conduct? Does he course in signs?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Has he thereby cultivated either the perception of signs or the perception of signlessness?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. Thus the Blessed One spoke on the profundity of non-duality:
"In that regard, Subhūti, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cultivate either the perception of signs or the perception of signlessness?"
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not apply himself in this way: 'I shall cultivate the sign,' or 'I shall cultivate the signless.'"

Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, Blessed One, this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which skillful means he does not make any phenomenon either existent or non-existent. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the bodhisattva mahāsattva stands in the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*) of all phenomena.
And abiding therein in the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), he enters into the three concentrations;
for the sake of sentient beings, he brings them to maturity by means of those concentrations.
Thus, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the three concentrations.
And there, Blessed One, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the three samādhis, applies those beings who practice with aspiration to the aspirationless;

and those beings who practice in conceptualization, the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes them in emptiness; and those beings who practice in signs, the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes them in the signless.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom matures sentient beings through the three concentrations.
Thus has been described the group of those in training who are irreversible, characterized by skillful means and profundity.
Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, enters into the three concentrations— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
does he thereby increase in the perfection of wisdom?"
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, if one increases through cultivation during the day, then one likewise increases even while in a dream. For what reason?"
It is non-conceptual. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, there is neither dream nor day;
if, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom during the day, [then he possesses it at all times].

"Then, even for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered into a dream, there will be the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. When this non-conceptualization regarding existence and peace had been thus stated, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs an action while in a dream..."
There is neither accumulation nor increase of that karma;
for as all phenomena have been described by the Blessed One as being like a dream, so there is for him neither accumulation nor increase. Why is that?
For in a dream, no decrease or increase of any dharma whatsoever is perceived. However, once one has awakened, one may conceptualize it, and for that person there is decrease or increase.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Venerable Śāriputra:
And suppose someone has committed the taking of life during the day, and having killed it in a dream, upon waking he conceptualizes it, thinking:
"Oh, I have killed it! It was well killed!"
"Regarding that, Venerable Śāriputra, what does 'action' say?
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, action does not arise without an objective support; action arises only with an objective support."

Subhūti said: "It is so, venerable Śāriputra. Karma arises with various objects; volition arises with various objects. Indeed, venerable Śāriputra, karma arises only with an object; volition arises only with an object."
It does not have various objects. Cognition proceeds by means of phenomena that are seen, heard, thought, or cognized;
cognition does not proceed by means of phenomena that are unseen, unheard, unthought, or uncognized. In this regard, some cognition grasps defilement, while some cognition grasps purification.
"Therefore, then, venerable Śāriputra, action arises only with an object, not without an object; volition arises only with an object, not without an object.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, if all actions and all volitions have been declared by the Blessed One to be secluded,"
"In that case, how is it that karma arises only with an object and not without an object,
and volition arises only with an object and not without an object?
Subhūti replied:

"Venerable Śāriputra, having taken a sign as its object, karma arises only with an objective support, not without an objective support; volition arises only with an objective support, not without an objective support.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the elder Subhūti:

Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, should give a gift, guard his moral discipline, fulfill patience, exert vigor, enter meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom— and should dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment— then it is dedicated to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the venerable Subhūti the Elder said this to the venerable Śāriputra:

"Venerable Śāriputra, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is present here; he is bound by only one more birth and has been prophesied by the Blessed One as being irreversible. He should be questioned; he will answer."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "This Elder Subhūti has spoken thus: 'This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is present here, bound by only one more birth; he has been prophesied by the Blessed One as irreversible. He should be questioned; he will provide the answer.'"
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya answer by means of a name, or will he answer by means of form?"
Will feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness be relinquished?
That which is the emptiness of form will relinquish it.
Is that which is the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations,
and the emptiness of consciousness that which will relinquish [them]?
And that which is the emptiness of form is not capable of relinquishing it.
Is that which is the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, and the emptiness of consciousness capable of relinquishing anything?
What, then, will it relinquish? I do not perceive any such dharma that would relinquish.
I do not perceive that dharma which he will relinquish, nor that wherein he will relinquish it.
That dharma which has been predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
that by which it was predicted;
or that in which it was predicted—
“I do not perceive even that dharma; all these dharmas are non-dual and without division.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
“Maitreya, have you personally realized these dharmas in the same way that you speak of them?”
Maitreya said:
"I have not realized these dharmas in the way that I speak of them.
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:
Profound indeed is the wisdom of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya! For just as he has practiced the perfection of giving,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom,
so too is this teaching for one who practices non-apprehension, being itself non-apprehensible.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "What do you think, Śāriputra?
Do you perceive that dharma by which you are designated as an arhat?"
Śāriputra said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
In the same way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:

"This dharma will predict [enlightenment], this dharma is being predicted, or this dharma has been predicted; he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Coursing in this manner, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
And no doubt arises in him:
"I shall not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; I will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in this way courses in the perfection of wisdom. Coursing in this way, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not afraid, nor does he tremble.
He does not fall into terror;
he thinks, "I shall not fail to awaken, I will indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This succession of challenges is called the equality of existence and peace.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity, upon seeing beings who are hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, inadequately dressed, and lacking beds and seats, should reflect as follows:"
"I shall practice the perfection of generosity in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

all these faults of these sentient beings will not exist at all, nor will they be found, just as [they are absent] among the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin."

for the enjoyment and utilization by the gods of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Śuddhāvāsa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Aspṛha, Atapa, and Akaniṣṭha heavens;

Such will be the enjoyments and resources of sentient beings in that buddha-field. Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of generosity and draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline [encounters] those who take life...

Having seen beings who take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, speak harshly, utter divisive words, indulge in idle chatter, harbor covetousness, possess malevolent thoughts,

and hold wrong views— beings who are short-lived, afflicted by many ailments, full of distress, ugly, lacking in influence, possessing little wealth, born into low families, following base livelihoods, and deprived of limbs— one should examine them in this way:
"In such and such a way will I practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
these faults shall neither exist nor be perceived among those beings in that buddha-field.
Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline and draws near to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience, upon seeing sentient beings whose minds are full of mutual malice— beating one another with clods of earth, striking one another with weapons, depriving one another of life, and engaging in combat with staffs against staffs, clubs against clubs, pulling each other by the hair, and tearing each other’s hair— should examine the situation in this way:
In such a way will I practice the perfection of patience that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
these faults shall neither exist nor be perceived among those beings in that buddha-field; and all beings shall possess minds equal toward one another as toward a mother.
They will have minds equal toward their fathers,
they will have minds equal toward their brothers, and they will have minds equal toward their sisters.

They will possess a mind equal toward sons and daughters, and they will possess a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*). Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) and will draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) [should look upon] those of inferior vigor...
Seeing sentient beings who are indolent, lazy, lacking in effort, and of little strength— beings who have set out by means of the three vehicles,
whether by the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas— one should examine oneself thus:
"I shall practice the perfection of vigor in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [my followers will not be so]."

In that buddha-field, these faults of those beings will not exist and will not be perceived. Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of vigor and draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration sees beings engaged in the five hindrances— the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt— [he should reflect as follows].

[He beheld] beings who were proceeding [in saṃsāra], deluded and of confused mindfulness, devoid of the first dhyāna, devoid of the second dhyāna, devoid of the third dhyāna, and devoid of the fourth dhyāna; devoid of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and devoid of the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Seeing beings thus deprived [of these qualities], one should reflect:

"I shall practice the perfection of meditation in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, those beings in that buddha-field will neither possess nor even perceive these faults. In this manner...
Subhūti, practicing thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of meditative concentration and draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom [should regard] those of poor wisdom...
Seeing sentient beings who have fallen away from wisdom— beings devoid of mundane and supramundane right view, who are proponents of non-action,

nihilism, annihilationism, eternalism, and those who propound identity, difference, or both— one should reflect thus: "I shall practice the perfection of wisdom in such a way that [I may attain] my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

When he has attained perfect awakening in that buddha-field, all these faults of those beings will not exist at all, nor will they even be known. Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of wisdom and draws near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing beings existing within the three categories— those fixed in rightness, those unfixed, and those fixed in falsehood— should examine them in this way:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections."

I shall purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, such that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, even the sound of the words "fixed," "unfixed," or "fixed in falsehood" will not exist, even as a mere report, among the sentient beings in that buddha-field.

It will not be perceived. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections sees beings in the hells, beings in the animal realm, and beings in the world of Yama, he should think as follows:
In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections, purify a buddhafield,
and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, even the sound of the three lower realms shall not exist in that buddhafield.
It will not be perceived.
Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, these great terrestrial stumps, thorns, thickets, precipices, ravines, gullies, cesspools, and dung-heaps [are to be regarded as such].
Having seen them thus fulfilled, one should examine it in this way:
"In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections and I shall purify the buddha-field."

"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, those faults shall not exist for those sentient beings in that buddha-field,

and my buddha-field shall be as level as the palm of a hand. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, seeing this great earth as consisting of mere clay and devoid of gold and silver, should reflect:
"In such and such a manner will I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,

this great earth in that buddha-field will be covered with golden sand. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and draws near to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees beings existing in a state of possessiveness and grasping, he should examine himself in this way:
"In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections and purify a buddhafield."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

those sentient beings in that buddha-field will have no sense of 'mine' or possessiveness, nor will such things be perceived. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing the four castes— the kṣatriyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras— should examine himself thus:
"In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

there will not even be the sound of the four castes in that buddha-field, nor will they be known. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
And he becomes one who practices [this].

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections sees the inferior, superior, and middling states of beings, as well as the inferior, middling, and superior birth-statuses of beings—
Having seen this, one should examine it thus: "In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections,
purify the buddha-field,
and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, [it shall be so] there."
