In that buddha-field, these defects of sentient beings will not exist and will not be perceived. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, upon seeing the diversity of the appearances of sentient beings, should investigate in this manner:
In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections, purify the buddha-field,
and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, there will be no diversity of appearance among the sentient beings in that buddha-field.

Except for this, all beings will be handsome, pleasing, and beautiful, endowed with the excellence of a most sublime complexion. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing a sovereign ruler, should examine himself in this way:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddhafield."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity in such a way that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

even the designation of a sovereign will not exist nor be known in that buddha-field, except for the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, who has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, practicing in this manner, a bodhisattva...
The mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, having seen the differentiation of the destinies of sentient beings, should investigate thus:
"In such and such a way shall I practice in the six perfections."

I shall purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will be no differentiation of destinies for sentient beings in that buddha-field, nor will it be perceived; there will be no hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, gods, or humans, but rather all sentient beings will be of a single karma.
They will be never separated from the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the noble truths, and the [three doors of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

By means of the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the superknowledges, and so on up to the four analytical knowledges— practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, having seen the four modes of birth of sentient beings— the egg-born, the womb-born, the moisture-born, and the spontaneously born—
Having seen this, one should examine it thus:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."

"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in that buddha-field, there will be no three modes of birth for sentient beings; there will be no egg-born, no womb-born, and no moisture-born, but all sentient beings will be of miraculous birth. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, seeing sentient beings devoid of the five superknowledges, should reflect as follows:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

all sentient beings in that buddha-field will possess the five superknowledges. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing the excrement, urine, and so forth of all sentient beings, should reflect in this way:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

all sentient beings in that buddha-field will have the joy of the Dharma and meditative concentration as their sustenance. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of omniscience."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing beings devoid of light, should reflect:
"In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

all sentient beings in that buddhafield will be self-luminous. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of all-knowledge."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, having observed sentient beings throughout nights, days, months, half-months, and years, should examine himself in this way:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."

"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in that buddha-field, there will be no sound and no perception of nights, days, months, fortnights, or years among those sentient beings. Subhūti, practicing in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections."
And he becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing beings deficient in lifespan, should reflect:
"In such and such a way shall I practice the six perfections."
"I shall purify a buddhafield and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
the beings in that buddhafield will have immeasurable lifespans. Subhūti, it is by practicing in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [proceeds].
He fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, seeing that sentient beings are devoid of [intrinsic] marks, should examine himself thus:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections."
I shall purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
the sentient beings in that buddha-field will be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. Thus...
Subhūti, while practicing, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing beings who are devoid of roots of virtue, should reflect in this way:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections."

"I shall purify a buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all sentient beings in that buddha-field will be endowed with roots of virtue,
and by means of those roots of virtue they will attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections.
And he becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing beings afflicted by disease, should examine himself thus:
"In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections and purify a buddha-field."

"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in that buddha-field, four types of diseases will not exist among those beings, nor even be known. What are the four?

Those arising from wind, those arising from bile, those arising from phlegm, or those arising from a combination of the humors. Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and trains for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, upon seeing sentient beings afflicted by the three defilements, should reflect:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice the six perfections and purify the buddha-field."
I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, three afflictions will not exist nor be known in that buddha-field.
Which three?
Lust, hatred, and delusion. And all sentient beings there will be free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.
Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, upon seeing sentient beings of inferior inclinations, should reflect:
"In such and such a manner shall I practice in the six perfections."

I shall purify a buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in that buddha-field there will be no sound of, nor even the name of, two vehicles— neither the vehicle of the śrāvaka nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.

"Except for those who will set out toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and becomes one who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, upon seeing beings who are conceited, should reflect as follows:"
In such and such a manner I shall practice the six perfections, purify a buddha-field,

and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, even the sound of the word "arrogant beings" will not exist in that buddha-field.
It will not be perceived,

except that all sentient beings will become free from conceit. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who cultivates the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections should generate this thought:
"I shall not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as long as the measure of my lifespan in that buddha-field is limited, and the measure of my radiance is limited."
The community of monks is limited;
nevertheless, I shall practice the six perfections in such and such a manner,
and I shall purify a buddha-field.

"And I shall bring sentient beings to maturity so that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the measure of my lifespan in that buddha-field will be immeasurable, my radiance will be immeasurable,

and my community of monks will be immeasurable. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections should examine himself in this way:
"I shall not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening as long as my single buddha-field has not become as vast as as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges;
rather, I shall practice the six perfections in such and such a manner."

"I shall purify a buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity, so that when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges shall become my single buddha-field."
Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections should investigate in this manner:
"Alas, this saṃsāra is indeed long!"

This realm of sentient beings is vast; therefore, one should attend to it properly in this way: "Alas, this saṃsāra is as limitless as space; alas, this realm of sentient beings is as limitless as space."

And herein no one at all will transmigrate, nor will anyone at all attain final nirvana. Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six perfections and becomes one who practices for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects.
Now, at that time, a sister named Gaṅgadevā was present and seated in that assembly.
Rising from his seat, draping his upper robe over one shoulder, and placing his right knee upon the ground, he bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, Sugata, having practiced the six perfections, I shall take hold of a buddha-field of such a nature as has been described here by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in this Perfection of Wisdom."
Then that woman, having taken golden flowers,
having taken silver flowers,
and having taken flowers both born of water and born of land, [proceeded].

Having taken all the ornaments and having taken a pair of garments of golden-yellow hue, he cast them toward where the Blessed One was. As soon as that pair of fine cotton cloths was cast, by the power of the Buddha, they immediately rose up into the sky above the Blessed One.

At the summit of the joint, there stood a gabled pavilion— quadrangular, with four pillars, symmetrical, constructed part by part, well-proportioned, and beautiful. Then that woman, having made that gabled pavilion common to all sentient beings, dedicated it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the woman’s resolute intention, manifested a smile at that moment.

Now, it is the natural law of the Blessed Buddhas that whenever they manifest a smile, rays of light of many colors and various hues issue forth from the Blessed One’s mouth. At that very instant, such rays indeed issued forth.

Just as if they were blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, or the color of crystal and silver, they went to those infinite and boundless world-systems, and having returned once more, circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.
Then, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and [extended] his right...
Placing his knees upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause? What is the condition?"
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, this sister Gaṅgadevā, in a future time, will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One named Suvarṇapuṣpa."

Ānanda, in the world during the aeon known as Tārakopama, this sister Gaṅgadevā will experience her final existence as a woman. Having cast off her female state and attained the male state, Ānanda, this sister Gaṅgadevā will be reborn in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Akṣobhya.
In the world-system Abhirati, he will practice the holy life there. Furthermore, Ānanda, this bodhisattva mahāsattva shall have the name Suvarṇapuṣpa.
Moreover, Ānanda, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvarṇapuṣpa has passed away from there, he will travel from buddha-field to buddha-field.
And he shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Ānanda, it is just as when a universal monarch (cakravartin) walks from palace to palace;

throughout his life, until the time of his death, he does not touch the earth with the soles of his feet. In the same way, Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvarṇapuṣpa [will travel] from buddha-field to buddha-field.
"until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Ānanda:
"As many bodhisattva mahāsattvas as there will be assembled in that buddha-field,"
That should be known as an assembly of Tathāgatas.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Ānanda, said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"It is so, Ānanda, just as you say."

That gathering of bodhisattva mahāsattvas which occurs in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Suvarṇapuṣpa should be known as a "Tathāgata-gathering"; there will be a community of monks there that is not limited by measure, and it is impossible to determine the number of that community of monks.
There are this many disciples, or this many hundreds of disciples,
or this many thousands of disciples.
There are this many hundreds of thousands of disciples, or this many millions of disciples, or this many hundreds of millions of disciples.
There will be either this many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of śrāvakas,
or this many hundreds of thousands of niyutas of koṭis of śrāvakas;
indeed, there will be incalculable, immeasurable, and limitless hundreds of thousands of niyutas of koṭis of śrāvakas belonging to Suvarṇapuṣpa.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
all these defects that have been described here in the Perfection of Wisdom will, in every way and in every respect, no longer exist nor even be known in that Buddha-field.
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, where was this Gaṅgadevā planted the roots of merit?
The Blessed One replied:
Ānanda, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṅkara, this sister planted roots of merit and resolved her mind upon unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment; she dedicated those roots of merit toward unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment, and while aspiring for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, she scattered golden flowers over that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṅkara.
Ānanda, when I scattered five blue lotuses over the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara while aspiring for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
I was then endowed with roots of virtue by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.

Having understood this, he was prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment: "In a future age, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni—an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. At that time...
Upon hearing this prophecy concerning me from her sister, she conceived this thought:

"O, may I too in a future time be prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment just as this young man has been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus, Ānanda, it was by this sister...
"In the presence of that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, his first thought was generated for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, this sister Gaṅgadevā has performed the preliminary preparations for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is."
"As you say,
sister Gaṅgadevā, this Ānandā has performed the preparatory practices for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having said this, the supreme purification of the field was declared.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, by what means should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivate mastery over emptiness?
How should emptiness be meditated upon?"
How is there mastery over the signless?
How is the signless to be cultivated?
How should mastery be achieved over the wishless?
How should one cultivate the wishless?
Up to: how should one achieve mastery in the factors conducive to awakening?
How should the factors conducive to awakening be cultivated?
Thus ends the section on the domain of skill in means.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate that form is empty."
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are to be contemplated as empty;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are to be contemplated as empty.
Dependent origination should be contemplated as empty;
the factors of dependent origination should be contemplated as empty;
and so on, up to the realm of desire, which should be contemplated as empty.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) should be contemplated as empty;
the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) should be contemplated as empty. And it should be contemplated in such a way that, while contemplating, one does not distract that mind.
With an undistracted mind, he does not perceive that dharma which would be realized; he does not perceive that dharma.
Not perceiving [them], he does not realize them. Why is that?

Because, having been well-trained in phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), he does not effect the exclusion of any phenomenon, nor is there anything for him to realize.
Whatever he might realize, or that by which he might realize it—
he perceives all those phenomena as neither conjoined nor disjoined.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Regarding what the Blessed One has said—
that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize empty phenomena— how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while abiding in emptiness, not realize emptiness?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects,
he does not contemplate it thinking, 'I shall realize it directly.'"
He does not contemplate that "it must be realized," but he contemplates, "I shall bring it to mastery.

He contemplates, "this is not the time for realization"; he contemplates, "this is the time for mastery, this is not the time for realization. While still not yet concentrated, the bodhisattva mahāsattva...
He fixes his mind upon an object of focus;
during this interval, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall away from the factors conducive to awakening, yet he does not personally realize the destruction of the outflows. Why is that?
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will be endowed with such sublime knowledge. Why is that?
Because one who stands firm in the factors conducive to awakening knows thus: "This is the time for mastery; this is not the time for direct realization.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should reflect in this manner:
This is the time for the perfection of generosity;
this is the time for the perfection of ethical discipline;
this is the time for the perfection of patience.
This is the time for the perfection of vigor;
this is the time for the perfection of meditation;
this is the time for the perfection of wisdom.
This is the time for the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness;
likewise, this is the time for the cultivation of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;
this is the time for the cultivation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

This is the time for internal emptiness; this is the time for external emptiness; this is the time for internal and external emptiness; up to this is the time for the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
This is the time for the cultivation of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments;
this is the time for the cultivation of the noble truths.
This is the time for the cultivation of the five superknowledges;
this is the time for the cultivation of the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs;
this is the time for the acquisition of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

This is the time for the attainment of the four grounds of self-confidence; this is the time for the attainment of the analytical knowledges; this is the time for the fulfillment of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
this is the time for the attainment of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
This is not the time for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry;
this is not the time for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; this is not the time for the realization of the fruit of non-returning.
"This is not the time for the realization of the fruit of arhatship; this is not the time for the realization of the knowledge of a pratyekabuddha;
this is the time for the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates mastery in emptiness."
He dwells in emptiness,
masters the signless,
and dwells in the signless.

He masters the wishless and dwells in the wishless. He cultivates the applications of mindfulness and dwells by means of the applications of mindfulness, yet he does not realize them. Likewise, he cultivates the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, as well as the noble eightfold path, and he dwells by means of the noble eightfold path, yet he does not realize it.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva masters the factors conducive to awakening, cultivates the factors conducive to awakening, and dwells in the factors conducive to awakening; yet he does not realize the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor does he realize the fruit of arhatship. This is the application of skillful means.
Subhūti, it is just as if there were a certain man who would be brave, heroic,
and firmly established.
He would be handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.
He would be endowed with the excellence of most beautiful complexion and form,
he would have reached the highest mastery in archery and weaponry,
and he would have taken up firm weapons.
He would be fully accomplished in all sixty-four arts, he would have mastered every field of craftsmanship and every sphere of activity,
and he would be dear and pleasing to many people.
Whatever action he might undertake, in every instance he would be endowed with gain and honor;

and by means of that, he would honor, revere, respect, and worship many people, becoming all the more delighted, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness toward his mother, father, children, and wife.

Having taken them with him for some particular business, he might have entered a great, terrifying, and formidable forest wilderness, which is frightening to the foolish and causes one's hair to stand on end;
and having entered there, that man [left behind] those parents, children, and wife.
He should invite them with words of fearlessness, saying:

"Do not fear, do not fear! I shall quickly lead you away from this great, terrifying, and formidable wilderness and forest—this place that strikes fear into the foolish and causes one's hair to stand on end—and I shall quickly set you free. And to him...
In that forest wilderness, many enemies, murderers, adversaries, and foes would be encountered by that man;
yet that man would be endowed with supreme power of wisdom,
and having delivered them— having led his mother, father, sons, and wife out from that forest wilderness— he would [further...]
Having thus gone to a village, or a city, or a town, or a district, or a region, he should dwell having given rise to joy and gladness, unhurt and unharmed,
and he should not allow his mind to become corrupted toward those beings who are adversaries or enemies. Why is that?
For he would thus become proficient in all the arts;
by means of that, in that forest wilderness, other more noble adversaries and enemies— more numerous, more heroic, and more skilled with firm weapons than those [initial] adversaries and enemies—
would be conjured up for them.
They would all be freed from that fear. Then that man, having safely delivered his parents, children, and wife, would dwell in happiness.

In the same way, Subhūti, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells having pervaded all sentient beings with a mind directed toward loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and with a mind directed toward compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), in that interval, Subhūti, the bodhisattva—
The Mahāsattva is not defined by the signless, nor does he abide on the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha through the realization of the signless samādhi.
This is the means for transcending obstructive dharmas.
Subhūti, it is just as if a winged bird moves through the air and does not fall to the ground;
it dwells in the sky, in the intermediate space, yet it neither stays nor rests there. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva masters emptiness and dwells by means of emptiness.
He masters the signless and dwells in the signless; he masters the wishless and dwells in the wishless;
yet he does not personally realize emptiness, the signless, or the wishless.
By which realization one might fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha—
[realization] that is devoid of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha.
Having practiced, one attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus is the method of dwelling without fixation (*apratiṣṭhitavihāra*).
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a powerful master of archery who was well-trained in the science of archery;
he would shoot an arrow upward and, with other arrows, [strike] that previous arrow in succession.
It would not fall to the earth as long as that man so desired; indeed,
this arrow would only fall to the earth when he no longer wished to cast another subsequent arrow upward.
In this way, that succession of arrows would fall upon the earth.

In the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, being sustained by skill in means, does not realize that ultimate limit of reality as long as those roots of virtue [are not yet complete].
They become matured for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
when those roots of virtue have become matured for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, then one realizes that supreme limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
"Practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should thus contemplate and examine the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena.
This is the method for following through with the momentum of one's vow.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult who trains here in the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), trains in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), trains in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), trains in absolute emptiness (atyantaśūnyatā), and so on, up to training in the emptiness of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā),
and even up to training in the three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha).
And he does not fall into despondency regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
it is marvelous, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:

For it is thus, Subhūti: all sentient beings have not been abandoned by the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, for one who has not abandoned all sentient beings, there is such a specific excellence of vow as this, Subhūti:
the bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought, "All sentient beings have not been abandoned by me; I must liberate them."
Abiding by means of dharmas that do not exist, he brings forth the gate of liberation that is the peaceful concentration on emptiness;
he brings forth the gate of liberation that is the signless concentration; he brings forth the gate of liberation that is the wishless concentration.

At that time, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as being endowed with skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), and he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the interim until he has attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the uncommon means.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to contemplate those profound points, he should be known as being endowed with skill in means.
That is to say: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and the three gateways to liberation—one should thus bring forth the production of the thought [of awakening].

For a long time these beings have wandered in the sphere of apprehension, dwelling upon the notion of a self, the notion of a being, the notion of a soul, the notion of a creature, the notion of a nourisher, the notion of a person, the notion of an individual, the notion of a human, the notion of a youth, the notion of an agent, the notion of an experiencer, the notion of a knower, and the notion of a seer.

In order to abandon their view of apprehension, I shall awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and teach the Dharma. At that time, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the gateway to liberation of the concentration on emptiness,

cultivates the gateway to liberation of the signless concentration, and cultivates and enters the gateway to liberation of the wishless concentration, yet does not realize the limit of reality— that realization by which one would attain the fruit of stream-entry— [he remains thus].
He might attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship;

he might attain solitary enlightenment— at that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva would not attain the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor would he attain arhatship.
He would not attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and these roots of merit,
does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim, nor does he fall away from the four immeasurables and the four meditative absorptions.

By means of the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, he does not fall away.
He does not fall away from the perfection of generosity, he does not fall away from the perfection of ethical discipline,
and he does not fall away from the perfection of patience.
He does not fall away from the perfection of vigor, he does not fall away from the perfection of meditation,
and he does not fall away from the perfection of wisdom.
He does not fall away from the noble truths;

he does not fall away from all the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; and he does not fall away from the five superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges.
He does not fall away from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
nor does he fall away from great loving-kindness and great compassion. Thus, at that time,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with all the factors conducive to awakening and does not fall away from them until he reaches unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

He attains full awakening. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, embraced by skill in means, increases in pure qualities, and his faculties become so exceedingly sharp that they are not like those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This is the method of [overcoming] incapacity.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "For a long time these beings have had their minds perverted by the four perversions—namely, the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of purity, and the perception of self. For their sake, I shall likewise awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and teach the Dharma."

In such a way that even the mental application [of the thought] "it is impermanent," "it is suffering," "it is impure," or "it is not-self" will no longer occur. Endowed with this production of the thought and through skill in means, he courses in the perfection of wisdom;
he enters the meditative absorption of the Buddha-qualities, yet the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four [fearlessnesses] remain unfulfilled.

At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and enters into the gateways of liberation— the concentrations on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— by means of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
And he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "For a long time these beings have practiced with the notion of apprehension, thinking 'this is self.'"
"Sentient being," "living soul," "creature," "nourisher," "person," "individual," "human," "man," "agent," "experiencer," "knower," or "seer";
or "form," or "feeling," or "perception," or "mental formations," or "consciousness"; or "aggregates," or "elements," or "bases," or "dependent origination," or "factors of dependent origination."

"Or, by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, I shall act in such a way that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, these faults of apprehension will no longer exist for sentient beings.
Endowed with these productions of the thought of awakening and practicing this skill in means within the perfection of wisdom, he...

At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) because the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), as well as great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), are not yet complete; rather, at that moment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation consists of the gate of liberation that is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatāsamādhi-vimokṣamukha*).
It reaches fulfillment. Thus is the method of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it occurs to him: "For a long time these beings have practiced with signs—whether with signs of women, or signs of men, or signs of form, or signs of the formless."
"Or rather, I shall act toward those beings in such a way that, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
these faults will no longer exist for them. Endowed with that production of the thought of awakening and endowed with this skill in means,
while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not realize the limit of reality midway, as long as [the perfections] are not yet fulfilled.

By means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great loving-kindness and great compassion— at that time, for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with that production of the thought [of awakening], the gateway to liberation that is the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) reaches fulfillment through cultivation. This is the skillful means of the signless (*ānimittopāya*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it occurs to him: "For a long time these beings have practiced with aspiration; that is to say, they long for the state of Śakra, the state of Brahmā, the state of a world-protector, and the state of a universal monarch; they long for form, and likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations."
"Those who long for consciousness—

for their sake, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall teach the Dharma in such a way that those faults regarding the aspirations of those beings will no longer exist. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva..."
Through these productions of the thought of awakening, these roots of virtue, and this skill in means, as the Mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom,
his cultivation of the gate of liberation that is the concentration of wishlessness reaches fulfillment,
yet he does not realize the limit of reality.

Subhūti, it is impossible and there is no occasion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing the six perfections, practices in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without having fulfilled the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Practicing in the four foundations of mindfulness, practicing in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment;

practicing in the paths; practicing in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; practicing in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion; and practicing until he has mastered the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
It is impossible that one who is thus endowed with the qualities of knowledge would fall into the state of non-conditioning or dwell together with the triple world; such a thing cannot occur.
This, Subhūti, is the method of the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*)...
While practicing and mastering the dharmas, one should inquire: how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to fully awaken to unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment, practices and masters the dharmas conducive to awakening, yet does not personally realize emptiness?

And yet, he would not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nor would he attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
how then could he directly realize emptiness, the signless, the wishless, the unconditioned, the unarisen, or non-existence, while also cultivating the perfection of wisdom? Thus [he asks].

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being thus questioned by bodhisattva mahāsattvas, should answer in this way: "He should attend to emptiness alone; he should attend to the signless alone."
He should attend to the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and he should attend to non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and existence itself;

yet he must not abandon all sentient beings. Subhūti, it should be known by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has received the prophecy (*vyākṛta*) regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
For what reason?
Because he indicates, predicts, and elucidates that which demonstrates the mastery of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if, when asked, he were to explain it in this way:

He should not cultivate mastery in emptiness, nor in the signless, nor in the wishless, nor in the unconditioned, nor in non-arising, nor in non-existence; he should not cultivate mastery in the factors conducive to awakening, nor should he take all sentient beings as his object. Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not been predicted for unsurpassed [perfect enlightenment].
Regarding perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because that which does not indicate, does not predict, and does not manifest the mastery of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and furthermore, that which does not indicate, does not predict, and does not cultivate the Dharma of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti, it should be understood by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having completed his mastery, has transcended from that stage to the stage of irreversibility belonging to an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
This is the means for the signs of irreversibility.
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, could there be a way in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva would be irreversible?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, suppose there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having heard or not having heard the six perfections, would give such an answer as an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does; those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is irreversible."
Subhūti said:
"In that case, Blessed One, many bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, practice for the sake of awakening;
but few, Blessed One, are those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who will respond in such a manner."
Just as irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas [abide] either on the stage of preparation or the stage beyond preparation.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been thus prophesied for the stage of irreversible gnosis are few indeed.
But as for those who will be prophesied, they alone will answer in this way."

Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as having refined roots of virtue, being unshakable by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Thus has been explained the means regarding the immeasurable domain;
thus has been explained skill in means;
thus has been explained the complete awakening to all aspects.

In the Noble *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, as revised in accordance with the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, this is the chapter on Suchness, belonging to the section on the Perfect Awakening to All Aspects.
